By contrast, COVID-19 illness itself has caused millions of deaths worldwide.

claim: "There was a raid on the Biden residence yesterday by the military!"
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official statements indicating the U.S. military conducted a raid on President Biden’s residence yesterday; an action of that magnitude would be widely reported and publicly documented. U.S. law and longstanding norms severely restrict domestic military law-enforcement actions, making an unreported military raid on the president’s home implausible.

claim: "Mitt Romney has been asked to lead Health and Human Services in Biden administration."
rationale: There is no credible public reporting that President Biden asked Senator Mitt Romney to lead Health and Human Services. Biden nominated Xavier Becerra as HHS Secretary, who was subsequently confirmed, and Romney continued serving in the Senate rather than joining the Biden administration.

claim: Says Jon Ossoff is "a socialist."
rationale: Jon Ossoff is a Democratic U.S. senator who identifies with mainstream/center-left Democratic policy positions and has publicly rejected being a "socialist." His record and statements support market-based and incremental policy approaches rather than socialist ideology.

claim: "March 2019 and on-going food benefits WILL NOT be available until further notice. Clients are encouraged to use their food benefits as soon as possible in case SNAP benefits are unavailable in March."
rationale: There is no evidence that SNAP or other food benefits were universally suspended for March 2019; benefit issuance is handled by states on monthly schedules and such a blanket, nationwide stoppage would have required clear federal or state announcements. The claim is alarmist and could be a mistaken or fraudulent local message rather than an accurate nationwide policy change.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: This is false. Impeachment of a U.S. president is performed by the U.S. House of Representatives, whose members cast the impeachment votes; state governors do not vote in that federal process. Phil Scott is the Republican governor of Vermont and is not a member of Congress, so he could not have 'just voted to impeach' President Trump.

claim: "There's not a single, solitary example that" signing the bill to end Glass-Steagall "had anything to do with the financial crash."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: the 1999 repeal (Gramm–Leach–Bliley) removed barriers between commercial and investment banking and many major banks expanded into mortgage securitization and risky investment activities afterward. Multiple investigations and academic studies (including the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission and later research) identify links between post-repeal consolidation/affiliations and exposures that contributed to the 2007–2008 financial crisis, even though it was not the sole cause.

claim: Says Marco Rubio endorsed Obamacare for his own family.
rationale: There is no reliable record that Marco Rubio publicly 'endorsed Obamacare for his own family.' Rubio has consistently opposed the Affordable Care Act and voted to repeal it, and mainstream reporting does not corroborate a claim that he endorsed ACA coverage for his family. Claims that he personally recommended or embraced Obamacare for his household appear to be mischaracterizations or unverified social-media assertions.

claim: Says many public-employee unions falsely told their Wisconsin members his budget-repair bill sought 12 percent to 13 percent of their incomes for health insurance premiums.
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes what the budget-repair bill (Act 10) actually did and what unions communicated. Act 10 required certain employee contributions (notably toward pensions and to health-plan premiums under negotiated terms) but did not impose a blanket 12–13%-of-pay requirement for health insurance; fact-checkers concluded the 12–13% figure was an exaggeration or a conflation of different figures. While some union messaging used alarming example percentages, the bill itself did not universally demand 12–13% of income for premiums.

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: U.S. reporting and government data have shown that thousands of people on terrorist watchlists (including the No Fly List / Terrorist Screening Database) were able to purchase firearms because placement on those watchlists does not automatically trigger a federal prohibition on gun purchases. Multiple news investigations have identified figures above 2,000 who appear on watchlists yet passed or circumvented background checks.

claim: "Nearly 70 percent of all federal spending will go towards Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid" in fiscal year 2014.
rationale: In fiscal year 2014, Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid together accounted for well under 70% of total federal outlays—roughly around 45–50% by standard CBO/OMB budget breakdowns—so the claim that nearly 70% of all federal spending went to those three programs is incorrect.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of CBO/OMB historical federal budget tables and typical shares of Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid in total federal outlays (combined about half, not near 70%).
safety_notes: Percentages vary slightly by source and whether one includes net interest or other mandatory programs, but under common definitions of total federal outlays the three programs do not approach 70%.

claim: Says a photo shows a "lithium mine for hybrid cars."
rationale: There is no way to verify from the statement alone that the pictured site is a lithium mine specifically supplying hybrid car batteries; images of mines are frequently miscaptioned or repurposed. Identifying a mine and its product requires provenance, geolocation, or authoritative sourcing, which are not provided, so the claim is unsupported and likely false as stated.

claim: "Under Rick Scott, homeowners are paying higher (home insurance) premiums for less coverage."
rationale: The claim attributes higher premiums and reduced coverage directly to Rick Scott, but publicly available information shows Florida homeowners’ insurance costs and coverage levels have been driven by multiple factors (hurricane risk, reinsurance costs, insurer insolvencies, assignment-of-benefits litigation and market exits) across several administrations. While policies and reforms enacted during various governors’ terms may have influenced market conditions, there is no clear, singular causal evidence that homeowners paid more for less coverage specifically and solely “under Rick Scott.”

claim: A video shows a nurse pretending to vaccinate actor Anthony Hopkins before squirting fluid in the syringe on the floor.
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated evidence that a nurse intentionally pretended to vaccinate Anthony Hopkins and then squirted fluid onto the floor. Viral clips of medical procedures are frequently edited or taken out of context and this specific allegation has not been supported by reputable reporting or documentation of the full, original footage.

claim: "Biden resigned, Pelosi was detained."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden resigned or that Nancy Pelosi was detained. Both would be major, widely reported events; up to my knowledge cutoff in June 2024 there were no such reports, so the claim appears to be false or a rumor. If the claim refers to a specific later date, it should be verified against current reliable news sources.

claim: "Barnes opposed the creation of the HOPE Scholarship and campaigned against Zell Miller on the issue."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that a politician named Barnes actively opposed the creation of Georgia’s HOPE Scholarship or mounted a campaign against Zell Miller over that issue. The HOPE Scholarship was authored and vigorously promoted by Zell Miller and established in 1993; public records and major accounts of Georgia politics do not show a prominent 'Barnes' leading opposition to its creation. Therefore the specific claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Members of Congress and their families and staff are exempt from repaying student loans.
rationale: There is no law or blanket policy that exempts members of Congress, their families, or staff from repaying student loans. Individuals in those groups are subject to the same federal loan rules as other borrowers, though they may qualify for general programs like Public Service Loan Forgiveness, income-driven repayment forgiveness, or discharge for disability/death.

claim: Says with "Gov. Chris Christie and bipartisan reformers" New Jersey had "the most job growth in 11 years."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported as written. New Jersey did see job gains during Gov. Chris Christie’s tenure, but official labor data show variable annual gains and do not clearly support an unqualified claim that the state had “the most job growth in 11 years” without specifying the exact year, period, or whether it refers to absolute or percentage gains and private vs. total jobs.

claim: "We have the lowest beer tax in the nation."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which jurisdiction “we” refers to or the time period; beer tax rates vary widely by state and locality and change over time. Without a specific jurisdiction and date, the assertion that ‘we’ have the lowest beer tax in the nation cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says NASCAR "bans the confederate flag but FORCES all their drivers to do Muslim prayer."
rationale: While NASCAR did implement a policy in 2020 banning display of the Confederate flag at its events, there is no evidence that NASCAR forces drivers to perform Muslim prayer. Forcing employees or contractors to engage in religious practices would violate U.S. norms and employment law and would have been widely reported; no credible sources support that claim.

claim: Ted Cruz "helps run two national organizations that have been leading the push to give amnesty to illegal immigrants."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Ted Cruz 'helps run' two national organizations leading a push for amnesty; Cruz has publicly opposed broad amnesty measures and led efforts against comprehensive immigration bills. The claim conflicts with his voting record, public statements, and known affiliations, which do not include leadership of pro-amnesty national groups.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted to keep the shutdown going."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsupported as presented because it does not identify which shutdown or which specific roll-call vote is meant. Without a precise vote to check, the claim cannot be verified; public roll-call records would be needed to confirm whether Rep. Steve Southerland cast a particular vote that directly ‘‘kept the shutdown going.’’ Given the lack of specific evidence, the blanket assertion is not verifiable and therefore treated as false.

claim: "Hillary ignored multiple requests for security, didn’t respond for 13 hours, & let 4 Americans die in Benghazi. Trump rushed in reinforcements, threatened to destroy Iran, & made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad."
rationale: This is a composite claim that mixes accurate facts with false or misleading assertions. Four Americans did die in the 2012 Benghazi attack, but multiple official investigations and the State Department Accountability Review Board found no evidence that Hillary Clinton personally ignored repeated requests for security or deliberately failed to respond for '13 hours' in a way that caused those deaths. Donald Trump did deploy forces to the region, made aggressive public statements about Iran and ordered the strike that killed Qasem Soleimani, but characterizing his actions as a threat to 'destroy Iran' and claiming he 'made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad' is exaggerated and not supported by the factual record of events and casualties.

claim: "Some people are going to die from the vaccine directly. But a large number of people are going to start getting horribly sick and get all kinds of autoimmune diseases."
rationale: While vaccines (including COVID-19 vaccines) have been linked to rare serious adverse events and very occasional deaths in specific, well-documented cases (for example anaphylaxis, VITT with some adenoviral vaccines, and rare severe myocarditis), broad high-quality surveillance and epidemiological studies do not show that a large number of people will become “horribly sick” or develop widespread new autoimmune diseases as a result of vaccination. Overall safety monitoring finds such severe outcomes are rare and far outweighed by the benefits of vaccination in preventing disease and death.

claim: "A new ruling by the EPA would force dairy farmers to comply with the Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure Program when dealing with spilt milk -- the same regulations oil and natural gas producers must follow."
rationale: The EPA's Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure (SPCC) program applies to oil and oil-based substances and to facilities that could reasonably be expected to discharge oil to navigable waters; it does not cover ordinary spilled milk. Public fact-checks and EPA guidance have clarified that dairy farmers would not be forced to treat routine milk spills as SPCC oil spills, though separate rules could apply to actual oil or oily wastes on farms.

claim: Potential Foxconn changes are due to "the wave of economic uncertainty" from Evers administration
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the Evers administration alone produced a 'wave of economic uncertainty' that caused Foxconn to alter its plans. Reporting and company statements attribute Foxconn’s scaled-back project to global market demand shifts, COVID‑19 disruptions, supply‑chain and corporate strategy decisions rather than solely to actions by the Wisconsin governor's administration.

claim: "You had (4,925) out-of-state voters… in Georgia."
rationale: The statement gives a specific count but provides no election, time period, or data source, so it cannot be verified as presented. Official verification of out-of-state voters in Georgia requires specifying the election cycle and consulting state voter rolls or certified post-election audits; absent that context, the precise figure is not demonstrably true.

claim: If you paid rent in March or April, "they got to give" you your money back.
rationale: There is no universal rule that landlords must refund rent paid in March or April. Whether rent must be returned depends on the lease terms and applicable local, state, or federal laws or emergency relief programs in effect at the time; some jurisdictions enacted eviction moratoria or rent-relief assistance during emergencies, but these did not automatically require universal refunds.

claim: "Moderna chief medical officer admits: mRNA alters DNA."
rationale: Moderna’s chief medical officer has not admitted that mRNA alters DNA; company representatives and molecular biology experts state that vaccine mRNA does not enter the nucleus or integrate into genomic DNA. The claim misrepresents public statements and contradicts standard cellular biology of mRNA vaccines.

claim: Says recent studies indicate that nationally, only 8 percent of white voting-age citizens but 25 percent of African-American voting-age citizens lack government-issued photo IDs.
rationale: Multiple national surveys (most notably a 2014 Brennan Center study) found that a small share of white voting‑age citizens (typically reported in the mid-to-high single digits) lack government-issued photo ID while about one quarter of African‑American voting‑age citizens do. The exact white percent varies by study and definition (often reported as 6–8%), but the 8% vs. 25% comparison matches published estimates showing a pronounced racial disparity.

claim: Under Mayor Angel Taveras "Providence’s bond rating was downgraded from A to BBB, two steps above junk-bond status."
rationale: The statement mixes rating scales and overstates the precision: credit ratings are issued by different agencies with different notches, and public records do show downgrades for Providence during Taveras’s tenure but not the simple “A to BBB, two steps above junk” formulation. BBB is an investment-grade category and whether it is ‘two steps above junk’ depends on the agency and which notches are counted; the commonly used S&P/Fitch sequence does not support the exact phrasing. Because the claim lacks the rating agency and timeframe and misstates the notch/count, it is misleading.

claim: GOP candidate for California governor Travis Allen "on the floor vote … refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens."
rationale: I cannot find reliable evidence that Travis Allen specifically 'refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens' on a named floor vote; California passed a law allowing driver licenses for undocumented immigrants (AB 60) and most GOP legislators opposed it, but the claim asserts a particular action by Allen that isn’t corroborated by readily available vote records. Without a precise vote date or roll-call citation the statement appears unverified and likely misleading.

claim: The Republicans' alternative health care plan "will still let insurers raise premiums four times faster than wages."
rationale: The statement gives a specific numeric outcome that is not supported as a general fact for ‘‘the Republicans' alternative health care plan.’' Independent analyses (including CBO reviews of particular GOP proposals like the 2017 AHCA) produced mixed projections about premium changes and did not conclude insurers would universally be able to raise premiums “four times faster than wages.” Premium growth projections depend on the exact bill text, timeframe, and assumptions, so the blanket four-times claim is unsupported.

claim: Republican state Sens. Paul Newton and Warren Daniel "refused to even give testimony" in North Carolina’s latest redistricting case.
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated reporting that both Republican Sens. Paul Newton and Warren Daniel 'refused to even give testimony' in North Carolina’s most recent redistricting litigation. Coverage of the cases indicates legislators either provided testimony or depositions, invoked legislative privilege, or were not subpoenaed—not an outright, documented joint refusal to testify.

claim: President Joe Biden was confused, "turned around and shook hands with thin air" after a speech.
rationale: Video clips show President Biden extending his hand after a speech, but the assertion that he was ‘confused’ and deliberately ‘shook hands with thin air’ is an interpretive claim not supported by clear evidence. Multiple fact-checks and the available footage indicate the action is ambiguous (he may have been acknowledging staff or someone off-camera), so calling it definitive confusion is misleading.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Alec Baldwin, a total loser, has taken his impression of me to a new low by testing out this theory" by shooting someone.
rationale: There is no credible record of Donald Trump saying that quoted line about Alec Baldwin "testing out this theory" by shooting someone. Coverage of the Baldwin shooting and Trump's public statements and tweets did not contain that phrase, and such a provocative comment would have been widely reported by major outlets if made.

claim: "Dr. Oz releases COPD gummies that help quit smoking, detox lungs and stop COPD."
rationale: There is no credible clinical evidence that any 'COPD gummies' released by Dr. Oz can make people quit smoking, 'detox' lungs, or stop COPD. COPD is a chronic, largely irreversible lung disease that requires evidence-based treatments; smoking cessation is aided by nicotine replacement, medications and counseling, not unproven gummies. Claims of a gummy product curing or reversing COPD are inconsistent with medical consensus and lack supporting clinical trials.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: This is a specific, personal claim about the contents of a letter and the payment history of correspondents that cannot be independently verified from the statement alone. Without the original letter or payment records to confirm the numbers, the assertion should be treated as unverified and thus labeled false.

claim: "The United States was paying for anywhere from 70 to 90 percent of (NATO), depending on the way you calculate."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The U.S. does not pay 70–90% of NATO’s budgets: depending on the measure, the U.S. accounts for roughly two‑thirds of total NATO members’ aggregate defense spending in recent years, but only about one‑fifth of NATO’s relatively small common-funded budgets. Saying the U.S. pays 70–90% of NATO conflates different accounting measures and overstates the U.S. share of NATO’s formal budgets.

claim: Says opposing the Paycheck Fairness Act is part of the Koch brothers’ agenda.
rationale: Koch-affiliated groups and allied business interests have publicly opposed the Paycheck Fairness Act and similar federal pay-equity measures. That opposition fits within the Koch network’s broader, well-documented agenda of opposing workplace regulations and promoting business-friendly, limited-government policies.

claim: "Mayor Barrett saved Milwaukee $25 million, thanks to Gov. Walker’s reforms."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that Mayor Tom Barrett personally "saved" Milwaukee $25 million as a direct result of Gov. Scott Walker’s reforms. While Walker’s 2011 collective-bargaining and budget changes changed municipal labor costs and produced contested savings estimates, city audits and budget documents do not clearly corroborate a discrete $25 million saving credited to Barrett; the figure appears in partisan statements rather than neutral fiscal accounting.

claim: "Virginia papers called (Scott) Rigell’s campaign ‘Mostly False.’"
rationale: There is no clear evidence that multiple Virginia newspapers collectively labeled Scott Rigell’s entire campaign 'Mostly False.' Fact-check ratings such as 'Mostly False' are used by outlets like PolitiFact for specific statements, but I could not find contemporaneous Virginia papers using that exact characterization of his campaign as a whole, so the claim appears imprecise or unsupported.

claim: "COVID ends next Wednesday."
rationale: There is no evidence or authoritative forecast that SARS‑CoV‑2 will stop circulating on a specific forthcoming day; infectious diseases do not abruptly 'end' on a given weekday. Public health agencies monitor trends but have not predicted a single-day end to COVID‑19, and the virus continues to circulate globally.

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
rationale: Both Representatives Luke Messer and Todd Rokita voted in favor of granting Trade Promotion Authority (commonly called "fast-track") to the Obama administration, which allowed expedited consideration of trade agreements such as the Trans-Pacific Partnership. Their recorded House votes supported the 2015/2016 fast-track/TPA measures.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: I cannot find independent, authoritative confirmation that a 13-year-old in Halifax is in critical care due to her heart stopping immediately after a vaccination. Claims of individual medical incidents require verification from hospitals or public health authorities; temporal proximity to vaccination does not establish causation. Without corroborating statements or credible news reports this specific causal claim is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: In Hillary Clinton's tax returns, "you saw a lot of income coming from donors to the Clinton Foundation and people who benefitted from her State Department term as well."
rationale: Clinton tax returns and public reporting show large sums from speaking fees and book deals, but investigations found only a limited overlap between those payers and major Clinton Foundation donors or parties that benefited from State Department actions. Characterizing the returns as showing "a lot" of income from donors/beneficiaries overstates the documented overlap; most reported income came from corporations, universities, and financial firms that were not major Foundation donors or proven State Department beneficiaries.

claim: Says video shows "Ukrainian forces shoot down Russian plane carrying hundreds (of) troops on Kyiv airport."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Ukrainian forces shot down a Russian plane carrying ‘hundreds’ of troops at Kyiv airport; such a large, deadly incident would have been widely and reliably reported. The claim appears to be based on a misattributed or misleading video and exaggerates passenger numbers beyond typical military transport capacity.

claim: Says Barack Obama "endorsed a total ban on the manufacture, sale and possession of all handguns."
rationale: There is no credible record of Barack Obama endorsing a blanket ban on the manufacture, sale, and possession of all handguns. His public positions and policy proposals have focused on measures such as universal background checks, reinstating the assault weapons ban, and limits on high-capacity magazines, not an outright prohibition of all handguns.

claim: Says U.S. Senate rival Tommy Thompson said he wants to "do away with Medicare."
rationale: There is no clear record of Tommy Thompson explicitly saying he wanted to 'do away with Medicare.' He has supported proposals to restructure Medicare (such as premium‑support/defined‑contribution approaches) and opponents ran ads accusing him of wanting to end traditional Medicare, but Thompson did not publicly call for abolishing the program outright.

claim: Says Matt Rosendale "consistently supported land use rules that would help developers like him and hurt farmers in Montana."
rationale: There is insufficient publicly documented evidence that Matt Rosendale has 'consistently supported' land-use rules specifically designed to help developers like himself while harming Montana farmers. The claim is a broad, sweeping assertion that would require citation of a pattern of specific bills, votes, or policy actions; without those specifics it is not verifiable. Available summaries of his record show some pro-development positions but not a clear, consistent pattern as stated in the claim.

claim: No one "with a concealed carry permit ever committed a mass shooting."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but is contradicted by documented exceptions: some perpetrators of mass shootings have legally held concealed-carry permits according to news reporting and datasets tracking mass shootings. Because 'mass shooting' definitions and permit laws vary by jurisdiction, counts differ, but the universal negative ('no one ever') is demonstrably incorrect.

claim: Says Scott Walker supports "a health care plan that would gut protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Scott Walker publicly stated he would protect coverage for people with pre-existing conditions and has not been documented as endorsing an explicit proposal that openly abolishes those protections. He has backed repealing the ACA and measures (like state waivers and less prescriptive benefit rules) that critics say could weaken protections in practice, but that is not the same as a clear, explicit policy pledge to “gut” protections.

claim: The Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine contains an "undisclosed ingredient. … How is informed consent possible?"
rationale: Regulatory filings, the FDA emergency use authorization documents, and the vaccine’s package insert publicly list the active and inactive ingredients in the Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine (the mRNA and the specific lipid components, cholesterol, salts, sucrose, and water). There is no credible evidence that the marketed vaccine contains an additional secret or undisclosed ingredient, so the claim is false and informed consent can be based on the available disclosed information.

claim: "The number of killings of citizens by police is at a two-decade high."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which country and which years it refers to, and cannot be verified as stated. In the United States some datasets show a peak around 2020, but whether killings are at a 'two-decade high' depends on the data source, definitions, and exact years compared; globally the pattern is different. Because the statement lacks crucial context and is not clearly true as written, I rate it false.

claim: "One man (New Castle, Del., County Executive, Chris Coons) thought property taxes should be hiked almost 50 percent."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that New Castle County Executive Chris Coons formally proposed raising property taxes by nearly 50%. Public records and contemporary reporting on Coons’s county budgets do not support a single-person proposal of that magnitude; the claim appears to be an exaggerated or misleading characterization of budget or assessment changes.

claim: "If you stop testing (for COVID-19) it all goes away and people just have colds like before."
rationale: Stopping testing does not make the virus disappear — it only reduces detection and reporting. SARS‑CoV‑2 continues to circulate and can cause severe illness and death, unlike typical common colds, and testing is important for diagnosis, treatment, isolation, and public-health surveillance.

claim: Over the last 10 years, incomes for the top 1 percent "have grown." Meanwhile, the bottom half of the country, "they've seen their wages stagnate."
rationale: Multiple empirical analyses over recent decades show that income gains have been concentrated at the very top: the top 1%’s share and real incomes increased while median and lower-half workers saw little real wage growth. Broadly speaking, IRS/academic income-share data and BLS/CE wage statistics support the characterization that the top 1% grew while the bottom 50% experienced stagnation in real wages over the last decade.

claim: "United Nations Resolution is the single largest economic sanctions package ever on North Korea. Over one billion dollars in cost to N.K."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not definitively supported. While multiple UN Security Council resolutions in 2016–2017 were widely described as the toughest sanctions on North Korea and collectively reduced export revenues substantially, calling a single "United Nations Resolution" the "single largest economic sanctions package" is ambiguous and independent estimates of the economic impact vary; there is no definitive, universally accepted accounting that a single resolution imposed over $1 billion in costs.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's "been very clear where she stands on trade."
rationale: Hillary Clinton's positions on trade have changed over time—she supported NAFTA in the 1990s and initially backed the Trans‑Pacific Partnership before reversing to oppose it during the 2016 campaign—producing public confusion and criticism about consistency. Because of these shifts, the blanket claim that she has "been very clear where she stands on trade" is inaccurate.

claim: "Biden won’t allow Delta-variant COVID patients to get proven and effective monoclonal treatments even though there are 50,000-100,000 Americans infected by Delta EVERY DAY."
rationale: The Biden administration has not prohibited monoclonal antibody treatments; several monoclonal therapies retained emergency use authorization and have been distributed by HHS, though specific products have been limited or withdrawn when data showed reduced effectiveness against particular variants. The claim’s daily infection figure (50,000–100,000 Americans infected by Delta every day) is an unsupported, time‑specific assertion—daily case counts varied substantially and attribution solely to Delta depended on sequencing and timing.

claim: "Wisconsin Republicans have not passed a single bill in 6 months."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that is implausible without a clearly defined timeframe or criteria. State legislative records show bills being passed regularly in Wisconsin; even during contentious periods legislatures typically pass some measures within six months. Without a specific date range or definition of 'passed' (floor passage vs enacted into law), the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: "92 million Americans aren't working."
rationale: The claim is vague and misleading because it gives no date or definition of “aren’t working.” Bureau of Labor Statistics data distinguish ‘not in the labor force’ (roughly 90–95 million people in some recent months) from ‘not employed’ (which includes unemployed people and is larger) and from the count of employed (around 150–165 million), so the plain statement as presented is not reliably true without context.

claim: "In Harrisburg, I passed more bills than all the Democrats combined, in terms of legislation affecting the city."
rationale: The claim asserts an individual passed more bills affecting Harrisburg than all Democrats combined, but there is no presented evidence and such a comparison would require detailed legislative records and clear definitions. Without specifying the actor, timeframe, legislative body, and what counts as 'affecting the city,' the assertion is unverified and implausible as stated.

claim: Says swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball is a "safe, easy way" to remove them from skin.
rationale: Major public health guidance recommends using fine-tipped tweezers to grasp a tick close to the skin and pull straight out; they advise against smothering or home-remedy techniques. Swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball is not endorsed as reliably safe or effective and could provoke the tick to regurgitate, increasing infection risk.

claim: Marco Rubio's "income skyrocketed while his power increased."
rationale: The statement is vague and not supported by public records: Marco Rubio’s annual financial disclosures and mainstream reporting show income and asset changes over time (salary, investments, occasional book/speaking income) but do not document a sudden, dramatic "skyrocketing" tied to an increase in political power. Major, verifiable spikes of the sort implied would have been reported and are not evident in available summaries of his disclosures.

claim: Video shows Biden saying "salute the Marines" after hearing the words in an earpiece before his inauguration.
rationale: While a short clip circulated in which Biden appears to mouth or say words that some interpret as 'salute the Marines,' independent fact-checks found the audio and lip movements are ambiguous and there is no verifiable evidence he was repeating words fed through an earpiece. Official inauguration footage and reporting show no clear earpiece prompt and the claim that the video proves he heard and repeated an earpiece instruction is unsubstantiated.

claim: "We paid down the debt for four years -- paid down $600 billion on the national debt."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the U.S. federal government ‘‘paid down’’ the national debt by $600 billion over any recent four‑year span as a matter of record; over most recent administrations the total federal debt rose, and the only period of modest declines in debt held by the public was in the late 1990s and was smaller and shorter than this claim asserts. The statement lacks precision about which debt measure (gross debt vs. debt held by the public) and which four years are meant, and under typical definitions the claim is not supported by Treasury/CBO data.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: While multiple reputable studies find voter fraud in the U.S. and in Texas to be very rare, documented cases and prosecutions in Texas demonstrate it is not literally non-existent. Absolute phrasing ('non-existent') is contradicted by public records and news reports of isolated incidents.

claim: Says Alaska Sen. Mark Begich "is on record supporting a carbon tax, even pushing Harry Reid to make it a priority."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Senator Mark Begich formally called on Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to make a carbon tax a priority. While Begich has at times expressed openness to market-based measures to reduce emissions, contemporary news and congressional records do not support the specific claim that he publicly pushed Reid to prioritize a carbon tax.

claim: "Justin Amash is rated Michigan’s No. 1 conservative" by National Right to Life.
rationale: National Right to Life issues pro‑life scorecards and votes‑based ratings, not broad statewide rankings labeling someone the "No. 1 conservative." There is no clear evidence that the organization formally declared Justin Amash to be "Michigan’s No. 1 conservative"; the phrase appears to be a subjective or misattributed claim rather than an official NRL designation.

claim: "Welders make more money than philosophers."
rationale: The claim is too general to be universally true. Earnings depend on the country, experience, and whether by 'philosopher' one means academic philosophers (professors) or people with philosophy degrees; in some places experienced welders earn more than entry-level philosophers, while tenured philosophy professors often earn more than many welders. Because wages vary by role, location, and measurement (median vs mean), the blanket statement is false.

claim: Says that according to a report, "the tech sector now drives more than one-quarter of Austin’s economy."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not supported by a single, widely cited report phrased that way. Austin’s tech sector is large and growing, but estimates of its share vary by metric (employment, GDP, wages) and authoritative sources do not universally state that tech ″drives more than one-quarter″ of the entire Austin economy without qualification. Without the specific report, year, and metric, the unqualified statement overstates what typical data show.

claim: Says Bill White is refusing to debate.
rationale: The statement lacks crucial context (which Bill White, what debate, and when) and cannot be verified as a factual claim from the information given. Without a specific event or citation, there is no reliable basis to conclude that a person named Bill White is refusing to debate.

claim: "A lot of the move to free the slaves ... did not come from the federal government. It came from a growing movement among the people, particularly people of faith."
rationale: Historical evidence shows that abolition was driven significantly by grassroots activism—abolitionist societies, the Underground Railroad, enslaved people's resistance, and organized religious groups (Quakers, evangelicals, Black churches) played major roles in shifting public opinion and pressuring leaders. While final legal emancipation required federal actions (Emancipation Proclamation, Civil War measures, and the 13th Amendment), much of the momentum originated outside the federal government, especially among people of faith.

claim: "It is more difficult to obtain a Costco membership than it is to get a NYC Municipal ID"
rationale: The claim is not generally true: joining Costco typically requires paying a membership fee and presenting a basic photo ID and can be completed in-store or online quickly. By contrast, the NYC Municipal ID (IDNYC) requires documented proof of identity and proof of New York City residency and an application process, making it at least as or more document‑burdensome for many applicants.

claim: "Obama-Nelson economic record: Job creation ... at slowest post-recession rate since Great Depression."
rationale: The statement overstates the case. While the post-2009 job recovery under Obama was relatively slow compared with many postwar recoveries and has been described by analysts as the weakest since World War II, mainstream data and analyses do not support the stronger claim that it was the slowest recovery 'since the Great Depression.'

claim: Tapping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve would immediately lower gasoline prices
rationale: Releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve increases crude supply and can put downward pressure on crude prices, but retail gasoline prices typically do not fall immediately. Gasoline prices reflect refined-product inventories, refinery capacity and turnaround times, distribution logistics, taxes, and retailer margins, so changes at the SPR usually take days to weeks (and may be muted) to affect pump prices.

claim: "[The] unemployment rate in the Philadelphia metro area is now at its lowest level ever recorded."
rationale: The claim gives no date or source and therefore cannot be verified as a current factual statement. Metropolitan unemployment series from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and state labor agencies vary over time and by definition; while Philadelphia-area unemployment has fallen to near pre-pandemic lows in recent years, I cannot confirm it is definitively the lowest ever without a specific date and dataset.

claim: "I certainly supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden. ... I was there both times for them."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who is speaking or provide independent evidence of their stated support and presence. Without a named person and corroborating records (public endorsements, attendance lists, photos, or contemporaneous statements), the assertion that they 'supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden' and 'was there both times' cannot be confirmed.

claim: Rubio's "got more experience than Obama had."
rationale: The claim is vague and not objectively verifiable as stated: “experience” can mean years in elected office, federal vs. state experience, executive vs. legislative experience, or other public-sector roles. Barack Obama had both Illinois state senate service and a U.S. Senate term plus legal and community-organizing experience before becoming president; Marco Rubio had substantial Florida legislative service and later a U.S. Senate seat. Without a clear metric or timeframe, asserting Rubio definitively "got more experience than Obama had" is unsupported.

claim: Says scientists are "in dispute" over whether being gay is a choice.
rationale: Major medical and psychological organizations and the bulk of scientific literature treat sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, developmental, and environmental factors rather than a conscious choice. While researchers continue to study the precise causes and relative contributions of genes, hormones, and environment, there is not a substantive scientific dispute framed as 'is being gay a choice?' among credible scientists.

claim: The federal government requires "COVID passports to visit the movies."
rationale: There is no general federal requirement that people present COVID vaccination passports to attend movie theaters. Where COVID-passport or proof-of-vaccination rules existed, they were typically set by states, provinces, municipalities, or by private venues, not imposed as a blanket federal mandate.

claim: The Obama administration "was successful in rushing a massive spending bill through Congress in just two days — after which it sat on the president's desk for three days, while he was away on vacation."
rationale: The claim is vague and does not match the documented timelines for major Obama-era spending bills. Major measures like the 2009 Recovery Act were debated and amended over weeks in Congress, not simply rushed through in two days, and there is no clear record that a massive spending bill sat unsigned on the president’s desk for three days while he was away on vacation as described. The claim appears to conflate or distort legislative timelines and presidential signing practices.

claim: "We’re also using a sterilization process ― some great equipment that will sterilize masks up to 20 times per mask. So that’s like ordering 20 times more masks."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While a specific vaporized-hydrogen-peroxide decontamination system received emergency authorization to reprocess certain N95 respirators up to 20 times, most sterilization methods and mask models cannot be safely reprocessed that many times and reuse degrades fit and filtration. Reprocessing capacity, regulatory limits, and compatibility mean it is not equivalent to simply having '20 times' the number of new masks.

claim: When the United States "first created the federal income tax, frankly, nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything."
rationale: This is false: when the modern federal income tax was established after the 16th Amendment (1913), the Revenue Act imposed a 1% tax on incomes above a few thousand dollars and surtaxes on higher brackets — not only on millionaires. Earlier federal income taxes (for example during the Civil War) also taxed much lower incomes.

claim: "We only have 2 percent of the oil reserves in the world, and we consume 25 percent of the world's oil on a daily basis."
rationale: The first part (about 2% of global proven oil reserves) is roughly correct for the United States, but the consumption figure is overstated. The U.S. consumes closer to about 18–20% of world oil on a daily basis (varies by year), not 25%.

claim: The Democratic Party "is the oldest continuous political party in the world."
rationale: The U.S. Democratic Party traces its roots to the Jeffersonian Republican movement and is conventionally dated to the 1828 formation around Andrew Jackson; by that standard it is widely described as the oldest continuously operating political party in the world. While historians sometimes debate exact lineage or definitions of what counts as the same party over time, no other major national party predates the Democrats and remains continuously active under a clear organizational line.

claim: "Our state economic development agency under Walker, WEDC, actually isn’t even using the funds that are appropriated to it."
rationale: The Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation (WEDC), created under Governor Walker, received legislative appropriations and actively issued loans, grants and tax-credit programs during his administration. Independent state audits and reporting criticized WEDC for governance, transparency, and documentation problems, but did not conclude the agency simply refused to spend appropriated funds across the board.

claim: Under President Barack Obama, "We’ve got the lowest labor force participation in over three decades, since 1978."
rationale: During President Obama's time in office the civilian labor force participation rate fell to levels not seen since the late 1970s. BLS series show the participation rate in the mid-2010s dipped to roughly the same range as 1978, making the statement broadly accurate as an approximate comparison.

claim: The national debt is "larger than our entire annual economy."
rationale: Interpreting 'annual economy' as GDP, many countries’ total national (federal) debt has recently exceeded one year’s GDP — for example, U.S. total federal debt has been larger than annual U.S. GDP in recent years. However, whether the statement is true depends on the country, the time period, and which debt measure is used (gross debt vs. debt held by the public).

claim: "Drug overdose deaths decreased in 2018 for the first time in 30 years."
rationale: U.S. provisional CDC data released in early 2019 showed a small decline in drug overdose deaths in 2018 compared with 2017, which was widely reported as the first decrease after decades of year-over-year increases. This decline was modest and noted as the first drop in roughly 30 years of rising overdose mortality.

claim: Ketanji Brown Jackson "says she gave pedophiles lighter sentences (because) it’s different when they use computers vs mail to get volumes of child porn. This makes ‘total sense’ according to Jackson."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Ketanji Brown Jackson saying the quoted line that she gave pedophiles lighter sentences because “it’s different when they use computers vs mail” or that “this makes ‘total sense’.” Reporting from her confirmation and past sentencing hearings shows critics cited and criticized some of her sentencing decisions and nuanced courtroom explanations, but the specific phrasing in the claim is a mischaracterization and not a verbatim or supported quote. Context around sentencing often involved guideline considerations and distinctions among offenses rather than a categorical statement as presented.

claim: "28.2 million Americans are still waiting under Obamacare and remain uninsured!"
rationale: The statement is misleading. While annual estimates of uninsured Americans have been in the mid-to-high tens of millions in some recent years, the specific figure '28.2 million' is not a verified current count and the claim that they are 'still waiting under Obamacare' mischaracterizes why people are uninsured — many are ineligible (e.g., undocumented), live in states without Medicaid expansion, or choose not to enroll, rather than simply 'waiting' for ACA coverage.

claim: "Queen Elizabeth d-e-a-d at age 95."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Queen Elizabeth II was born 21 April 1926 and died on 8 September 2022 at age 96, not 95. Other historically notable Queen Elizabeths died at very different ages (e.g., the Queen Mother at 101), so 95 is not correct for the widely referenced Queen Elizabeth II.

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I could not verify the specific figures in this claim from available descriptions of Portland’s composting pilots; municipal reports and media summaries of such pilots often show different sample sizes and satisfaction percentages. Without a primary source citation (city report or peer-reviewed study) confirming 2,000 households and an 87% satisfaction rate, the claim remains unverified and treated as false.

claim: "Medicare does just as good, if not better, at keeping people healthy" as Medicare Advantage.
rationale: The evidence is mixed and does not clearly support the blanket claim that traditional (fee‑for‑service) Medicare performs as well or better than Medicare Advantage (MA) at keeping people healthy. Many studies and CMS quality metrics show MA enrollees often receive more preventive services and sometimes have better adjusted outcomes, while other analyses note selection effects and variation across plans and measures. Because results depend on which health outcomes, populations, risk adjustment, and study methods are used, the categorical claim is not reliably supported.

claim: Twenty-seven percent of Californians, almost 11 million, "were born in a foreign land."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census Bureau/American Community Survey estimates show that roughly 27% of California residents are foreign-born, which converts to about 10.5–11 million people given California’s ~39–40 million population. The phrasing "born in a foreign land" corresponds to the Census concept of "foreign-born," so the claim matches available estimates.

claim: Says President Barack Obama wants to raise "the lowest (income) tax rate from 10 to 15 percent."
rationale: This is false: President Obama’s major tax proposals during his presidency and 2012 campaign targeted higher-income earners (e.g., restoring higher rates for incomes above $250,000) and closing certain tax breaks, not raising the bottom individual income-tax bracket from 10% to 15%. Assertions that he sought to increase the lowest bracket were political mischaracterizations rather than accurate descriptions of administration or legislative proposals.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution "doesn’t say anything about (redistricting) being fair. … it’s set up to be partisan."
rationale: The Constitution does not contain an explicit requirement that redistricting be 'fair' or nonpartisan; it vests primary authority over the time, place, and manner of congressional elections and apportionment in states (Article I) and assigns seats by population. That structure means state legislatures historically control mapmaking and can pursue partisan advantage, though later amendments and court decisions constrain some abuses (e.g., racial vote dilution and population-equality requirements).

claim: Says Fox News gave Republican senators twice the air time as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State.
rationale: I cannot find independent evidence or a published timing analysis confirming that Fox News gave Republican senators exactly twice the airtime as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State. Numerical claims about airtime require precise measurement of broadcast logs or third‑party media monitoring; absent a cited study or timing data, the assertion is unverified. While analyses and critiques often note Fox News favors Republican voices, that general bias does not validate this specific 2:1 airtime claim.

claim: Say Ohio Reps. Marcia Fudge, Marcy Kaptur and Dennis Kucinich are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Marcia Fudge and Marcy Kaptur are Democratic members historically associated with mainstream/progressive positions but are not known to openly identify as socialists, and Dennis Kucinich is a former congressman who left the House in 2013. None of the three are documented as openly serving in the U.S. Congress as self‑identified socialists.

claim: Benzene has "never been proven to be harmful."
rationale: Benzene is a well-established human carcinogen and has been linked by numerous epidemiological and toxicological studies to blood cancers (including acute myeloid leukemia), bone marrow suppression, and other health harms. International and national health agencies classify benzene as carcinogenic and regulate occupational and environmental exposure limits.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh "refused to uphold key patient protections in the past."
rationale: The statement is a broad, categorical claim lacking specifics; Brett Kavanaugh has in some cases ruled against particular health regulations or favored limits on agency authority, but that is not the same as a documented, blanket refusal to uphold "key patient protections." Whether any particular protection was undermined depends on the specific law, case, and statutory interpretation. Without a named protection or ruling, the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "Schumer and Pelosi sneak funding into COVID bill."
rationale: The statement is a vague, unsubstantiated accusation of secretive behavior. While congressional leaders including Schumer and Pelosi have negotiated and supported adding funding or provisions to large bills, that is a routine part of the legislative process and does not by itself prove they "sneak" funding into a COVID bill; specific evidence or a particular instance would be required to substantiate the claim.

claim: "The minimum number of infrastructure (needs) in Atlanta is $900 million."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported: there is no widely recognized single “minimum” infrastructure need for Atlanta set at $900 million. Infrastructure funding estimates vary by sector (roads, water, transit, stormwater) and by report and timeframe, and many assessments produce different or larger figures. Without a clear source, scope, and date, the claim is unverified and likely incorrect.

claim: "If a statue of a person in the park on a horse has both front legs in the air, the person died in battle. If the horse has one front leg in the air, the person died as a result of wounds received in battle. If the horse has all four legs on the ground, the person died of natural causes."
rationale: This is a widely circulated folk belief but not a factual rule. There is no standardized or historical convention that links a horse’s leg position in equestrian statues to how the rider died; sculptors choose poses for aesthetic, structural, or symbolic reasons, and many notable statues contradict the claimed code.

claim: "In 2009, Jim Doyle and the Democrats rushed through a budget repair bill with billions in tax increases and held no public hearings."
rationale: This statement conflates events and is inaccurate. There was no widely reported "budget repair bill" rushed through by Governor Jim Doyle in 2009 without public hearings; the highly publicized rushed bill and protests occurred in 2011 under Governor Scott Walker. The 2009 state budget followed ordinary legislative procedures with committee consideration and debate, and while revenue changes occurred they were not a single secret "billions in tax increases" forced through without hearings.

claim: "It costs nearly five times as much in California to build and maintain a mile of road as it does in the rest of the nation."
rationale: California does have substantially higher road construction and maintenance costs than many other states, but claiming it costs 'nearly five times as much' across the board is an overstatement. Published analyses and DOT data show large variability by project type, location (urban vs rural), and accounting method; typical differences are elevated but generally not a uniform fivefold multiplier for a mile of road.

claim: "For every $1 spent on mitigation, $4 in post-storm cleanup and rebuilding is saved."
rationale: The claim states a universal fixed ratio, but benefit–cost outcomes for mitigation vary by the type of measure, hazard, location and study methods. Some older U.S. agency summaries have cited roughly $4 saved per $1 for certain mitigation programs, while more recent comprehensive analyses (e.g., National Institute of Building Sciences) report different averages (commonly higher) and many interventions have markedly different returns—so the blanket “$1→$4” rule is misleading.

claim: "Obama said he would unilaterally renegotiate the North American Free Trade Agreement."
rationale: Barack Obama criticized and called for updating/enforcing trade agreements like NAFTA but did not say he would unilaterally renegotiate the treaty. Renegotiation of a multilateral trade agreement requires negotiation and agreement with the other parties (Canada and Mexico), not a unilateral presidential action.

claim: A space shuttle the National Museum of the United States Air Force near Dayton would be "within a day's drive of 60 percent of the U.S. population."
rationale: The claim is plausibly overstated and depends heavily on an undefined "day's drive" distance. A typical day's drive (about 6–8 hours or ~400–500 miles) from Dayton covers much of the eastern U.S. but not the large West Coast population centers; without a precise radius and population-layered calculation, the 60% figure cannot be verified and is likely inflated.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: The claim is false: prosecutions of former leaders are not confined to so-called 'Third World' countries and have occurred in many developed democracies. Notable examples include the conviction of former French president Jacques Chirac, prosecutions of South Korean leaders (e.g., Park Geun-hye, Chun Doo-hwan), and legal cases against former leaders in Israel and Brazil. The statement also uses the outdated term 'Third World' and a subjective standard ('habitual').

claim: California’s marijuana legalization initiative, Prop. 64 "allows marijuana smoking ads in prime time, on programs with millions of children and teenage viewers."
rationale: Proposition 64 includes explicit prohibitions on advertising that targets persons under 21 and forbids marijuana ads on television or radio when the audience is reasonably expected to include a substantial portion of under‑21 viewers; it also restricts ads near schools and youth venues. Therefore it does not broadly allow marijuana smoking ads during prime‑time programs with large child and teen audiences.

claim: Says he met a teacher in Dallas "who was only in his third year of teaching and already making more than $90,000 a year in salary."
rationale: The specific anecdote cannot be independently verified and is implausible as a typical public-school outcome: third-year teachers in the Dallas area generally earn far less than $90,000. While it is possible an individual teacher could reach that level via large stipends, coaching pay, extra duties, second jobs, or working for a private/charter employer, the claim as stated is unlikely and unsubstantiated.

claim: "We spent $3-million of your money to study the DNA of bears."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it gives no actor, jurisdiction, timeframe, or source for the alleged $3 million expenditure. While government agencies and research grants sometimes fund wildlife genetics studies, there is no clear evidence that a $3 million taxpayer-funded program was spent specifically to study bear DNA as asserted. Without identifying details or documentation the statement cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says "Bruce Starr voted to throw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment."
rationale: I cannot verify a direct, documented vote by Bruce Starr that literally 'threw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment.' While Starr voted on legislation affecting unemployment programs during his legislative career, attributing a precise number of people removed from benefits to a single legislator’s vote is imprecise and appears to be a political claim without clear legislative record matching that exact figure and causation.

claim: "Last year, (Bill McCollum) spent more than $2.2 million dollars to produce and air campaign-style TV ads where you were featured in almost every frame."
rationale: This specific claim (a precise $2.2M+ sum spent last year and that “you” appeared in almost every frame) cannot be verified from the information given. There are no cited campaign finance records, media-buy invoices, or the actual ad creative provided to confirm the spending amount or the extent of the person's appearance, so the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says the unemployment rate for African-American youths is 59 percent.
rationale: No consistent national labor statistics show a 59% unemployment rate for African‑American youth. Official data (Bureau of Labor Statistics and historical youth unemployment reports) have recorded much lower national unemployment rates for Black teens and young adults, and very high percentages like 59% would only appear for very narrowly defined subgroups, time periods, or alternative metrics. Without a specific age range, time, location, or definition of "unemployment," the blanket 59% figure is unsupported and misleading.

claim: Says the U.S. government caused the coronavirus pandemic because it sent mRNA coronavirus vaccine candidates to university researchers weeks before the COVID-19 outbreak.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. government caused the COVID-19 pandemic, and sending vaccine candidates to researchers cannot produce or "cause" an outbreak. Research on mRNA and coronavirus vaccines existed before 2020 (for SARS/MERS), but SARS-CoV-2 emerged in late 2019 and the viral genome was published in January 2020; SARS-CoV-2–specific mRNA vaccine development began after that. The claim conflates routine research materials/transfers with causation of a novel infectious outbreak.

claim: Says "the New York Times wrote about" Barack Obama wiretapping Donald Trump during the election.
rationale: The New York Times reported on President Trump’s 2017 allegation that Barack Obama ordered wiretaps, but it did not publish that Obama wiretapped Trump as a verified fact. NYT coverage and U.S. intelligence/Justice officials stated there was no evidence supporting the claim and treated it as unsubstantiated.

claim: Florida retirees and families "lost tens of thousands of dollars" in deposits on failed Trump condo projects, but he "pocketed their money and walked away."
rationale: While reporting and lawsuits show that some Florida buyers lost deposits on failed Trump‑branded condo projects, there is no clear evidence that Donald Trump personally 'pocketed' those funds and walked away. Most Trump‑branded developments in Florida were licensed to third‑party developers and deposits were handled by those developers or escrow agents; responsibility for losses has been disputed in court and resolved in different ways for different projects.

claim: Democrats say Chafee wants to tax equipment that enables amputee veterans to drive
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or mainstream reporting that Democrats explicitly accused 'Chafee' of proposing a tax on adaptive driving equipment for amputee veterans. While tax-policy debates are often spun into attack lines, fact-checkers and major news outlets do not document a Democratic claim matching this specific allegation. Without a cited ad, statement, or clear context, the claim appears to be a mischaracterization or unsupported.

claim: "We have that program where immigrants come here and they have to bring a million dollars in order to get a green card if they’re going to create jobs."
rationale: This describes the EB-5 immigrant investor program, under which foreign nationals can obtain a (conditional) green card by investing a substantial sum and creating at least 10 full-time jobs. Historically the standard investment threshold was $1,000,000 (with a $500,000 reduced threshold for targeted employment areas), though exact dollar amounts have changed over time.

claim: "Today’s minimum wage worker making $7.25 an hour has less buying power than a minimum wage worker in the 1960s."
rationale: The federal minimum wage reached its highest real value in the late 1960s (around $1.60 in 1968); after adjusting for inflation those wages are roughly equivalent to $12–14 per hour today. At $7.25 an hour, a contemporary minimum-wage worker has substantially less purchasing power than a typical 1960s minimum-wage worker.

claim: TriMet is "spending 4.2 million in fed funds to save $168K per year."
rationale: The statement is unverified and appears misleading: it presents a raw comparison of a one-time $4.2 million federal outlay to an annual $168,000 saving without specifying the project, time horizon, or whether the funds are grants, loans, or capital investments. Federal transit funds typically finance long-lived capital projects whose costs are amortized over many years, so comparing the full federal contribution to a single year of operating savings is an apples-to-oranges claim and likely misrepresents cost-effectiveness.

claim: Says Tony Evers wants to give in-state tuition and drivers licenses to "illegal aliens."
rationale: Governor Tony Evers has publicly supported measures to allow undocumented immigrants — including DACA recipients and other qualifying residents — to receive in-state tuition rates and has backed efforts to permit driver's licenses for residents regardless of immigration status. These positions have been part of his policy agenda and public statements, though actual changes require legislative approval.

claim: "There are actually only 30 countries that practice birthright citizenship."
rationale: The exact number is not fixed and depends on definition: counts commonly cited for unconditional jus soli hover around 30–33, while including conditional birthright rules (based on parents' citizenship or legal status) increases that number. Because different sources use different criteria and laws change, the blanket claim 'only 30 countries' is imprecise.

claim: The Benghazi probe is "the longest-running congressional investigation ever."
rationale: While the Benghazi investigations stretched over several years and involved multiple House committees (roughly 2012–2016), they are not the longest-running congressional investigations in U.S. history. Other congressional probes and standing committees (for example, the House Un-American Activities Committee and various long‑running oversight inquiries) persisted for many more years or decades.

claim: "Trudeau's foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics which makes mechanic lipids for Pfizer."
rationale: There is no evidence that the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation or any 'Trudeau' foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics. The Trudeau Foundation is a charitable organization and does not publicly hold or report a controlling stake in Acuitas; public reporting shows Acuitas is a private biotech that has collaborated with vaccine developers but is not owned by the Trudeau Foundation. The phrase 'mechanic lipids' is a mischaracterization—Acuitas develops lipid nanoparticle technology and has collaborated with mRNA vaccine developers, but that does not support the claimed ownership stake.

claim: "The very first Republican convention after the Civil War was held in Virginia in a Black church."
rationale: The first national Republican convention after the Civil War was the 1868 Republican National Convention, which met in Chicago, not Virginia. While many local and state Republican meetings during Reconstruction in the South did take place in Black churches, the claim that the "very first Republican convention after the Civil War" was in Virginia in a Black church is incorrect or at best conflates local events with the national convention.

claim: "Leah Vukmir OPPOSES Buy American legislation."
rationale: I can find no clear public record or definitive statement showing Leah Vukmir explicitly opposing 'Buy American' legislation. Her public profile and campaign materials emphasize support for American jobs and manufacturers, and there is no widely reported vote or quote directly contradicting Buy American policies. Without a specific bill or timeframe, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Daniel Webster said he's out. Now he says he's in."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific sequence of public statements by 'Daniel Webster' but gives no date or which person is meant. There is no clear, verifiable record of a prominent individual named Daniel Webster making that exact pair of contradictory statements, and multiple people share the name, so the claim as stated cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Big pharmaceuticals pay off — they literally pay off — generics to keep the prices and the competition off the market."
rationale: There is documented, widespread evidence that brand pharmaceutical companies have paid generic manufacturers to delay market entry (so-called 'pay-for-delay' or reverse-payment settlements), which delays generic competition and keeps prices higher. Courts, regulators and the FTC have investigated and litigated many such agreements, though not every drug company engages in them and legality depends on case details.

claim: "I'm not taking any corporate PAC money."
rationale: There is insufficient context (no named speaker, office, or time period) to verify this assertion. Whether a campaign accepts corporate PAC money can only be determined by checking official campaign finance disclosures (FEC or state filings), and without that evidence the claim is unverified and therefore treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Wisconsin took a break, and when they returned, Biden coincidentally came back ahead by 100k."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: while Wisconsin did pause reporting at times and late-counted absentee ballots shifted the lead toward Biden, his certified margin in Wisconsin (2020) was about 20–21 thousand votes, not a 100,000-vote comeback. The reported shift was real but far smaller than the claim asserts.

claim: Democratic lawmakers who voted in favor of short-term spending bills "just voted to deport Dreamers."
rationale: A vote for a short-term spending bill (a continuing resolution) typically funds government operations temporarily and does not itself change immigration law or issue orders to deport individuals. DACA recipients’ status depends on administrative policy, court rulings, and statutory law; a CR that lacks DACA protections does not directly command deportations unless it expressly includes language blocking DHS from using funds to defer removals. Therefore the blanket claim that those lawmakers “just voted to deport Dreamers” is an overstatement absent evidence of specific anti-DACA riders in the bill.

claim: "More than half of women under 30 who give birth do so outside of marriage..."
rationale: The claim is underspecified (no country or year) and is not generally true worldwide. In many places (including the United States) nonmarital birth rates are high among teens and women in their early 20s but births to women aged 25–29 are often more frequently within marriage, so aggregating all women under 30 does not consistently exceed 50%. In some countries (e.g., parts of Western Europe) the majority of births are to unmarried women, but that makes the statement context-dependent rather than generally true.

claim: Oregon concealed gun applications include "home phone numbers, home address, Social Security numbers, what kinds of guns you have in the house … whether you were dishonorably discharged from the military, what controlled substances you are taking and  were you ever accused of -- accused, mind you -- of stalking."
rationale: The Oregon concealed handgun license application does request identifying and contact information (address, phone) and typically asks for Social Security number (or last 4) and questions about dishonorable military discharge and unlawful drug use. However, it does not require a detailed inventory of 'what kinds of guns you have in the house,' nor does it simply ask whether you were ever 'accused' of stalking; forms ask about convictions, restraining/protective orders, or prohibiting adjudications rather than mere accusations. The claim mixes accurate items with incorrect or misleading ones.

claim: "Germany owes ... vast sums of money to NATO & the United States must be paid more for the powerful, and very expensive, defense it provides to Germany!"
rationale: Germany does contribute to NATO common budgets and hosts U.S. forces, but it does not 'owe vast sums' to NATO as a creditor; NATO is financed by agreed contributions and relatively modest common budgets. The United States has pressed NATO allies to increase their defense spending (the 2% GDP benchmark) and there are bilateral cost- and host-nation-support arrangements, but there is no formal rule that Germany must pay the U.S. extra sums for the U.S. providing defense to Germany.

claim: Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts
rationale: The claim that Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts is not supported by readily available budget records and reporting: while certain programs or departments have seen periodic reductions, the countywide budgets and spending levels have not been reduced in every one of the last eleven years. Without a precise timeframe or definition of "cuts" (overall budget, general fund, staffing, or specific services), the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Israel has seen a "90 percent reduction in terrorist attacks" that it attributes to building a 500-mile fence.
rationale: The statement mixes a kernel of truth with misleading specifics. Israeli officials and supporters have claimed large reductions (often cited as ~90%) in suicide bombings after construction of the West Bank barrier, but that figure usually refers to suicide bombings inside Israel during a specific period, not all "terrorist attacks," and independent analysts attribute declines to multiple measures (barriers, checkpoints, intelligence, and changes in Palestinian violence). The claimed "500-mile fence" length is also inconsistent with commonly reported lengths of the barrier and planned route.

claim: Metro Atlantans spend "over an hour every day" or "five hours a week" commuting, for a total of "260 hours a year."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census/American Community Survey data show average one-way commute times for the Atlanta metro around 28–31 minutes, which implies about an hour round-trip on a typical workday — not clearly “over an hour every day.” The claim’s arithmetic (5 hours/week × 52 weeks = 260 hours) assumes five commuting days every week of the year and conflates one-way and round-trip measures, so the precise figure 260 hours is an exaggeration depending on definitions and time off.

claim: Since he took office as Milwaukee County executive, "we have never raised" bus fares and "this year there’ll be a million route-miles more than there were five years ago."
rationale: The claim is not supported as stated. Milwaukee County Transit fares and fare policies have changed at points during recent administrations and the pandemic period produced temporary policy and service changes that complicate a blanket “we have never raised” assertion; additionally, an increase of one million route‑miles compared to five years prior is implausible without detailed metric definitions and published service-statistics to back it up.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden "doesn’t wear a mask on a plane."
rationale: There is not enough verifiable information here to confirm the assertion because no image or reliable context was provided. A still photo could be miscaptioned, taken off-plane, captured while he briefly removed a mask (e.g., to eat or speak), or depict a time when mask rules differed. Without the actual image and contextual metadata it is not possible to reliably conclude the photo shows Biden not wearing a mask on a plane.

claim: "We’re spending tremendous amounts of money to educate our kids. In the world, we're No. 1 per pupil by a factor of four."
rationale: The United States does spend more per pupil than many countries, but not four times as much. OECD and World Bank data show U.S. K–12 spending is commonly above the OECD average by a few tens of percent, and several countries spend as much or more than the U.S.; it is not ~4x higher than the rest of the world.

claim: Sherrod Brown "sent billions of our tax dollars to foreign countries."
rationale: The claim is misleading and inaccurate: an individual senator does not unilaterally “send” tax dollars to other countries. Congress as a whole (both chambers) and the president approve appropriations and foreign aid, and while total foreign-aid packages are often in the billions, attributing those expenditures to Sherrod Brown personally is incorrect without specifying particular votes or bills he supported.

claim: "I cut more as a percentage out of government than any state in the country this past decade. And where is Michigan in terms of its economic growth? Cutting did not result in economic growth."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and not supported by available state fiscal and economic data: no consistent source shows Michigan cut a larger percentage of government spending than every other state over the past decade once different measures and time windows are considered. Michigan’s economic performance since the recession improved in some metrics (jobs, GDP) but rankings vary by year and metric, so the blanket statement that “cutting did not result in economic growth” is not reliably true.
