Analysts and agencies have found the Keystone XL cancellation would have had at most a modest, localized effect on U.S. crude flows and negligible direct impact on retail gasoline prices.

claim: "There are 300,000 babies born deformed every year in this country because of women who are alcoholics while they're carrying those children to term."
rationale: The claimed figure is greatly inflated and causation is misstated. Even in high-income countries with millions of births per year, credible estimates of fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) or fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD) are far lower than 300,000 births annually, and not all birth defects are caused by maternal alcoholism or prenatal alcohol exposure.

claim: An election worker in Georgia threw away a ballot.
rationale: There is no verified, documented instance showing a Georgia election worker intentionally throwing away a valid ballot; widely circulated videos were investigated and explained by fact-checkers and officials as showing spoiled ballots, ballot envelopes, or misinterpreted actions rather than lawful ballots being discarded. Claims asserting otherwise relied on ambiguous footage and lacked corroborating evidence that a counted or valid ballot was destroyed.

claim: "Pro-Lifers Declare 'Ejaculation Is Murder: Every Sperm Cell Is A Life.'"
rationale: This claim mischaracterizes mainstream pro‑life positions. While some extreme fringe individuals or satirical posts online have made hyperbolic statements about sperm, major pro‑life organizations and typical advocates do not characterize ejaculation or every sperm cell as murder and do not promote criminalizing ejaculation. The claim therefore overgeneralizes rare rhetoric as a widespread declaration.

claim: "More Americans have lost their jobs under Barack Obama than any president in modern history."
rationale: This is false: the largest recent job losses occurred during the 2007–2009 Great Recession, whose big payroll declines began before and around the time Obama took office and are commonly attributed to the recession that began under George W. Bush. Over his two terms Obama presided over a long period of job growth (millions of net payroll jobs added after early 2010), and far larger employment collapses in modern U.S. history occurred during the 1930s.

claim: "As compared to last year, Texas has about 15% more power generation capacity."
rationale: A one-year, ~15% increase in Texas generation capacity is unlikely based on typical annual additions. Texas (ERCOT) has total capacity measured in the tens to low hundreds of GW, and recent yearly additions of wind, solar, and storage have been a few GW—generally single-digit percent changes, not ~15%.

claim: "20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of (Obamacare)."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did lead to cancellation of some noncompliant individual plans, but the specific claim that exactly 20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance is not supported by consistent official data. State and federal reports documented cancellations and transitions to new plans, and counts vary by source and by whether people actually became uninsured versus moved to replacement coverage.

claim: Says George LeMieux was one of two Republicans who voted for President Barack Obama's jobs bill.
rationale: George LeMieux served in the U.S. Senate from 2009 to early 2011 and therefore was not in office when President Obama proposed the American Jobs Act in September 2011. Because that high-profile 'jobs bill' vote occurred after LeMieux left the Senate, he could not have been one of two Republicans to vote for it.

claim: "There are at least 23 countries that refuse to take their people back after they’ve been ordered to leave the United States, including large numbers of violent criminals."
rationale: Independent fact-checks and U.S. government data show the count of countries that categorically 'refuse' to take back nationals varies by definition and time and is smaller or more complicated than the blanket claim. Public records do not support that those countries are sending back 'large numbers of violent criminals' — many had few or no removals and some later cooperated or accepted limited returns.

claim: During his time as House speaker, "unemployment came down from 5.6 percent to under 4 (percent)."
rationale: The claim lacks a named speaker and does not match U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly unemployment data for any recent Speaker’s full tenure. No recent House Speaker began their term with unemployment at 5.6% and finished with unemployment below 4%—typical speaker tenures and monthly unemployment series (U-3) show different start/end values.

claim: Says El Chapo testified in court that he paid off Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open for drug cartels.
rationale: There is no record in El Chapo's trial testimony or official court transcripts accusing Nancy Pelosi of being paid to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open. Major news organizations and fact-checkers reviewed the trial and found no evidence linking Pelosi to any payments by Guzmán or his cartel; the claim appears to be a fabricated social-media rumor.

claim: "The average Republican voter thinks there should be some revenue as part of this deal."
rationale: The claim is too vague and unsupported as stated — it refers to “this deal” and “some revenue” without definition, and there is no cited polling or evidence showing the average Republican holds that view. Public opinion among Republican voters varies by issue, timeframe, and question wording, so a blanket statement about the 'average' Republican is not verifiable. Without specific poll data about that particular deal, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Josh Mandel doctored an image in a campaign ad but "forgot to Photoshop the hands that clearly show he put his face on the body of a Black soldier."
rationale: There is no reliable, widely reported evidence that Josh Mandel published a campaign ad in which he clearly left unedited Black hands showing his face was pasted onto a Black soldier’s body. While contentious campaign images are sometimes scrutinized, the specific allegation about visible hands revealing an obvious Photoshop has not been substantiated by credible news or forensic reporting.

claim: Says "if current trends continue, by 2040, one out of three Texas workers will not have a high school diploma."
rationale: Historical and projected educational attainment data for the U.S. and Texas show the share of adults without a high school diploma has declined for decades and is expected to continue falling, not rise to one-third of workers by 2040. Absent a credible source showing a dramatic reversal in trends or unusual modeling assumptions, the claim is implausible.

claim: "Michigan just refused to certify the election results!"
rationale: The claim is false as stated: there are no credible reports that Michigan 'just refused' to certify statewide election results. Michigan's statewide results (including the 2020 presidential race) were ultimately certified after canvassing, and while some local boards have occasionally delayed or initially deadlocked, the state-level certification was completed.

claim: If women seeking an abortion see their ultrasound, "the odds are pretty high they're going to keep the baby."
rationale: Empirical research on mandated ultrasound viewing shows at most modest or mixed increases in the likelihood of continuing a pregnancy; many women who see an ultrasound still choose abortion. The blanket statement that "the odds are pretty high" overstates the evidence and ignores variation by context, gestational age, counseling and whether viewing is voluntary or forced.

claim: Judge Jeff Davis "spent years defending a convicted cop killer" and "tried to get him off the hook."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable, public evidence that a judge named Jeff Davis spent years defending a convicted cop killer or repeatedly tried to get such a person off the hook. The claim appears to conflate identities or allege a specific legal history that is not documented in accessible public reporting or court records under that name.

claim: Wisconsin’s economy has "tanked" under Gov. Scott Walker and "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014."
rationale: The assertion that over 6,685 people were laid off in Wisconsin in 2015 and that this already exceeded all of 2014 is not supported by state and federal labor data; moreover calling the state's economy "tanked" is a subjective characterization contradicted by job growth and falling unemployment during much of Scott Walker's tenure. Official labor-series and state reports show overall private-sector job gains and a declining unemployment rate through 2015, and the specific 6,685 figure and comparison to 2014 appear to be misleading or based on an incomplete counting method.

claim: Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now," so they should address election social distancing concerns.
rationale: The claim that Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now" is inaccurate: while the governor is a Democrat, the state legislature is controlled by Republicans and many statewide offices and representation are split. Responsibility for election procedures and pandemic-related measures is shared across state and local officials, so blaming a single party is misleading.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Rep. Bob Dold "continues to side with his Republican leadership and the NRA in blocking consideration of a bill that would keep firearms out of the hands of people on the terrorist watch list."
rationale: The claim asserts that Rep. Bob Dold specifically "continues to side... in blocking consideration" of a particular bill, but it lacks a clear reference to a specific procedural vote or date tying Dold personally to blocking floor consideration. While Dold has often voted with House Republicans and held pro-gun positions and NRA support, there is no clear, documented single action by Dold alone that ‘‘blocked consideration’’ of a named bill; such blocking is typically a collective leadership or procedural decision. Without a specific vote or bill, the statement is unsubstantiated as phrased.

claim: Says Rep. Betty Sutton supports allowing "welfare fund withdrawals from strip clubs, casinos and liquor stores."
rationale: This claim mischaracterizes Sutton’s position. She backed ensuring EBT cardholders could access cash at ATMs and opposed blanket restrictions that would limit access, but she did not endorse allowing welfare benefits to be spent at strip clubs, casinos, or liquor stores; federal benefit rules already prohibit using SNAP for alcohol and adult entertainment, and available fact-checks found the claim to be a misleading framing from political ads.

claim: "All of the records, as far as I know, about what we did with health care, those are already available."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unverified assertion that all records about actions on health care are already publicly available. In practice, government and organizational records often include exempt, redacted, or classified materials and private health information that are not publicly released, so the universal claim is unlikely to be true without specification.

claim: Video shows that Sûreté du Québec officers "removed their identifying names and badge numbers from their uniforms in Ottawa."
rationale: While videos circulated during the Ottawa protests showed officers covering or removing identification, available, verified reporting and fact-checks found the footage’s attribution to Sûreté du Québec was unproven or ambiguous. SQ publicly disputed systematic removal and investigations emphasized uncertainty about which agencies appeared in particular clips, so the specific claim that video shows SQ officers removing names and badge numbers in Ottawa is not substantiated.

claim: "I personally am pro-choice. I always have been. And I made no qualms about that when I was elected governor."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks attribution to a specific person and timeframe; whether someone was personally and consistently pro-choice and made that clear when elected governor depends on that individual's public record and campaign statements. Without identifying the speaker, I cannot confirm the accuracy of the self-description. Because the assertion is unverified and potentially falsifiable with public records, I classify it as false under uncertainty.

claim: Under the North American Free Trade Agreement, "we lost millions of jobs."
rationale: Empirical economic studies do not support the unqualified claim that NAFTA alone caused "millions" of lost jobs. Most authoritative analyses attribute at most several hundred thousand U.S. job displacements directly to NAFTA, while the multi‑million decline in manufacturing employment reflected a mix of factors including automation and trade with other countries (notably China). Thus the statement overstates the consensus about NAFTA's direct job impact.

claim: Medicaid "is contributing to 70 percent of our budget deficit right now. It’s the one that is in our lap because of Obamacare."
rationale: Medicaid does not contribute 70% of the federal budget deficit. Federal deficits are driven by multiple factors—revenue shortfalls, tax policy, rising interest payments and large mandatory programs (Social Security and Medicare); Medicaid is a meaningful but much smaller portion. The ACA did expand Medicaid eligibility, but CBO/OMB analyses do not show Medicaid as the dominant source of current federal deficits and the ACA was projected to reduce deficits over its budget window.

claim: Asked what his administration would be doing about "the gun problem," said, "We have done much more than most administrations. … We’ve done, actually, a lot."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it lacks a named speaker, date, or source and I cannot confirm that exact quote in reliable reporting or official transcripts. Without attribution or corroborating evidence, the statement cannot be established as factual.

claim: Says that PolitiFact Ohio confirms that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt"
rationale: There is no clear evidence that PolitiFact Ohio explicitly "confirmed" that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt." PolitiFact typically evaluates specific claims and would publish a precise ruling and citation; no known PolitiFact Ohio item endorses that exact, absolute phrasing about Sutton.

claim: "Close to half of the folks in this country illegally entered legally (but) overstayed (their ) visas."
rationale: Multiple authoritative analyses (DHS entry/exit estimates and Pew Research Center studies) report that roughly 40–45% of the undocumented population entered lawfully and then overstayed visas. Saying 'close to half' is a reasonable concise characterization of those published estimates.

claim: "The job [of correctional officer] lowers your life expectancy . . . Metropolitan did a study in, I believe it was 1998, and the life expectancy was 58."
rationale: There is evidence that correctional officers face elevated health risks (stress, cardiovascular disease, suicide) that can reduce longevity, but I am not aware of a reputable 1998 'Metropolitan' study reporting an average life expectancy of 58 for correctional officers. No widely cited peer-reviewed or governmental source supports a population mean life expectancy that low for correctional officers in the U.S.; the specific 58-year figure and the cited 1998 'Metropolitan' study appear unverified or misattributed.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers "wants to force residents to fund Planned Parenthood abortion business."
rationale: This is a partisan mischaracterization. Tony Evers has voiced support for reproductive health services and family-planning funding and has defended Planned Parenthood as a healthcare provider, but he has not proposed a policy that would "force" residents to directly pay for elective abortions. Wisconsin law and typical public-funding rules limit use of state funds for elective abortion, and Planned Parenthood also delivers many non-abortion health services.

claim: Says Dr. Robert Gallo, the man who helped discover the HIV virus, confessed he was "forced" to "create the HIV virus as a secret weapon to wipe out the African race."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Dr. Robert Gallo confessed to being forced to create HIV as a weapon to wipe out Africans; this allegation is a baseless conspiracy. Scientific consensus holds that HIV arose from cross-species transmission of simian viruses, and the claim has been repeatedly debunked by public health experts and reputable fact-checkers.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Trey Gowdy’s 8-year-old son found dead "in a dumpster in D.C."
rationale: There are no credible news reports, official statements, or reliable records that Rep. Trey Gowdy’s 8-year-old son was found dead in a dumpster in Washington, D.C. Major news organizations and fact-checkers have debunked similar social-media hoaxes about the families of public figures. The claim appears to be fabricated and defamatory.

claim: "When I was speaker, we had four consecutive balanced budgets."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits who “I” is, which legislative body, and the exact years; without that context it cannot be confirmed. Whether a speaker presided over four consecutive balanced budgets depends on the country, accounting definitions, and timeframe, and many speakers did not oversee such a run. Because the statement lacks essential identifying details it should not be accepted as factual.

claim: Gas prices during the Obama-Biden administration were $5.49 a gallon.
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. gasoline prices averaged $5.49 per gallon during the Obama-Biden administration (2009–2017). National average pump prices during those years generally remained well below $5.49; while some stations in high-cost states occasionally charged prices that high, it was not a common or national average price.

claim: "I have spent virtually every weekend since Memorial Day in the Panhandle."
rationale: This is a first‑person claim about past personal activity with no supporting evidence provided. Without travel records, timestamps, photos, receipts, or third‑party corroboration, the statement cannot be independently verified and therefore is treated as not established.

claim: Republican candidate for Georgia governor "dabbled" in birther conspiracy theories.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated because it does not name a specific Republican candidate or timeframe. Public records and reporting on prominent Georgia gubernatorial candidates do not document that major contenders broadly 'dabbled' in birther conspiracy theories; without a named individual the assertion is unsupported. It is possible that a minor or fringe candidate made such claims, but the blanket statement is not verifiable.

claim: Says that when Republicans held Congress and the presidency, they "doubled the size of the (U.S.) Department of Education."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Republicans, while holding both the presidency and Congress, doubled the size of the U.S. Department of Education. Historical staffing and budget records do not show a doubling in those windows; Republican administrations have more often proposed cuts or limits to the department rather than expanding it twofold.

claim: "Hillary interned with Bob Treuhaft, the head of the California Communist Party."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Rodham (Clinton) interned for Robert (Bob) Treuhaft. Treuhaft was a left‑wing attorney who at times represented Communist clients and was active in progressive causes, but he was not the head of the California Communist Party, and Clinton's documented early internships/employment do not list working for him.

claim: Obama "says he'll raise taxes on electricity."
rationale: There is no credible record of Barack Obama explicitly saying "I'll raise taxes on electricity." He supported carbon-pricing mechanisms and emissions regulations (e.g., cap-and-trade proposals and the Clean Power Plan) that critics said would raise energy costs, but those policy proposals are not the same as a direct pledge to impose an "electricity tax." The claim appears to conflate opponent messaging with a direct quote or promise.

claim: "I never was in favor of shutting down the government. … (I) voted to fund the government fully."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who made the statement or specify which funding vote is referenced. Whether someone ‘never’ favored a shutdown and whether they ‘voted to fund the government fully’ are factual assertions that require checking that person’s public statements and specific roll-call votes; absent that context they cannot be confirmed. The two parts also require separate evidence and could be inconsistent over time.

claim: Scott Maddox is a "lobbyist."
rationale: Scott Maddox is best known as a former Tallahassee mayor and chair of the Florida Democratic Party who was arrested and convicted in a corruption probe; he is not generally described as a lobbyist. News coverage links him to dealings with lobbyists during the investigation, but does not identify lobbying as his primary occupation.

claim: Says Governor Cooper has vetoed "every single teacher pay raise we've ever passed."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Governor Roy Cooper has vetoed some budget bills but he has not vetoed every teacher pay raise passed by the legislature. Public records and news coverage show that some teacher pay increases were enacted during his tenure without a veto or were included in budgets he signed or that became law despite vetoes/overrides.

claim: Says Bill Nelson "skipped 45 percent of the hearings on national security."
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated evidence that Senator Bill Nelson 'skipped 45 percent of the hearings on national security.' The claim is unsourced and fails to specify a timeframe or which committees/hearings are meant; publicly available attendance and hearing records do not substantiate such a blanket 45% absentee rate.

claim: "We had the Democratic Governors Association and the Obama political machine come into a Republican primary to try and rig the election by spending $1 million against me in the last couple of days."
rationale: The claim alleges a specific $1 million intervention by the Democratic Governors Association and the vaguely defined 'Obama political machine' in a particular Republican primary in the last couple of days. I could not confirm this precise allegation from public campaign finance disclosures or reputable reports; the phrase 'Obama political machine' is not a formal organization and the DGA's activities would be documented and reported if it had made such a late, large expenditure. Absent verifiable, specific evidence tying those groups to a $1 million spend in the stated timeframe, the claim is unverified and treated as false.

claim: Medicare insurance premiums will be rising to "$120.20 per month in 2013 and $247.00 per month in 2014."
rationale: The numbers are incorrect for standard Medicare premiums. The Medicare Part B standard premium for most beneficiaries was roughly $104.90 per month in 2013 and remained about the same in 2014; it did not rise to $120.20 in 2013 or $247.00 in 2014. While higher-income enrollees pay additional income-related amounts, the claim as stated is inaccurate for Medicare generally.

claim: "Pasco County has the second highest population of homeless in all of Florida."
rationale: Available homelessness counts (e.g., HUD point-in-time and state reports) show Miami-Dade, Broward, Orange, Hillsborough and other large Florida counties having the largest absolute homeless populations; Pasco County is not reported as the second-highest. The claim is inconsistent with typical county-level HUD and state data unless a very specific year or unusual metric is being used.

claim: Hepatitis outbreak in kids may be related to Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: Major public health agencies (WHO, CDC, ECDC) investigating the unexplained pediatric hepatitis cases have not found evidence linking the outbreak to the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine. The J&J vaccine uses an adenovirus 26 vector and was not widely administered to young children; the cases have been epidemiologically associated with other causes such as adenovirus type 41 or prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, and no causal signal to J&J vaccination has been established.

claim: Says Bubba Watson wrote a viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter.
rationale: There is no widely reported or verifiable record that professional golfer Bubba Watson authored a viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter. A post by a celebrity that went viral would typically have been covered in mainstream media and fact-checked, and I am not aware of such coverage linking Watson to a viral BLM post.

claim: "Senator Robert Hurt voted for a bill that’s raised your electric rates seven times."
rationale: The claim is not supported. Robert Hurt is better known as a former U.S. Representative (not a U.S. Senator), and there is no verifiable, specific bill tied to him that can be shown to have 'raised your electric rates seven times.' The statement conflates office title, omits which bill and timeframe, and asserts a causal link between a single vote and multiple rate increases without evidence.

claim: "We could build 30 walls with the $150 billion Obama gave to Iran."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the U.S. did not 'give' Iran $150 billion. The $100–150 billion figure commonly cited refers to Iran’s total frozen foreign assets and restrained access changes under the nuclear deal, many of which were held outside the United States and were not a direct cash transfer by President Obama. Separately, cost estimates for a U.S. border wall vary but are far lower per-wall than implied, so the arithmetic asserting 30 walls from $150 billion is not supported.

claim: Photo shows Rihanna is pregnant
rationale: A single photo alone does not prove pregnancy; without corroborating information (an official announcement from Rihanna or reporting by reputable news outlets) the claim is unverified and likely misleading. Photographs can be affected by clothing, posture, camera angle, or editing and therefore are insufficient evidence of pregnancy.

claim: In Japan, executives of failing companies "say 'I'm sorry' and then either do one of two things: resign or go commit suicide."
rationale: This statement is an exaggeration and stereotype. While Japanese corporate culture often emphasizes public apology and resignation as taking responsibility, suicide by executives is a rare and tragic occurrence, not one of only two routine outcomes; executives may also be dismissed, face legal consequences, remain in post, or pursue other remedies.

claim: Says "Rep. Ann Wagner, a three-term incumbent, has never held a town hall in the Second District."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: public schedules and news coverage indicate Rep. Ann Wagner has conducted constituent outreach in the 2nd District, including town-hall–style meetings and telephone/virtual town halls during her tenure. The statement overgeneralizes by claiming she 'never' held any town hall.

claim: The U.S. Justice Department "conservatively estimated that guns are used 1.5 million times per year to save lives."
rationale: There is no record that the U.S. Department of Justice itself issued a ‘‘conservative’’ estimate of 1.5 million defensive gun uses per year. That figure is most closely associated with academic survey estimates (notably Kleck’s survey-based estimates) and advocacy citations; federal crime-survey data (Bureau of Justice Statistics / NCVS) produce much lower annual counts and researchers have criticized the survey methods that produced multi‑million estimates.

claim: "Dying nurse on deathbed claims she swapped more than 5,000 babies for ‘fun.’"
rationale: This is a recurring urban-legend style claim that has no credible evidence or named, verifiable sources. Swapping more than 5,000 babies would be logistically implausible given hospital record-keeping, parent identification procedures, and the lack of any major investigative reporting or prosecutions tied to such an extraordinary confession.

claim: "Japan drops vax rollout"
rationale: The terse claim that "Japan drops vax rollout" is inaccurate as a general statement—Japan did not abandon its COVID-19 vaccination program. Japan authorized vaccines, carried out mass rollouts beginning in 2021, and continued booster and routine vaccination campaigns thereafter; there were only limited, temporary pauses or adjustments for specific lots or age groups at times.

claim: House Republicans required the use of Styrofoam cups in House cafeterias that are "part of Koch Industries."
rationale: There is no evidence that House cafeterias are part of Koch Industries; congressional dining facilities are operated under the Architect of the Capitol/House administrative entities, not by a private corporation. While there have been news reports of cost-cutting decisions in House cafeterias that led to continued or increased use of foam cups, those actions were administrative choices and not because the cafeterias belonged to or were run by Koch Industries.

claim: "U.S. government reports record tax haul after Trump tax cuts spur economic growth."
rationale: The claim mixes two assertions that are not supported together: while nominal federal receipts rose in some years after the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the tax cuts reduced revenue relative to prior-law projections and increased deficits. Independent analyses (CBO, Treasury, and other fiscal analysts) found that the TCJA did not pay for itself and that any economic growth that occurred was insufficient to create a ‘record’ revenue haul attributable to the cuts.

claim: A flight crew took a knee and stranded the New Orleans Saints on an airport runway.
rationale: There are no credible reports that a flight crew 'took a knee' and thereby stranded the New Orleans Saints; such an event involving a high-profile NFL team would have been widely reported. Airline and charter operations have procedures and regulatory oversight (including replacement crews) that make this scenario unlikely as stated, suggesting the claim is unverified or false.

claim: "In fact, there’s more state funding for education today than any other time."
rationale: The claim is unqualified and therefore misleading. While nominal state education spending (raw dollars) is larger today than in the distant past due to inflation and larger budgets, that does not prove spending is higher in real (inflation‑adjusted) terms, per‑pupil, or as a share of GDP — measures where trends differ by state and period. Without specifying the timeframe, geographic scope, and whether amounts are nominal or inflation‑adjusted, the statement cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Anthony Fauci was on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and "currently serves on Gates Foundation."
rationale: Public records and multiple fact-checks show Dr. Anthony Fauci was never a member of the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years, nor is he a serving board member of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. Fauci is a long-time federal official who has collaborated with many public health organizations, but those collaborations do not equate to board membership.

claim: Says David Dewhurst "went out for drinks" during Senate debate on abortion bill.
rationale: There is no reliable contemporary reporting or documented evidence that David Dewhurst left the chamber to "go out for drinks" during the high‑profile Texas Senate debate on an abortion bill. Major news accounts and records of the debate describe him presiding and managing proceedings rather than departing for socializing.

claim: "Twenty-five percent of our kids in foster care are there because their parents are involved in drugs."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and cannot be confirmed as a general fact. While parental drug use is frequently identified as a significant factor in child removals, the percentage attributed to parental drug involvement varies by jurisdiction, year, and whether it is counted as a primary reason or a contributing factor, so an unqualified '25%' claim is not reliably verifiable.

claim: Says private-sector job growth in 2011 "places New Jersey in the top third among all of the states."
rationale: State employment data sources (such as BLS state employment reports) do not clearly support the assertion that New Jersey’s private-sector job growth in 2011 was in the top third of states; New Jersey’s private-sector gains that year were modest and generally ranked around the middle or lower half in many published comparisons. Without a specific data source or definition of the metric, the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: Since 2009, "we've cut homelessness (among veterans) by a third."
rationale: The statement is misleading as written. Federal data from HUD and the VA show veteran homelessness declined substantially since 2009, and in some official comparisons (depending on the years and measure used) the reduction was larger than one-third; moreover counts vary by whether one uses point-in-time counts, annual counts, or different baseline years. Because the claim gives a single unsourced fraction without specifying the measure or exact timeframe, it is not an accurate, verifiable statement as presented.

claim: "A million people … could get health insurance right away" if Texas expanded Medicaid under Obamacare.
rationale: Multiple nonpartisan analyses have concluded that roughly one million (around 1.0–1.2 million) low‑income adults in Texas would become newly eligible for Medicaid if the state expanded under the Affordable Care Act. Those people would generally be able to enroll and gain coverage once expansion is implemented, though exact timing depends on how the state rolls out enrollment.

claim: Says Debbie Wasserman Schultz "voted repeatedly to send terminally ill patients to prison."
rationale: There is no credible evidence in congressional voting records or reputable fact-checks that Debbie Wasserman Schultz repeatedly voted to imprison terminally ill patients. Claims like this have circulated as distortions of votes on unrelated health or criminal statutes and often lack reference to any specific bill or amendment that would criminalize terminally ill patients themselves.

claim: "There's no such thing as a lone wolf. ... That was a phrase invented by the last administration to make Americans stupid."
rationale: The claim is false: 'lone wolf' is an established term in criminology and law enforcement describing individuals who act alone, and there are well-documented historical cases (for example the Unabomber and numerous lone-actor mass shooters). The phrase predates recent U.S. administrations and was not invented by any single administration as a tactic to 'make Americans stupid.'

claim: Image shows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky "has joined the front lines with his troops."
rationale: An image alone does not prove that Zelensky 'joined the front lines' in combat; verified reporting and official Ukrainian communications document he makes supervised visits to troops but do not support claims he took up arms on active front-line positions. Verification would require image metadata, geolocation, and independent corroboration, which are not provided here.

claim: Coca-Cola, Ben & Jerry’s and other companies support rioting.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coca-Cola, Ben & Jerry’s, or most other major companies have officially endorsed or funded rioting. Public corporate statements and reporting show these companies have expressed support for racial justice or peaceful protest and in many cases condemned violence; critics sometimes misrepresent those statements as support for rioting.

claim: Says federal regulations adopted in 2011 increased the cost of each vehicle for his business by $10,000.
rationale: The claim is specific (a $10,000 per-vehicle increase due to federal regulations adopted in 2011) but provides no evidence or identification of which regulation, vehicle type, or cost study. Regulatory compliance costs vary widely by rule, manufacturer, and model year, and independent regulatory-impact analyses would be needed to substantiate a uniform $10,000 increase per vehicle. Without that supporting data, the precise monetary assertion cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: Says she "called for addressing risks of derivatives, cracking down on subprime mortgages and improving financial oversight" early on in the financial crisis.
rationale: The claim refers to "she" but does not identify who is being quoted, so it cannot be verified as stated. While many public figures did call for addressing derivatives risks, cracking down on subprime mortgages, and improving oversight early in the financial crisis, the lack of a named person or source means the specific assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Biden concedes 6 million votes."
rationale: There is no record or credible reporting that President Joe Biden ever "conceded 6 million votes." A concession in electoral terms means admitting defeat in an election, and Biden has not issued any statement conceding an election or specifically conceding 6 million votes.

claim: Says Marilinda Garcia supports "$150 billion in new taxes."
rationale: I find no credible evidence that Marilinda Garcia publicly endorsed or proposed a policy to raise $150 billion in new taxes. The specific $150 billion figure does not match Garcia’s known campaign positions or any documented legislative proposal attributed to her, and such a precise national-tax claim appears to be a mischaracterization by opponents.

claim: "25,000 businesses have been created since (Scott) Walker took office."
rationale: The statement gives a precise count but provides no source or clear end date; official business formation statistics are reported by state and federal agencies and vary by timeframe. Without a verifiable source tying the 25,000 figure to a defined period 'since Walker took office' the claim is unverified and likely misleading or cherry-picked.

claim: Wisconsin state lawmakers worked seven days in 2012 but got "paid for a whole year."
rationale: The claim is misleading and lacks supporting evidence. Wisconsin legislators receive an annual salary and perform year-round duties (committees, constituent work, interim activities), and public records do not clearly support the assertion that they only 'worked seven days' in 2012; without a precise definition of "worked" (floor days vs. committee or other official business) the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: Health care premiums for consumers have doubled since 2001.
rationale: The claim is too general to be judged true as written: health insurance premiums have risen substantially since 2001, but the magnitude differs by country, by type of plan (employer-sponsored, individual/marketplace, Medicare supplemental), and by whether you measure family vs. single coverage or premiums vs. out‑of‑pocket costs. Some U.S. employer family premiums have more than doubled over long periods, while other measures (individual market premiums after ACA subsidies, or single-worker premiums in some years) have increased less or changed differently, so a blanket "doubled" statement is misleading. Without specifying country and which premiums, the claim is not reliably supportable.

claim: Data on violent crime shows Wisconsin "has become less safe than it was when Scott Walker took office."
rationale: The claim is too categorical and not supported by a single clear trend: Wisconsin violent-crime measures have fluctuated since Scott Walker took office in 2011, with increases in some years and declines in others. Whether the state is "less safe" depends on the specific metric (violent-crime rate, total offenses, homicide rate), the comparison years chosen, and local variation, so the blanket statement is not supported without a defined timeframe and metric.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton called the Trans-Pacific Partnership "the gold standard. You called it the gold standard of trade deals. You said it’s the finest deal you’ve ever seen."
rationale: In 2015 Hillary Clinton publicly praised the Trans-Pacific Partnership, describing it with phrases such as the 'gold standard' for trade agreements and commending its terms; the claim is a reasonable paraphrase of her earlier statements. She later reversed her position during the 2016 campaign, but the quoted praise reflects her prior public remarks.

claim: A U-Haul operated by antifa activists distributed "shields, weapons & black bloc" to protesters in Louisville, Ky., and is linked to "a George Soros-funded initiative."
rationale: Multiple reputable news outlets, local authorities, and fact-checkers found no evidence that a U-Haul in Louisville was operated by 'antifa' activists, that it distributed shields, weapons and black bloc gear to protesters, or that it was linked to any George Soros-funded initiative. Public records and reporting did not corroborate the claimed chain of custody or funding connection, and the specific allegation appears to be unverified misinformation.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum is running "from the FBI."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Andrew Gillum is literally 'running from the FBI.' Public reporting around investigations involving Gillum has not documented him fleeing, and he has publicly cooperated with inquiries rather than evading law enforcement. The claim appears to be a sensational or metaphorical characterization rather than a documented fact.

claim: During her tenure as county attorney in Minnesota, "there was a 65 percent decrease in incarceration of African-Americans."
rationale: The claim is vague and I find no corroborating public data or reputable reporting showing a 65% decrease in African‑American incarceration attributable to a Minnesota county attorney’s tenure. County incarceration statistics are reported by specific jurisdictions and timeframes; without a named county, dates, or source, the claim is unsubstantiated and likely misleading.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers has declared Wisconsin "permanently closed" for business.
rationale: Governor Tony Evers issued temporary emergency orders and business restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic, but he never declared Wisconsin "permanently closed" for business. The "permanently closed" wording circulated as a mischaracterization or misinformation of his temporary public-health orders and guidance.

claim: "Over-vaccination causes faster mutation of the (COVID-19) virus, which causes a super virus we may not have the ability to fight off."
rationale: Vaccination does not 'cause' faster mutation; viral mutation rate is driven by the number of replications and transmissions. Vaccines generally reduce infections and viral replication, thereby lowering the opportunity for new variants to arise. While immune pressure can favor immune-escape mutations in some situations, that is not the same as vaccines creating a guaranteed 'super virus' we cannot combat.

claim: Obamacare is a "massive, massive income redistribution" with "$250 billion a year in Medicaid expansion (and) in the subsidy structure that's basically being paid for by people on Medicare, through Medicare cuts, and a lot of tax increases."
rationale: The claim mixes some accurate elements with exaggerated and incorrect specifics. The ACA did expand Medicaid and created subsidies for exchange coverage and it included Medicare payment reductions and new taxes to help finance the law, but the specific figure of "$250 billion a year" for Medicaid expansion is not supported by mainstream budget estimates and the assertion that subsidies are "basically being paid for by people on Medicare" mischaracterizes how Medicare savings (largely provider and plan payment reductions) and targeted tax increases were used. Overall the statement overstates and distorts the financing and redistributive effects.

claim: "The Railroad Commission of Texas has nothing to do with railroads."
rationale: Despite its name, the Railroad Commission of Texas no longer regulates railroads and today primarily oversees oil and gas production, pipelines, and mining. The agency’s name is historical—railroad oversight was its original 19th-century purpose but that authority has long since been transferred to other entities.

claim: In 1988, in response to Iran’s attack on the U.S.S. Samuel Roberts, President Ronald Reagan "destroyed half of Iran’s Navy."
rationale: While the U.S. retaliatory Operation Praying Mantis in April 1988 (after USS Samuel B. Roberts struck a mine) sank or damaged several Iranian surface ships and oil platforms, it did not literally destroy half of Iran’s navy. U.S. forces sank a frigate and some smaller patrol craft and damaged others, but Iran retained the majority of its naval fleet and other maritime forces after the clashes.

claim: Countries were exporting COVID-19 "diagnostic test instruments" in 2018.
rationale: SARS-CoV-2 and the disease COVID-19 were not identified until late 2019 and diagnostic tests specific to COVID-19 were developed only after the viral genome was published in January 2020. While general-purpose diagnostic instruments (PCR machines, immunoassay analyzers) were exported in 2018, instruments specifically for COVID-19 could not have been produced or exported in 2018.

claim: The wife of the Ferguson, Mo., police chief said African-Americans in Ferguson "are feral and violent."
rationale: There are no credible contemporaneous news reports or official transcripts that attribute the exact phrase "feral and violent" to the wife of the Ferguson police chief. While there were social-media posts and public criticism connected to Ferguson officials and their spouses during the 2014 protests, major outlets did not document this precise quoted statement by the chief's wife. Given the lack of reliable sourcing, the specific quote is unsubstantiated.

claim: If you know someone's name and date of birth you can change their votes on Oregon’s voting website.
rationale: Oregon’s public voter tools (e.g., My Vote) allow lookup of registration and ballot status but do not provide any function to alter someone’s cast ballot. Oregon uses a secure vote-by-mail process with county custody, signature verification and other checks, so merely knowing a person’s name and date of birth is not sufficient to change their votes via the state website or official systems.

claim: Wisconsin is "38th in the country in terms of proficiency standards" in student testing.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and not supported as a general fact: there is no single, widely accepted nationwide ranking that places Wisconsin exactly 38th on 'proficiency standards' without specifying the test, year, or methodology. Wisconsin's position varies substantially by assessment (NAEP, state tests) and by year, and in many common measures Wisconsin is near or above the national average rather than 38th. Absent a cited source, the claim is misleading.

claim: "Trump's Cabinet is more white and more male than any first Cabinet since President Ronald Reagan’s."
rationale: Contemporary analyses of the incoming Trump administration noted its Cabinet was overwhelmingly white and male compared with first-term Cabinets of presidents since Reagan. Trump’s initial slate included very few women and few racial minorities relative to the first Cabinets of George H.W. Bush, Clinton, George W. Bush and Obama, making it the least gender- and racially-diverse first Cabinet since Reagan’s.

claim: Says Obama said black people have the "worst jobs, the worst housing" and face rampant police brutality, "but when so-called black committeemen came around election time we’d all line up and vote the straight Democratic ticket, sell our souls for a Christmas turkey."
rationale: This wording appears in Barack Obama’s memoir Dreams from My Father, where he recounts South Side political patronage and describes Black residents having the worst jobs and housing and enduring police harassment while still lining up to vote the straight Democratic ticket — “sell our souls for a Christmas turkey.” The passage is widely cited as Obama’s own description of local politics and voting behavior.

claim: "Individuals and small businesses will be hit by increases in health insurance premiums as high as 39 percent."
rationale: The claim is unqualified and presents a specific nationwide increase as certain, but there is no universally applicable evidence that all individuals and small businesses "will be hit" with premium rises of up to 39%. Health insurance premium changes depend heavily on the specific policy, state, plan, age mix, and regulatory assumptions; some analyses for specific scenarios or subgroups have shown large increases, but that does not validate a blanket, certain prediction. Without a cited study, timeframe, or jurisdiction the assertion is unsupported.

claim: House Republican plan would increase costs for Oregon seniors by $6,000 with health care vouchers instead of Medicare
rationale: The claim as stated is unverified because it names no specific House Republican bill or timeframe; independent analyses (including CBO studies of various Medicare “voucher”/premium-support proposals) have shown that out-of-pocket costs for beneficiaries could rise under some proposals, but the dollar impact varies widely by proposal, year, and beneficiary circumstances. No single, authoritative estimate universally shows Oregon seniors would pay exactly $6,000 more under a generic “House Republican plan.”

claim: "42 percent of (Walmart’s) associates are black."
rationale: Publicly available corporate diversity/EEO-1 data and Walmart’s own diversity reports do not support a claim that 42% of Walmart’s overall associates are Black; reported Black representation in Walmart’s U.S. workforce has generally been substantially lower (commonly in the low-to-mid teens). The 42% figure is inconsistent with typical published workforce breakdowns and lacks supporting context (country, year, or specific division).

claim: Says after Hurricane Sandy, New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg "refused to allow the National Guard into the city to restore civil order because Guardsmen carry guns!"
rationale: This claim is false. The mayor of New York City does not unilaterally control activation of the National Guard, and after Hurricane Sandy the New York National Guard was in fact mobilized to assist with response and security. There is no credible evidence Bloomberg "refused" Guard entry because they carried guns; that narrative circulated as a debunked viral rumor.

claim: "Wind powers nearly 13 million homes across the country."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and cannot be verified as presented because it lacks a country and a date; the common “homes powered” metric is a derived estimate that has varied year to year and by calculation method. Industry and government reports sometimes reported figures near 13 million for specific years or definitions, but the number is not a universally true, standalone fact without that context.

claim: He "stood up to Barack Obama by passing legislation that prevents you from being forced to join government health plans or buy health insurance against your will."
rationale: The claim is misleading: no single state or legislator can unilaterally 'prevent' federal law from imposing an individual coverage requirement, and the federal individual mandate was a matter of federal law and Supreme Court review. While Congress later set the federal penalty to $0 in 2017 and some states have enacted or repealed their own mandates or protections, that outcome was not simply the result of one person 'standing up to Barack Obama' by passing a law that unilaterally prevents being forced to buy coverage.

claim: "Only the fully vaccinated should fear the new ‘worst ever’ Covid-19 variant; data shows they already account for 4 in every 5 Covid deaths"
rationale: This claim is misleading and likely false: vaccines substantially reduce the risk of severe illness and death, and unvaccinated people have generally remained at higher risk. Reports that a large share of deaths are among the “fully vaccinated” are often driven by high vaccine coverage in vulnerable groups, age and health confounding, and waning/booster status — not evidence that only vaccinated people should fear a new variant.

claim: Says Marco Rubio took "three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives" during the 2016 Senate election.
rationale: I cannot find clear, verifiable evidence that Marco Rubio personally received exactly $750,000 from 'fossil fuel executives' in his 2016 Senate race. Campaign finance records and summaries typically report contributions from the oil and gas industry or related PACs in aggregate and may not match that specific figure or donor category. The claim appears to conflate different funding categories (industry PACs, employees, and executives) and lacks precise sourcing.

claim: "Lots of studies seem to indicate that minors find it very easy to get marijuana, easier than to get alcohol."
rationale: The research is mixed rather than clearly supporting the claim. Large national youth surveys (e.g., Monitoring the Future, NSDUH) and academic studies show adolescents commonly report easy access to both alcohol and marijuana, and in many samples alcohol is reported as equally or more accessible than marijuana; results vary by year, age group, and locality. Therefore it’s not correct to state that ‘lots of studies’ indicate minors find marijuana easier to get than alcohol overall.

claim: The Democratic health care bill in the House would "create 53 new government bureaucracies."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that a Democratic House health bill literally 'creates 53 new government bureaucracies.' Counts like this have been used as political rhetoric; how many new entities exist depends on loose definitions (offices, boards, programs, agencies) and different readings of the text produce very different totals. Independent fact-checkers and reading of legislative language do not support the definitive figure of 53 new bureaucracies.

claim: "Coolmath Games is being taken down cause it was run by the Mexican drug cartel?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that Coolmath Games was run by a Mexican drug cartel or that any takedown is for that reason. Company and domain ownership information and news coverage treat Coolmath as a legitimate gaming/education site, and claims tying it to a cartel appear to be baseless rumors.

claim: "Two Iraqis came here to this country, were radicalized and they were the masterminds behind the Bowling Green massacre. … It didn't get covered"
rationale: There was never a "Bowling Green massacre." Two Iraqi-born men were arrested in Bowling Green, Kentucky in 2011 on charges of attempting to provide material support to al-Qaeda in Iraq, and they pleaded guilty to related offenses; they were not masterminds of any massacre. Those arrests were reported at the time and later fact-checked when the false "massacre" claim circulated.

claim: As first lady, Clinton would travel to places that were "too small, too poor or too dangerous" for the president.
rationale: The phrasing appears to be campaign rhetoric rather than a documented, literal practice. While First Lady Hillary Clinton did travel widely and visited poor or sometimes unstable countries on diplomatic and humanitarian missions, there is no clear documentary evidence that she formally or consistently 'went to places that were "too small, too poor or too dangerous" for the president' as a categorical policy or routine. The quoted language is not a verified factual descriptor of her official travel program.

claim: Says Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins and Mitt Romney "are pro-pedophile."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins, or Mitt Romney endorse or are "pro-pedophile." These are inflammatory accusations that are unsupported by their voting records, public statements, or reputable reporting. The claim appears to be a rhetorical or defamatory attack rather than a factual description of their positions.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and incorrect: it is unclear whether 'America' means the United States or the continents, and by mid-2024 many countries already had >50% of their population fully vaccinated against COVID-19. Therefore claiming '50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated' is not supported by international vaccination data and conflates categories.

claim: "Mar-A-Lago (was) destroyed by (Hurricane) Irma (and) Jared Kushner (is) still missing."
rationale: Both parts of the claim are false. Mar-a-Lago sustained some damage from Hurricane Irma in 2017 but was not destroyed and remained in use afterward; Jared Kushner is alive and has continued to appear publicly and in news reports, with no credible reports of him being missing.

claim: Says Judge Amy Coney Barrett said that "gays have a right to be discriminated against because they are against God’s wishes" and that "white people are God’s chosen ones."
rationale: There is no reliable record or credible news report of Amy Coney Barrett making those statements; they appear to be fabricated or misattributed. Barrett has discussed her Catholic faith and religious-liberty views publicly, but did not explicitly say gays should be discriminated against or that white people are God's chosen ones.

claim: "For the first time in 35 years, we have more businesses closing than starting."
rationale: The claim gives no country or time period and cannot be verified as stated. National business statistics (e.g., business births vs. deaths data) vary by jurisdiction and year, and while closures rose during events like the COVID-19 pandemic, new business formations also increased in some datasets; there is no clear, universal evidence that for the first time in 35 years businesses closing exceeded startups. Without a specified jurisdiction and source, the statement is misleading and unsubstantiated.

claim: Says "over 40 percent of recent county bonds are for Precinct One, northeast Travis County," because he "is quick to identify projects that help make the East Side a desirable place to live."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise statistic (>40%) about recent Travis County bond allocations to Precinct One without citing a timeframe or source. County bond proceeds and project allocations are public and vary by bond package; absent a verifiable county bond report showing that share, the claim is unverified and implausible as stated.

claim: The Red Sox waited "87 long years" to win the World Series.
rationale: The Boston Red Sox's championship drought commonly called the 'Curse of the Bambino' lasted from their 1918 World Series win until their next title in 2004, a span of 86 years—not 87. Saying 87 years is off by one year based on the calendar difference between 1918 and 2004.

claim: Says he would be first CPA to serve as Texas comptroller.
rationale: The statement is unlikely to be reliably factual as written because it’s ambiguous who “he” refers to and the Texas Comptroller office has a long history with several holders having finance/accounting backgrounds. Without a specific named person and verification of every past comptroller’s professional certifications, the claim that any candidate would be the first CPA is not substantiated. Verification against official biographies of past Texas comptrollers is needed.

claim: Says "$57,000 is the mean [income] in our state" for a family.
rationale: The statement is unverified as written because it does not specify which state, which year, or the data source, and whether 'family' means household or Census family. State-level mean family incomes vary widely and official reports often publish medians rather than means, so $57,000 could be true for some states/years but cannot be accepted as a factual general claim without specifics.

claim: Says of flood of non-Mexicans being apprehended at the border: "These are people that are coming from states like Syria that have substantial connections back to terrorist regimes and terrorist operations."
rationale: Public data and reporting do not support that the recent surge of non-Mexican apprehensions at the southern border is dominated by people from Syria or that most have substantial ties to terrorist regimes. CBP/DHS statistics show the majority of non-Mexican migrants come from Central America, the Caribbean, and Latin America, and while isolated cases of nationals from countries of concern have occurred, there is no evidence of widespread terrorist connections among these migrants.
cited_knowledge: U.S. Customs and Border Protection/DHS reporting on migrant nationalities at the southern border, media and government briefings noting majority origins are Central America/Latin America and that extremist infiltration has been rare and not widespread.
safety_notes: The claim uses vague terms like "substantial connections" and does not specify timeframe; isolated incidents can occur so verify specific cases with official DHS/Intelligence statements.

claim: "Inequality in Texas is steadily getting worse, with very few rich people, a great many poor people, and fewer and fewer in the middle."
rationale: While income inequality in Texas has increased and the share of middle-income households has declined, the claim misstates the distribution: Texas also has a large and growing population of high-income households and many very wealthy individuals. Saying there are "very few rich people" is inaccurate, and terms like "great many poor" and "steadily getting worse" are vague without specific metrics and timeframes.

claim: Cher "is moving to Canada because of President Trump."
rationale: Cher did make public comments (largely on social media) after Donald Trump’s election suggesting she might leave the U.S., but there is no reliable evidence she actually moved to Canada and many reports treat her remarks as hyperbolic or rhetorical. The claim that she "is moving to Canada because of President Trump" presents intent or a joke as an established fact about an actual relocation, which is unsupported.

claim: On Donald Trump’s plan to cut federal funding to sanctuary cities, "because of a decision by the Supreme Court, no president's in a position to cut off funding across the board. It has to be very specific to the matter at hand."
rationale: Supreme Court precedent limits a president’s ability to withhold broad federal funding unilaterally: NFIB v. Sebelius held that threatening to cut all Medicaid funds was coercive and unconstitutional, and South Dakota v. Dole requires funding conditions to be related to the program. Presidents also cannot rescind appropriations passed by Congress without statutory authority. Therefore, broad across-the-board cuts are legally constrained and any conditions must be specific and tied to the federal program at issue.

claim: Under Republican-backed state budget, the state education agency estimates expansion of Wisconsin’s school voucher program "could cost nearly $2 billion annually"
rationale: Reports from Wisconsin news outlets and the Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction during consideration of the Republican-backed budget stated DPI estimates that a statewide expansion of the voucher program could cost on the order of billions per year, commonly described as nearly $2 billion annually. The phrasing matches published DPI cost projections and media summaries of that agency's estimate.

claim: Claims that Obama said, "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reputable fact‑checking finding that Barack Obama ever said the exact line, "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away." Versions of this phrase have circulated online as misattributed or fabricated quotes, and major fact‑checking organizations have debunked similar attributions.

claim: "Hair stylists are required to undergo more government scrutiny than foreclosure consultants."
rationale: This is a jurisdiction-dependent comparison and cannot be stated universally. Both hair stylists (cosmetologists) and foreclosure consultants are regulated in many places, but the type and intensity of oversight (licensing hours, inspections, consumer‑protection rules, bonding, criminal penalties) vary widely by state or country, so it’s incorrect to claim hair stylists are categorically subject to more government scrutiny than foreclosure consultants.

claim: Says that in three legislative sessions, his proposals opening pre-kindergarten to all Texas 4-year-olds never got heard or voted out of committee.
rationale: The claim lacks identifying details (which lawmaker, bill numbers, and which three sessions) needed to verify committee actions. While many Texas bills— including pre-K expansion proposals—do die in committee, I cannot confirm that this person's proposals in three separate legislative sessions were never heard or voted out without consulting specific session records, so the claim is unverified and treated as false.

claim: "About 95 percent of (Ohio’s) electricity comes from burning coal."
rationale: Ohio has historically relied on coal but never in recent decades has coal supplied as much as 95% of the state's electricity. Federal energy data show coal's share in Ohio has generally been in the tens of percent (often roughly 40–70% in the 2000s–2010s) and has declined further as natural gas, nuclear, and renewables supply larger shares.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown "voted to block American energy production and increase energy taxes."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unqualified assertion and cannot be verified as stated. Sherrod Brown has supported clean-energy investments and some environmental regulations, but there is no single record of him voting in a way that unambiguously "blocked American energy production" or directly enacted a broad "increase [in] energy taxes." Without a specific bill or roll-call, the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "Road projects across the state are staying on track or getting done sooner thanks to the good work of the team at the Wisconsin Department of Transportation."
rationale: The claim is a broad, causal assertion about statewide project timeliness that lacks specific, verifiable metrics or a defined timeframe. Without independent data (WisDOT performance reports or audits) showing that most road projects are on schedule or earlier and attributing that outcome specifically to the DOT team, the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Over the last two years since President Obama has taken office, the federal government has added 200,000 new federal jobs."
rationale: Official employment data from OPM/BLS for the period after Obama took office do not show a net gain of 200,000 ongoing federal jobs in his first two years. Temporary spikes (notably 2010 Census hires) inflated federal payroll counts briefly, but the net change in continuing federal civilian employment was far smaller and did not amount to 200,000 new permanent federal jobs.

claim: "The reason we even have colleges is that at some point there were politicians who said, ‘You know what? We should start colleges.’ "
rationale: Colleges and universities have many origins: medieval and early institutions were often founded by churches, cathedral schools, guilds, or private benefactors, not by secular politicians. Although governments and politicians later created many state and land‑grant institutions, it is inaccurate to attribute the existence of colleges solely to politicians deciding to start them.

claim: The Milwaukee County Board’s staff grew from four workers to 38 over four decades and now costs taxpayers "a lot more," while the total county workforce was more than cut in half in the same period.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim and the statement appears to conflate different time periods and categories of employees. Public records and reporting do not clearly support a straightforward increase from 4 to 38 staff over four decades nor an across-the-board county workforce cut by more than half without additional context on job classifications, outsourced services, and time frame. The phrase 'costs taxpayers a lot more' is subjective and unquantified, making the overall claim unreliable as stated.

claim: "In a very real sense, (Oklahoma has) flattened the curve. ... The number of cases in Oklahoma — it's declined precipitously."
rationale: The claim is time-dependent and provides no date or time window; COVID-19 case counts for Oklahoma have fluctuated with multiple surges and temporary declines rather than a single sustained, precipitous fall. Without a specific timeframe and accounting for testing rates and reporting lags, the assertion that Oklahoma has definitively “flattened the curve” and that cases have “declined precipitously” cannot be verified and is misleading.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut $700 million from water management."
rationale: The claim is misleading: there is no clear, single action by Rick Scott that represents a $700 million cut to 'water management.' The figure appears to aggregate multiple budget adjustments, vetoes, and reassignments across different years and programs rather than a discrete $700 million cut; fact-checkers and budget records show spending was often restructured and at times later increased for water projects.

claim: Says former President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominations "required 60 votes."
rationale: The Constitution and Senate practice require only a simple majority to confirm a Supreme Court nominee. Before the 2013 change to Senate rules, invoking cloture to end a filibuster on nominations did require 60 votes, which likely prompts the claim—but that 60-vote cloture threshold is a procedural hurdle to end debate, not the formal confirmation requirement.

claim: Says Meghan Markle was paid $7 million for giving an interview to Oprah.
rationale: Multiple reputable fact-checkers and major news organizations found no evidence that Meghan Markle was paid $7 million for the Oprah interview. The interview was produced and broadcast by CBS/Harpo and there is no verifiable documentation or credible reporting that the couple received that payment; the $7 million number appears unsubstantiated and may confuse later, separate media deals.

claim: Agriculture contributes $71 billion to Georgia’s economy annually, making it the state’s largest industry.
rationale: State agencies and university extension analyses commonly report that Georgia agriculture contributes just over $70 billion annually to the state economy (figures often cited in the low $70s to mid $70s billion range) and these reports characterize agriculture (including food, forestry and related industries) as Georgia’s top industry by economic impact. The $71 billion figure falls within the range typically reported and the designation as the state's largest industry reflects standard state economic-impact reporting.

claim: The Republican tax bill is "not being scored by the Congressional Budget Office, as it is traditionally."
rationale: Historically major tax legislation is scored by congressional scorekeepers: the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) provides tax/revenue estimates and the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) commonly provides budgetary and macroeconomic analyses. While timing can vary and CBO may sometimes delay publication, it is incorrect as a general statement that a Republican tax bill is simply "not being scored by the CBO" as a new tradition.

claim: Terry McAuliffe "wants to raise your taxes $1,700 to pay for his infinite promises."
rationale: The claim is a vague, partisan assertion and there is no concrete evidence that Terry McAuliffe proposed a universal, fixed $1,700 tax increase per household to fund unspecified “infinite promises.” Numbers like $1,700 typically come from partisan cost estimates that depend on which policies, time period, and household income are assumed; the phrase “infinite promises” is rhetorical hyperbole. Without a specific proposal or credible nonpartisan estimate matching that exact figure for all taxpayers, the claim is misleading.

claim: Says "Every time the Legislature 'suspended' the kicker, most recently the corporate kicker in 2007, Salem spent every penny and failed to stabilize the state's revenues."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. While Oregon’s “kicker” has been suspended in some years and those funds have at times been used to shore up budgets, it is not true that every suspension resulted in Salem literally spending “every penny” or uniformly failing to stabilize state revenues; outcomes have varied and depend on broader fiscal conditions.

claim: "Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have changed their positions (on the Iraq war withdrawal) to follow Chris Dodd."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton changed their Iraq-withdrawal positions specifically to follow Chris Dodd. While Clinton shifted toward supporting a withdrawal timetable after initially voting for the 2002 authorization, and Obama advocated withdrawal timetables from his 2007 campaign, these changes are documented as their own political evolutions and not as actions taken to follow Dodd. The claim asserts a causal link that is unsupported.

claim: "An attack on a healthy 22-year-old homosexual man would be more protected under the law than an attack on an eight-year-old child."
rationale: Across most legal systems, assaults on children are treated as especially serious and trigger child-abuse statutes, mandatory reporting, and enhanced penalties; that typically affords an eight-year-old stronger statutory protections than an ordinary adult victim. While many jurisdictions also enhance penalties for crimes motivated by bias against sexual orientation, those hate-crime provisions do not generally make an assault on a healthy 22-year-old inherently 'more protected' than an assault on a child.

claim: Says George Patton said, "Politicians are the lowest form of life on earth. Liberal Democrats are the lower form of politicians."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence or reputable biography showing George S. Patton uttered that phrasing. The specific wording including “Liberal Democrats” is anachronistic (Patton died in 1945; the modern UK Liberal Democrats were formed decades later) and the line appears to be a later political fabrication or misattribution.

claim: Atlanta Tea Party co-founder Debbie Dooley "wants gas taxes raised."
rationale: Debbie Dooley is best known as a Tea Party co-founder and public advocate against tax increases and big-government solutions; there is no clear, general record that she publicly advocates raising gas taxes. The broad statement that she "wants gas taxes raised" is misleading without a specific quote or context. While she has supported some market-based environmental measures, that does not equate to a general call for higher gas taxes.

claim: Says "former Democrat Kelli Ward attacked President Trump's plans to crack down on illegal immigration, saying Trump was making a mistake."
rationale: There is no known public record of Kelli Ward — a long-time Republican and former Arizona GOP chair — attacking President Trump’s plans to crack down on illegal immigration and saying he was making a mistake. Ward has generally been aligned with Trump on immigration issues, so the specific quoted attack appears to be a misattribution or false claim.

claim: "African-Americans are more likely to be arrested by police and sentenced to longer prison terms for doing the same thing that whites do."
rationale: Multiple government reports and academic studies document that Black/African-American people are arrested at higher rates than white people and, after arrest, often receive longer or harsher sentences than white defendants for similar offenses when controlling for comparable case factors. Disparities have been observed across policing (stops and arrests), charging decisions, plea bargaining, and sentencing outcomes. The magnitude of gaps varies by crime type, jurisdiction, and specific controls, but the overall pattern is well documented.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: Missouri does not rank among the states with the highest child uninsured rates; states like Texas, Oklahoma, and Florida have consistently had much higher percentages of uninsured children. Missouri’s child uninsured rate has tended to be near or below the national average, and expansion of Medicaid (voter-approved in 2020) further reduced uninsurance.

claim: "Last year we spent more than $40 billion on highways. And Lord knows we need that. But that's more than we spent on Amtrak in its entire 40-year history."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While federal highway program obligations in a recent year have been roughly $40–50 billion, Amtrak’s cumulative federal subsidies and capital grants since its 1971 founding through about a 40-year span are also on the order of tens of billions (commonly reported around $40B+), so it is incorrect to claim a single year of highway spending clearly exceeded Amtrak’s entire 40-year total without specifying exact years and accounting definitions.

claim: Ché Guevara "wrote extensively about the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent."
rationale: Che Guevara's published writings and speeches are centered on Marxist internationalism, anti-imperialism, and solidarity with oppressed peoples rather than asserting the superiority of white Europeans. While critics sometimes cite isolated, ambiguous or paternalistic remarks from private notes or translations, there is no body of extensive writing by Guevara advocating white European superiority over people of African descent.

claim: "Breaking: Santa Fe killer expresses his love for Obama."
rationale: There is no credible reporting that the Santa Fe (Texas) school shooter publicly 'expressed his love for Obama.' Major news investigations of the Santa Fe attack did not document any such statement and instead reported other motives and materials from the shooter. The claim appears to be a misattribution or fabricated headline.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: There is no known blanket order from the White House barring all people from photographing President Biden climbing stairs. In the United States, photographing public officials in public settings is generally protected by the First Amendment, though specific credentialing, pool rules, or security-based restrictions can apply in certain locations or events.
