claim: Says Oregonians for Food and Shelter "proudly features board members from Monsanto and Syngenta and the (Oregon) Farm Bureau also receives funding from biotech companies."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and organizational disclosures indicate that Oregonians for Food and Shelter's board has included representatives employed by major agrochemical/seed firms (historically Monsanto and Syngenta), and the Oregon Farm Bureau has accepted funding or sponsorship from biotech/agriculture companies. Those industry ties have been documented in news coverage and public filings.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: This claim is not supported by labor statistics: unemployment rates for recent college graduates are typically far below 50%, even during economic downturns. While underemployment or job–major mismatch can be substantial for some cohorts and fields, that does not equate to half of all graduating students being unable to find any job.

claim: Says we could have saved ourselves the cost of building the Powell Butte water reservoir.
rationale: The claim is a speculative value judgment without supporting evidence; whether the Powell Butte reservoir expense could have been avoided depends on technical, regulatory, and public-health constraints and on what cheaper alternatives (if any) were feasible. Public water-storage and seismic-safety projects are typically driven by legal requirements, aging infrastructure and engineering assessments, so a blanket assertion that the cost could have been saved is not demonstrably true without detailed analysis.

claim: "One would have to go back more than a century to find a scenario where a president’s nominee for the Supreme Court was confirmed by the opposition party in the Senate when the vacancy occurred during an election year."
rationale: The claim asserts that you must go back more than a century to find a case where an opposition‑controlled Senate confirmed a president’s Supreme Court nominee tied to a vacancy in an election year. Historical confirmation records show exceptions in the 20th century where nominees of a president were confirmed despite the Senate being of the other party in election‑year contexts, so the blanket >100‑year statement is incorrect. The precise count depends on the strict interpretation of “vacancy occurred during an election year,” which can affect which cases qualify.

claim: "She’s voted for 60 tax increases, hurting the middle class and small businesses."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “she” is or specify which 60 votes are counted as tax increases. Determinations about how many tax-related votes a legislator cast depend on definitions (tax increases vs. votes on complex bills, procedural motions, or budget packages) and the time period, and the alleged economic harm to the middle class and small businesses is a causal assertion requiring independent economic analysis. Without specific, corroborated vote records and supporting economic evidence, the statement cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: Repeal of Obamacare would "take away health care for 10.3 million Americans" who have received coverage since Oct. 1, 2013.
rationale: The 10.3 million figure matches HHS-reported marketplace enrollments during the first ACA open-enrollment period beginning Oct 1, 2013, but saying repeal would 'take away health care for 10.3 million Americans' is misleading. Repeal would eliminate marketplace plans and subsidies that enabled many enrollments, but it would not automatically strip coverage from every one of those enrollees (some have employer-sponsored or Medicaid coverage, and effects depend on legislative details and transition rules).

claim: "Hillary Clinton killed in monster truck mishap."
rationale: There are no credible reports, official statements, or major news coverage confirming Hillary Clinton was killed in any incident, and such a high-profile death would be widely reported. Claims like this have circulated as misinformation and hoaxes on social media rather than based on verifiable evidence.

claim: "Why would our president close the embassy to the Vatican? Hopefully, it is not retribution for Catholic organizations opposing Obamacare."
rationale: There is no evidence that the U.S. closed its embassy to the Holy See; the United States maintains diplomatic relations with the Vatican and operates an embassy to the Holy See in Rome. The suggestion that a president closed it as retribution for Catholic organizations opposing the Affordable Care Act is speculative and unsupported by documented actions or official statements.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted himself health care for life."
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Steve Southerland cast a vote that singularly gave himself "health care for life." Members of Congress participate in the Federal Employees Health Benefits program and may receive retiree coverage if they meet normal age/service requirements, but that is not a special lifetime benefit newly granted by a single vote he cast. Advertisements claiming he "voted himself health care for life" have been characterized as misleading.

claim: Says David Perdue wants to abolish the U.S. Department of Education, which would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans.
rationale: While David Perdue has publicly supported eliminating or rolling back the U.S. Department of Education in past statements, the claim that abolishing the department "would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans" is misleading. Federal education dollars to Georgia are substantial and could total around a billion depending on which programs are counted, but that number is an estimate and would depend on what replaces or reallocates those programs. Abolishing the department would not automatically erase existing federal student loan obligations — loans are federal obligations that would likely be transferred or managed differently, not simply eliminated.

claim: President Joe Biden will "control health care costs by slapping a 95% tax on prescription drugs."
rationale: There is no public Biden administration proposal or enacted law that imposes a blanket 95% tax on prescription drugs. Biden's health policy and the Inflation Reduction Act focus on Medicare drug price negotiation, caps on certain out‑of‑pocket costs, and penalties/refunds for unjustified price increases rather than a 95% across‑the‑board tax.

claim: Says Joe Biden stayed silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests.
rationale: This claim is false as stated. Joe Biden repeatedly spoke about the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, publicly condemning violence and looting while also expressing support for peaceful protest and calling for policing reforms; he made statements, speeches, and released press comments on these events. Critics sometimes argued his responses were insufficiently forceful in tone, but he did not remain silent.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that a specific Mizzou graduate-insurance problem was an inevitable or direct result of the Affordable Care Act; campus insurance disruptions are more commonly caused by university administrative decisions, contract/plan design, or state regulatory details. The assertion that Mizzou 'has to break the law to do the right thing' is unsupported — universities generally have legal avenues (plan changes, waivers, negotiations) to address coverage problems without illegal action.

claim: Student loans from the federal government issued between 2007 and 2012 are on target "to produce $66 billion in profits for the United States government."
rationale: The $66 billion number is a disputed, accounting-dependent projection rather than an established fact. Estimates of net profits or losses for federal student loans vary widely depending on whether one uses federal credit reform accounting or fair-value accounting and on assumptions about interest rates and defaults; CBO/GAO analyses do not unambiguously support a $66 billion guaranteed profit for the 2007–2012 cohorts.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "opposes faster broadband internet in small towns" and "got nearly $90,000 in campaign contributions from the telecom special interests."
rationale: The claim is a misleading summary of a nuanced record: Sen. Johnson has criticized federal broadband subsidies and voted against some broadband-related bills, but characterizing that as a blanket opposition to "faster broadband in small towns" misstates his stated preference for private-sector solutions. The specific contribution figure ("nearly $90,000") is not verifiable without a stated time period; industry contributions to his campaigns exist but the exact total requires checking campaign finance records.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: I am not aware of reliable, widely reported evidence showing that Rep. John Culberson was definitively caught using campaign funds to buy collectibles such as Civil War memorabilia and fossils. Public reporting and available campaign finance disclosures do not show a clear, substantiated finding of criminal misuse of campaign cash for personal collectible purchases.

claim: That Donald Trump said in 1998 if he were to run for president he would run as a Republican because "They’re the dumbest group of voters in the country. They believe anything on Fox News. I could lie and they’d still eat it up. I bet my numbers would be terrific."
rationale: There is no credible contemporaneous source—no verifiable audio, video, or reliable news report from 1998—showing Trump made this statement. Multiple fact-checking organizations have searched archives and found the quote appears to be fabricated or misattributed rather than traceable to a documented 1998 remark.

claim: Says a car driving former University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe "ran through the students, hit one of them" at the MU Homecoming Parade.
rationale: Contemporary news reports and police statements from the 2015 MU homecoming incident do not corroborate that a car driven by then-University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe ran through students and struck one. Eyewitness accounts conflicted, video evidence and police records showed no confirmed injuries and no charges were filed for hitting a student.

claim: "The stock market does better when you have a Democratic president in the White House."
rationale: While some historical analyses show average stock returns have been higher during Democratic presidencies over certain multi-decade periods, this is a correlation that varies by time frame and index and does not prove causation. Many other factors (economic cycles, monetary policy, global events, and start/end dates) drive market performance, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Says President Donald Trump's "effort to roll back regulations means that Big Ag now gets to inspect its own pork" and "they decided to stop testing for E. coli."
rationale: The claim overstates and misstates policy changes. The Trump-era USDA adopted a New Swine Inspection System that shifted some tasks to plant employees and allowed higher line speeds in qualifying facilities, but federal inspectors and FSIS oversight remained in place — it did not turn inspection responsibility entirely over to industry. Likewise, USDA/FSIS changed aspects of its testing and verification programs (notably adjustments around some non‑O157 STEC testing and sampling procedures), but it did not categorically stop all E. coli testing or remove regulatory responsibility for pathogenic E. coli such as E. coli O157:H7.

claim: Says Ted Cruz’s father "was with Lee Harvey Oswald" before the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rafael Cruz (Ted Cruz’s father) was ever with Lee Harvey Oswald prior to JFK’s assassination. The allegation circulated as an internet rumor and has been investigated and debunked by multiple fact-checkers and by reviews of Oswald’s known movements; no corroborating eyewitnesses or documents link the two men.

claim: This year’s state budget and my spending proposal for Fiscal Year 2016 represent an infusion of more than $1 billion in additional money for K-12 education.
rationale: The statement is time- and speaker-specific but gives no state or author, so it cannot be verified as presented. Whether a combined state budget and a FY2016 proposal added more than $1 billion to K–12 depends entirely on the particular state, accounting conventions, and budget documents. Without those specifics and supporting budget figures, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on gun control.
rationale: Mitt Romney’s public statements and policy positions on guns have changed over time—he took more moderate or regulatory stances while in Massachusetts and shifted to more pro-gun, GOP-aligned positions during his presidential campaigns. Media outlets, critics, and fact-checkers have documented these shifts and characterized them as a flip-flop.

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The statement conflates two different claims. While Texas Governor Rick Perry began his early political career as a Democrat before switching parties, he did not work as Al Gore’s campaign manager — Gore’s national campaigns were run by other staff and prominent Democratic operatives, not Rick Perry.

claim: The debt ceiling deal will result in "the lowest level of annual domestic spending since Dwight Eisenhower was president."
rationale: The statement is incorrect: the debt ceiling deal mainly limits discretionary spending caps and does not cut total annual domestic spending to Eisenhower-era levels. Total federal domestic outlays (including mandatory programs like Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid) remain far higher than in the 1950s in both nominal and inflation-adjusted terms, and most reporting about the deal described modest caps rather than a return to 1950s spending.

claim: "45.6 million people watched (the State of the Union), the highest number in history. @FoxNews beat every other Network, for the first time ever, with 11.7 million people tuning in."
rationale: Contemporary Nielsen and press reports showed the State of the Union audience was lower than 45.6 million when measured on television and that number was not the highest in history once prior SOTU and joint addresses and multiplatform totals are considered. While Fox News drew a large cable audience (reports around the low-to-mid millions), it has topped other networks for some SOTUs before, so the claim of 11.7 million being a first-ever network win is misleading.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: In the United States, violent crime broadly declined from the early 1990s through the 2010s, and federal and CDC data show a notable uptick beginning in 2020. Homicide counts and rates jumped sharply around 2020–2021; comparing 2019 to 2021 shows an increase exceeding 20% in the homicide rate, consistent with official crime-statistics reporting for that period.

claim: Says taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel jumped $100 million in closed-door sessions
rationale: I cannot corroborate that taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel 'jumped $100 million' as a confirmed outcome of closed-door sessions. Local reporting and public records I am aware of discussed subsidies and closed-session negotiations, but I find no reliable source confirming a $100 million increase disclosed from those sessions. Given the lack of verifiable evidence, the claim is judged false.

claim: Says "in Katrina, they approved $60 billion within 10 days of the storm on a voice vote."
rationale: Congress did not approve a single $60 billion package by voice vote within ten days of Hurricane Katrina. In the immediate days after the storm Congress passed much smaller emergency supplements (on the order of $10–12 billion) and the larger multi‑billion relief packages (totaling around $60 billion over time) were enacted later and involved multiple measures and formal procedures rather than a single voice vote within ten days.

claim: Says "some people in the Great State of North Carolina have been sent TWO BALLOTS. RIGGED ELECTION in waiting!"
rationale: While there have been isolated cases in North Carolina and other states where administrative or mailing errors caused some voters to receive duplicate ballots, those incidents were reported as mistakes and addressed by election officials. There is no credible evidence that these isolated mailings constitute a coordinated, statewide 'rigged' election as the claim asserts.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Major national polls consistently show a minority of Republicans approve of the Affordable Care Act as a whole, so an unqualified claim that 74% of Republicans support the ACA is incorrect. Polls do, however, often find large Republican majorities supporting specific ACA provisions (for example, protections for preexisting conditions), which can make such statements misleading without context.

claim: "There were 36 states where Republicans who were in charge refused to implement a state (health insurance) exchange."
rationale: While roughly 34–36 states ultimately relied on the federal ACA marketplace rather than creating their own exchange, it is incorrect to say there were 36 states where Republicans 'in charge' refused to implement a state exchange. The count of states using the federal exchange depends on timing and definitions (federal vs. partnership), and many of those states did not have unified Republican control or had Democratic officials who also declined to create a state exchange. Therefore the claim overstates both the partisan uniformity and a precise fixed number.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: I find no corroborating public records or credible reporting that Gerald Daugherty advocated reducing penalties for strangulation in domestic violence cases or uttered the quoted phrase; the claim appears unverified and likely a misattribution. A specific quote like that would typically be documented in news reports or official transcripts, which are absent in known sources.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The claim lacks any date or data source, so it cannot be verified as a timeless fact. COVID case trends fluctuate regionally and over time, and whether Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline" depends on a specific recent time window and metrics (cases, test positivity, hospitalizations). Without that context and current official surveillance data, the statement is not verifiable.

claim: If Missouri Amendment 1 passes, the auditor's office "could take one district, St. Louis here, and merge it with a district in southwest Missouri, a Republican district, and they don't even have to touch."
rationale: The claim overstates what a Missouri constitutional amendment would allow: redistricting authority is constrained by state law and constitutional requirements (including contiguity and equal population), and the state auditor does not gain unilateral power to splice noncontiguous parts of distant districts together. Even when courts or special officials enter mapmaking, they must follow redistricting standards and legal procedures, so the scenario of simply merging a St. Louis district with a distant southwest Missouri district without regard to contiguity or other rules is not supported.

claim: "The permission to engage was given before the word RPG was ever used."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific temporal ordering but provides no event, source, or evidence to verify that permission preceded the utterance of the word "RPG." Without a transcript, timestamped recording, or authoritative timeline, the claim cannot be substantiated. Absent supporting documentation, treating the assertion as false is appropriate.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The claim is categorical but provides no document or context ('here' is undefined), so it cannot be verified. Historically and practically, many pieces of legislation, regulations, or agreements include provisions that can substantially affect or advantage large Wall Street banks, so a blanket statement that none do is unjustified without the specific text.

claim: "If you’re a low-wage worker and you’re single and don’t have children, we’re literally taxing you into poverty."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. Whether a low-wage single childless worker falls below the poverty line after taxes depends on the country, wage level, hours worked, and available credits or benefits; payroll and income taxes can reduce take-home pay but do not universally push all such workers into poverty. In some cases (very low hours or very low pay) taxes can contribute to poverty-level disposable income, but many low-wage single workers remain above the poverty threshold after taxes and may receive offsets like tax credits or benefits.

claim: "U.S. teenagers have now fallen behind their counterparts in Ireland, Poland and even Vietnam in math and science."
rationale: International assessment results (notably OECD PISA in recent cycles) show U.S. students scoring below peers in countries such as Ireland, Poland and Vietnam in math and science, so the claim that U.S. teenagers have fallen behind those counterparts is supported by those comparisons. Vietnam in particular has outperformed the U.S. on recent PISA administrations.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate "is proposing the universal registration of all firearms and their owners."
rationale: No major recent Senate gun bill publicly introduced has proposed a legally defined, universal registry of every firearm and every owner; most proposals focus on expanded background checks, reporting requirements, funding for enforcement, or targeted measures (e.g., red flag laws). Opponents often describe certain record-keeping or background-check databases as 'registration,' but the legislative text typically does not create a comprehensive universal registry of all guns and owners.

claim: Says Texas "high school graduation rates are at all-time highs."
rationale: The statement lacks a specific timeframe; while Texas graduation rates have risen in recent years and the Texas Education Agency has reported record or near-record rates for particular cohorts, I cannot verify that they are currently or universally at 'all-time highs' without the latest official year-by-year data. Because the claim is ambiguous and depends on the specific year referenced, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "Two million more people just dropped out of Obamacare. It is in a death spiral."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that 'two million more people just dropped out' of the ACA marketplaces in a single recent change, and independent enrollment and policy analyses through 2023–2024 show marketplace enrollment was broadly stable or increased after expanded subsidies. Policy experts and insurers have not found the markets to be in a "death spiral"; premiums, insurer participation, and enrollment have generally stabilized after legislative and administrative measures.

claim: Says professional football coach Rex Ryan "won championships in New York. The AFC, I think, twice."
rationale: Rex Ryan did not win AFC conference championships in New York twice. His New York Jets reached the AFC Championship Game after the 2009 and 2010 seasons but lost both games, so he never won the AFC title as Jets head coach.

claim: "Most of Ted Cruz’s money comes from Washington, from outside the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while Ted Cruz has raised substantial national (out-of-state) campaign dollars, Federal Election Commission reporting and media analyses show a large share of his fundraising comes from Texas donors and from national networks rather than predominantly from "Washington" specifically. Without a clear timeframe or definition of “money” (personal income vs. campaign receipts) there is no basis to say most of his money comes from Washington or outside Texas as an absolute fact.

claim: President Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid support Rick Perry’s "decision to give in-state tuition to illegal immigrants."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that President Obama, Nancy Pelosi, and Harry Reid explicitly endorsed a particular decision by Rick Perry to grant in-state tuition to undocumented students. While the three Democrats have generally supported federal measures like the DREAM Act or policies expanding tuition access for undocumented students, that is not the same as publicly backing a specific action by Perry; presenting it that way is misleading.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: The claim is overly broad: whether a single-parent family working full time at the minimum wage lives in poverty depends on the exact current minimum wage, household size (number and ages of children), hours worked, taxes, and any public benefits or tax credits. Some single-parent households in New Jersey earning the state minimum could fall below federal or state poverty thresholds, but others—especially with higher state minimums or additional income/benefits—may be above the poverty line.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The claim is vague and not supported as a universal fact: insurer profits have varied widely by country, sector, and time period, and there is no consistent industry-wide increase of more than 400% since 2001. Public financial records and industry reports show volatility (early‑2000s, 2008 crisis, low interest rates) with some firms or segments experiencing large gains but many others not matching a 400% rise.

claim: "We borrow $4 billion every single day, much of it from China."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while the U.S. deficit in some recent years has equated to several billion dollars per day on average, the exact '$4 billion every single day' is an oversimplification and not a precise constant. Moreover, most new Treasury borrowing is financed by domestic investors and institutions; China holds well under a trillion dollars of U.S. Treasuries and does not supply 'much' of daily U.S. borrowing.

claim: Figures for September 2014’s job growth in Wisconsin mark the "largest private-sector job creation we've had in the month of September in more than a decade"
rationale: I cannot confirm from available knowledge that September 2014 was the single largest private‑sector September gain in over a decade for Wisconsin. Verifying the claim requires checking the state or BLS monthly private‑sector employment series back to at least September 2004; monthly job-change figures are volatile and subject to revision, so such a superlative claim is not reliably supportable without that data.

claim: The Wisconsin state Assembly chambers extend to the bathroom and the parlor, and rules allow members to vote for each other if the member is in the chambers.
rationale: This claim misstates Wisconsin practice. Wisconsin Assembly rules require members to be physically present at their assigned seat to cast a vote (the electronic system and rules do not permit one member to press the vote for another), and while there have been disputes about what areas count as 'in the chamber' for quorum purposes, ordinary bathrooms or private parlors are not automatically treated as part of the legislative floor for voting.

claim: Early morning election results from Michigan and Wisconsin show voter fraud.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that early-morning changes in vote totals in Michigan and Wisconsin constitute voter fraud. State election officials, bipartisan audits and recounts, and courts found no widespread fraud in recent contested elections, and late-night/early-morning swings are routinely explained by normal reporting of absentee and mail ballots.

claim: "People (are) paying more in taxes than they will for food, housing and clothing combined."
rationale: The claim is presented as a universal statement but gives no country, time period, or definition of "taxes" or the population referenced. Tax liabilities and household spending patterns vary widely by country, income level, and definitions, and it is not generally true that taxes exceed the combined outlays for food, housing, and clothing for most people. Without specific context or data this broad claim is unsupported.

claim: "The average life expectancy for African Americans in Saint Louis and Saint Louis County varies by as much as 18 years compared to the white population, with nearly half of all African-American kids under the age of 18 living in poverty."
rationale: Multiple local health analyses and reporting have documented life-expectancy differences of roughly 15–20 years between predominantly Black neighborhoods in the City of St. Louis and predominantly white neighborhoods in the St. Louis region, commonly cited as an 18-year gap. U.S. Census/ACS-based poverty statistics for the area also show extremely high child poverty among African-American households — often reported as nearly half of Black children living under the poverty line in parts of the city/region.

claim: New York is "leading the nation with the lowest imprisonment rate of any large state"
rationale: The claim is too broad and misleading: while New York has reduced its incarceration rate and is relatively low compared with many large states, other states (and some comparably sized states such as New Jersey or smaller states like Massachusetts and Maine) have had equal or lower imprisonment rates depending on the year and measure. Whether New York 'leads the nation' depends on the specific metric, year, and definition of 'large state', which the claim omits.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The statement that the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (OCC) office employs 74 lawyers is not supported by commonly available information; OCC is a relatively small state consumer-advocacy agency and publicly reported attorney headcounts have been much lower. The claim that funding them is “wasteful duplication” is a normative judgment, not an objective fact and cannot be verified as true or false without policy criteria and comparison to specific alternatives.

claim: Says New Hampshire had the fourth-lowest unemployment rate in the country during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state Senate.
rationale: Maggie Hassan served in the New Hampshire State Senate from 2004 to 2010, but state unemployment rankings change monthly and year-to-year. The claim gives no specific date, and available historical data show New Hampshire’s rank fluctuated during that period rather than consistently being exactly fourth-lowest. Without a precise timepoint and source, the assertion as stated cannot be verified.

claim: Supported in-state tuition in Arkansas for illegal immigrants "if you'd sat in our schools from the time you're 5 or 6 years old and you had become an A-plus student," among other things.
rationale: I cannot verify that a named Arkansas official publicly supported in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants using the quoted line; there is no clear, attributable source for that exact phrasing in major reporting or fact-checking. Arkansas law and debates on in-state tuition for undocumented students are specific and contested, so an un-attributed quotation cannot be treated as factual without corroboration.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: This line is widely attributed to Ayn Rand in quote collections, but there is no clear, verifiable primary-source citation in her published novels or essays showing she wrote or spoke it verbatim. Without a reliable source in her known works, the attribution is likely a misquote or later paraphrase rather than a confirmed Rand quotation.

claim: The debt is "nearly $6 trillion more than when President Obama was sworn into office."
rationale: The statement is misleading without a date; U.S. federal debt at Obama’s inauguration (Jan 2009) was roughly $10.6 trillion, and since then the total federal debt has risen by much more than $6 trillion over the following years. Depending on the cutoff date the increase is measured to, the rise is on the order of tens of trillions of dollars, not “nearly $6 trillion.”

claim: Insurance companies "have made a fortune with Obamacare."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While some large insurers and certain years saw substantial revenue and profits linked to the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplaces and expanded coverage, many insurers experienced losses early on and overall financial outcomes have varied widely by company, state, and year rather than uniformly producing large windfalls for the industry.

claim: "Most of these killers tend to be 18, 19 years old."
rationale: The statement is too vague and unsupported: it does not define what category or population 'these killers' refers to, and available criminological data do not show that a majority of killers are aged 18–19. Age distributions for homicide, mass shootings, and serial killings vary widely and typically include adults across a broader age range rather than concentrating at 18–19.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it does not specify the jurisdiction, the date Mark Sharpe took office, or whether the 18% refers to nominal tax rates, average bills, or assessed values adjusted for inflation. Without local tax records or a cited source, the precise 18% figure is unsupported and likely misleading.

claim: As Massachusetts governor, Mitt Romney used a line-item veto to cut "millions of dollars for firefighting equipment," including firefighters' "coats, pants, helmets and boots."
rationale: While Governor Romney used his line-item veto power and did cut or reduce some legislative earmarks—including a small number of items intended for fire departments—there is no clear evidence he eliminated 'millions of dollars' specifically for firefighters' coats, pants, helmets and boots as claimed. Contemporary news reports and fact-checking found the assertion exaggerated: some vetoes were for targeted grants/earmarks and many funding items were subsequently restored or were not for mass personal protective equipment purchases.

claim: "We've got 7.2 percent unemployment (in Ohio), but when you include the folks who have stopped looking for work, it's actually over 10 percent."
rationale: The statement gives no date and presents a time‑specific statistic as general fact. The official unemployment rate (U‑3) can be 7.2% at times, and a broader measure (U‑6) that includes discouraged and marginally attached workers is generally higher and can exceed 10% in some months, but that is not universally true for Ohio—whether it is over 10% depends on the specific month and year.

claim: An email from Hillary Clinton to Donna Brazile Oct.17th, 2016 stated: "If that f-----’ bastard wins, we’re all going to hang from nooses! You better fix this s---!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or authenticated release of Hillary Clinton’s emails showing that she wrote this quote to Donna Brazile on October 17, 2016. Such an inflammatory statement does not appear in the publicly available Clinton/DNC/Podesta email archives and has been debunked by fact-checkers and contemporaneous reporting.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: The statement mixes different measures and is misleading. While overall violent-crime rates in the U.S. remain well below their peak in the early 1990s, there were notable increases (especially homicides) around 2020–2021, so rates are not uniformly at historic lows across all measures and years. Gun availability (total number of firearms and recent purchases) is at or near record highs, but household or adult gun‑ownership rates by some surveys are not clearly higher than past decades; thus the paired claim as stated is not fully supported.

claim: Says "Rep. Jim Weidner proposed a bill taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children."
rationale: There is no record of an Oregon legislator named Jim Weidner proposing a bill to strip health care from 80,000 Oregon children; the name appears misattributed and such a large cut to children's coverage would have been widely reported. Changes to children's health coverage in Oregon are typically enacted through the state budget or federal Medicaid/CHIP policy, not a single privately framed bill without public notice.

claim: The STAR Ohio fund "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely misleading: whether STAR Ohio has the “highest possible credit rating” depends on which rating agency and which rating scale is meant, and the statement’s wording (“just received”) gives no date to confirm a recent action. Historically STAR Ohio has held top short‑term ratings from some agencies, but without specifying the agency and timing the blanket claim cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: "We work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese."
rationale: The claim is false: many countries in the industrialized world (and near-industrialized OECD members) report higher average annual working hours than the United States, and Japan, while known for long hours, is not the single longest. International data from organizations tracking average hours worked show several countries exceed the US on typical metrics.

claim: "Today and every day, an estimated 14,000 Americans will lose their health insurance coverage."
rationale: There is no authoritative, consistent statistic showing exactly 14,000 Americans lose coverage every single day. That figure appears to be a back-of-the-envelope derived by dividing certain annual estimates by 365; in reality rates of insurance loss vary by year, program (Medicaid vs employer vs individual), and include temporary “churn” versus permanent uninsured status.

claim: "Wisconsin is not as obese as the national average is. The national average, 35.7 percent of the population is obese. In Wisconsin, it's closer to 26 percent."
rationale: The claim understates national adult obesity and Wisconsin’s rate. Recent CDC measured estimates put U.S. adult obesity well above 35.7% (around 40–42% in recent multi-year estimates), and state-level BRFSS/self-report data generally place Wisconsin’s adult obesity in the low-to-mid 30 percent range, not about 26%.

claim: Says Jeff Foxworthy wrote a ‘fence test’ for Republicans and Democrats.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that comedian Jeff Foxworthy authored a widely recognized 'fence test' for Republicans and Democrats. Foxworthy is best known for his 'You might be a redneck' material, and the viral 'fence test' meme has not been credibly attributed to him in news archives or reputable sources and appears to be misattributed online.

claim: Georgia has saved $20 million through changes in criminal sentencing.
rationale: The claim is underspecified (does not state which 'Georgia' or which reforms and time period) and I cannot verify a widely reported, specific $20 million savings tied directly to sentencing changes. Reports on criminal justice reforms in the U.S. state of Georgia and in the country of Georgia describe various cost impacts and projections, but I am not aware of a definitive, sourced figure of exactly $20 million attributable to sentencing changes. Without a clear source and context the claim is unverified.

claim: There are "360,000 (deaths) a year from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that."
rationale: The figure is much higher than reliable estimates: the WHO reports roughly 200–240 thousand global drowning deaths per year (all settings), and deaths specifically in swimming pools are only a small fraction of that total. Therefore the claim that 360,000 people die annually from swimming pools is not supported by available data. The policy comment about not shutting the country down is an opinion and not a factual correction of the numeric error.

claim: "Russia has more diversity in its governmental representation than we do in Texas."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: Russia’s political institutions are dominated by a single party and a narrow political elite with constrained opposition, whereas Texas — while imperfect — elects officials across multiple parties and includes visible racial and ethnic minority and gender representation at many levels. Without a clear metric for “diversity in governmental representation,” there is no basis to conclude Russia is more diverse than Texas, and available evidence about Russian political centralization makes the claim unlikely.

claim: Bill Nelson’s vote for the Affordable Care Act "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
rationale: The ACA was estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to reduce projected Medicare spending by roughly $500 billion over a decade, but those were reductions in projected payments (e.g., to Medicare Advantage plans and providers) and slowing of spending growth, not direct cuts to Medicare benefits. The savings were used for a mix of purposes including deficit reduction and funding coverage expansions, so characterizing Nelson’s vote as simply "cutting $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs" is misleading.

claim: Federal spending is "the highest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years (and) revenue is the lowest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years."
rationale: This is misleading. Federal outlays did surge during the COVID-era, and receipts fell, but historical GDP-series show much higher spending shares in the WWII era and comparable spikes in earlier decades; likewise revenues fell sharply in 2009 (and other recession years) producing receipt/GDP ratios as low or lower than recent years. Whether the claim is true depends on the exact year and the specific series (unified budget vs on-/off-budget, fiscal year choice), so the blanket 60-year assertion is not supported without precise definitions.

claim: "As we watch the news from Colorado with horror and sympathy for the families, we should remember that each day more than 80 Americans are killed by gunfire, unnecessary tragedies."
rationale: Federal vital-statistics data show roughly 40,000–50,000 firearm deaths per year in recent years, which translates to well over 80 deaths per day, so the claim is supported. Note that those totals include suicides, homicides, unintentional shootings, and legal intervention deaths.

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no public record that Sen. Sherrod Brown promised the first COVID‑era stimulus bill would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. The first major stimulus (the CARES Act) focused on pandemic relief and did not include project‑specific funding for that bridge; Brown later supported seeking federal infrastructure funds for the bridge in subsequent legislation.

claim: Says Barack Obama "robbed Medicare (of) $716 billion to pay for ... Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included provisions that the Congressional Budget Office and Medicare actuary scored as roughly $716 billion in net Medicare savings over a 2010–2019 window, but those were projected reductions in future Medicare spending (largely lower payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans), not an unlawful 'robbery' of Medicare funds. Some of the projected savings were used on the score to help offset the cost of coverage expansions and reduce the deficit, so describing it as "robbing Medicare" is misleading about the mechanism and legality of the changes.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: This is a misleading exaggeration. The Biden-era nominee most often cited (Saule Omarova) proposed shifting core deposit-taking functions to a Federal Reserve-run platform to reduce systemic risk, not an explicit call to abolish all private bank accounts; she also said banks could continue to offer services. Multiple fact-checks and her Senate testimony show opponents’ phrasing distorted her academic proposals.

claim: "Newspapers have framed this election as my fight against the Illinois mafia."
rationale: The claim is a broad, general statement about how newspapers framed an unspecified election and lacks any specified time, person, or cited outlets. Media coverage and framing vary widely across newspapers; without evidence that a consensus of newspapers described the race as a fight 'against the Illinois mafia,' the assertion cannot be verified. Some individual pieces might have used confrontational language, but that does not support the universal claim.

claim: "There are no tax increases in this debt limit bill. Period."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about an unspecified "debt limit bill," which cannot be verified and is likely false because some debt-limit or budget-reconciliation packages have included revenue changes, fees, or offsets that effectively raise government receipts. Even if a particular bill contains no explicit headline income-tax rate increases, it may include tax-related provisions, fee hikes, or compliance measures that increase net revenue. Therefore the blanket "Period" assertion is unreliable without specifying the exact legislation.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim is likely false because U.S. super PAC fundraising totals in recent election cycles are typically much larger than $180 million and the exact breakdowns by donor type vary by cycle and reporting source. While a small number of very wealthy donors do often supply a large share of super PAC money, the specific figures (half from fewer than 200 people and ~20% from corporations) do not match standard FEC/analyst summaries and the statement gives no timeframe or data source.

claim: Between 40 and 50 percent of tax filers do not owe any income tax.
rationale: Multiple analyses of recent U.S. federal tax data show that roughly 40–50% of tax units/tax filers had zero net federal income tax liability in several recent years, largely due to low taxable incomes and refundable credits (e.g., EITC and Child Tax Credit). The exact percentage varies by year and by the population definition, but the stated range matches reputable estimates for recent periods.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: The claim is false: multiple studies and major public‑health agencies report that wearing cloth, surgical, or properly fitted medical masks does not cause clinically meaningful reductions in blood oxygen (SpO2) or dangerous rises in CO2 for the general public. While some individuals with severe, acute respiratory failure or specific medical conditions may find masks uncomfortable or intolerable and should follow medical advice, there is no evidence that routine mask use will 'kill quite a few people.'

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines contain tracking nanoparticles designed to be located by 5G networks. Authorized vaccine ingredient lists and regulatory reviews show components like mRNA (or viral vectors), lipids, salts and stabilizers, not electronic or powered tracking devices. Physically, 5G is a radio communications system and cannot remotely detect inert nanoparticles inside a person's body, nor could inert lipid nanoparticles act as transmitters without an internal power source and electronics.

claim: Perpetrators of school shootings "have been drugged in many cases … many of these young boys have been on Ritalin since they were in kindergarten."
rationale: The statement generalizes without evidence: investigations and academic reviews do not show that a majority of school shooters were "drugged" or put on Ritalin from kindergarten. Medication histories of perpetrators are mixed — some were never medicated, some received other psychiatric drugs, and a few had stimulant prescriptions — but there is no reliable evidence that many were continuously on Ritalin from early childhood or that this is a common pattern.

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: There is no evidence that six states collectively 'decided to stop counting' votes to freeze a favorable result for Donald Trump on election night. Election officials and jurisdictions continued counting ballots after polls closed (and in many places for days afterward), and any temporary pauses were procedural (e.g., end-of-day processing, poll closings, or rules about late-arriving ballots) rather than a coordinated halt to secure a win.

claim: "People were hopeless. Sixty percent of the population, 70 percent of the population wanted to live somewhere else. . . . By the time I left, 70 percent wanted to stay."
rationale: The quote asserts precise shifts in public sentiment with specific percentages but provides no source, timeframe, population, or poll methodology. Claims about opinion majorities require verifiable polling data; without named surveys or corroborating evidence the numbers cannot be confirmed. Therefore the statement is unsubstantiated and should be treated as false/unverified.

claim: "However, it took $19.5 million in Oregon Lottery funds for the Port of Newport to eventually land the new NOAA Marine Operations Center-Pacific."
rationale: Public accounts and government funding summaries show the NOAA Marine Operations Center–Pacific was financed primarily through federal NOAA funding together with Port of Newport financing and local contributions; there is no clear authoritative record that the project required or was paid for by exactly $19.5 million in Oregon Lottery funds. The specific $19.5 million lottery- funds figure does not appear in primary budget or reporting on the facility, so the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: In Sauk City, Wisconsin, "the ID office" that provides identification for voting "is only open on the fifth Wednesday of every month" -- a total of four days in 2016.
rationale: While 2016 did have four months with a fifth Wednesday (March, June, August, November), the claim that Sauk City’s “ID office” is open only on those days is not supported by standard practice or available local-office scheduling: municipal clerk offices and state DMV services normally maintain regular weekly hours or provide alternative locations and appointment options for issuing IDs. Without specific, contemporaneous evidence showing the office was legally or practically limited to only four annual days, the blanket claim is false.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act added a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, but it applies only to certain net investment income (including some capital gains) for taxpayers above income thresholds, not to every home sale. Proceeds from the sale of a primary residence are often excluded up to $250,000/$500,000 under existing tax rules, and investment-property sales can be subject to different rules.

claim: Says Amazon has removed "an educational game about Gettysburg."
rationale: There is no verifiable, specific reporting that 'Amazon removed an educational game about Gettysburg' as a general fact. The claim lacks critical details (which Amazon service, game title, and timing), and I cannot find corroborating evidence in major news or platform-removal reports to support it.

claim: Says Jennifer Aniston said, "Me and all the Trump supporter celebrities decide to make a company named ‘celebrities for Trump’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence Jennifer Aniston ever said that; public records and interviews show she has criticized Donald Trump and supported Democratic candidates. The quoted line appears to be a fabricated or satirical social-media claim inconsistent with her known public statements.

claim: "BREAKING: Trump family donates $1 billion to wall fund."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that the Trump family donated $1 billion to any wall fund; a gift of that size would be publicly disclosed and widely reported. Public campaign finance records and major news outlets show no such donation and prior contributions to border-wall efforts have been far smaller.

claim: "Obama admits he is not a citizen."
rationale: Barack Obama has never admitted he is not a U.S. citizen; he was born in Honolulu, Hawaii, and has produced a certified birth certificate and contemporaneous birth announcements. Claims that he admitted non-citizenship stem from misinterpretations or debunked 'birther' allegations and selective quoting. Multiple official records and court rulings have affirmed his U.S. citizenship.

claim: "Hillary Clinton leaves the country as Mueller indictment is announced."
rationale: There was no Mueller indictment charging Hillary Clinton, and credible news outlets did not report that she left the country in response to any Mueller announcement. The Mueller probe indicted others (e.g., Manafort, Flynn, Stone) and issued a report, but did not produce an indictment of Clinton or documented flight from the U.S.

claim: "Despite what you may have heard about Wisconsin’s finances, Wisconsin is on track to have a budget surplus this year."
rationale: The claim is time-sensitive and gives no specific year; I cannot verify current-year budget outcomes past my June 2024 knowledge cutoff. State budget balances depend on up-to-date revenue and expenditure forecasts that change frequently, so without current official reports I cannot confirm Wisconsin is "on track" for a surplus this year.

claim: "They (Clinton and Obama) have never to my knowledge been involved in legislation nor hearings nor engagement on this issue (climate change)."
rationale: The claim is false: both Barack Obama and members of the Clinton family (notably Hillary Clinton) have been actively involved in climate policy. Obama as President led major federal climate initiatives (for example the Clean Power Plan and U.S. engagement in the Paris Agreement) and worked with agencies and Congress on climate matters; Hillary Clinton as Senator and as Secretary of State participated in legislative debates, policy proposals, and international climate negotiations.

claim: Says former Clinton budget director Alice Rivlin said the stimulus bill "won't actually stimulate the economy."
rationale: I find no clear evidence that Alice Rivlin, former Clinton budget director, uttered the specific line 'won't actually stimulate the economy.' While Rivlin publicly critiqued aspects of stimulus proposals (arguing for better targeting, speed, or fiscal responsibility), reporting shows she generally acknowledged that stimulus could have some short-term effects rather than flatly claiming it would not stimulate at all. The precise quoted claim appears to be a mischaracterization or out-of-context paraphrase.

claim: "To children and the vast majority of young and middle-aged adults and the vast majority of teachers, (the coronavirus) poses virtually zero threat."
rationale: COVID-19 risk is lower on average for children and many younger adults than for older adults, but it is not zero: some children and substantial numbers of young and middle-aged adults have required hospitalization, died, or experienced long COVID. Teachers, because of workplace exposure and variable vaccination/mitigation, have also been affected by infections and outbreaks. Saying the virus poses "virtually zero threat" to these groups contradicts epidemiological data showing non-negligible severe outcomes and long-term effects across age groups.

claim: Brewpubs can't sell growlers of their beer to customers.
rationale: The statement is too absolute. In many jurisdictions brewpubs routinely sell growlers or allow beer to-go, though specific rules vary by state, province, or country and some places restrict or prohibit such sales.

claim: "We have 93 million people out of work. They look for jobs, they give up, and all of a sudden, statistically, they're considered employed."
rationale: The statement conflates distinct labor-force categories. By official U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics definitions, people who stop looking for work are counted as 'not in the labor force' (or as discouraged workers in a separate measure), not as employed; they are not 'suddenly... considered employed.' Additionally, the '93 million' figure typically cited refers to people not in the labor force (and includes retirees, students, caregivers, etc.), not 93 million unemployed or misclassified as employed.

claim: "There has been no net global warming for over a decade now."
rationale: Multiple independent datasets (surface temperature records and satellite analyses) show that global mean temperatures have continued to rise and that the most recent decade ranks among the warmest on record. Additional indicators — increasing ocean heat content, continued ice mass loss, and rising sea levels — corroborate ongoing net global warming, so the claim is incorrect.

claim: "Oregon, once again, remains among the top five hungriest states in the nation."
rationale: National food‑insecurity and hunger rankings published by sources such as the USDA and Feeding America typically list states in the Southeast and Mississippi Delta (e.g., Mississippi, Louisiana, New Mexico, Arkansas, Alabama/West Virginia) among the highest; Oregon is not usually in the top five. Because the claim gives no year or data source and current public datasets don’t routinely place Oregon in the top five, the statement is not supported.

claim: The United States "spends more on potato chips than we do on ALL energy R&D."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because U.S. spending on energy research and development (combining federal R&D budgets and private-sector R&D by utilities and energy companies) is substantially larger than consumer spending on potato chips. Annual U.S. retail sales of potato chips are in the low tens of billions of dollars, whereas federal energy R&D budgets plus private energy industry R&D add up to many tens of billions (and in some measures hundreds of billions over multi-year cycles). The statement conflates different categories of spending and ignores large private and governmental energy R&D investments.

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: Local reporting and official Milwaukee police/county traffic data for 2021 indicate roughly 65 people were killed in crashes attributed to reckless driving and that vehicle thefts exceeded 9,000 — about double the reported total in 2020. These numbers were widely reported by Milwaukee news outlets using police/crime statistics.

claim: Says "FBI and Texas State Police are both confirming that Raymond Peter Littleberry, the man accused of shooting up a Texas church, was an avid atheist on the payroll of the Democrat National Committee."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official statements from the FBI or Texas Department of Public Safety confirming that a person named Raymond Peter Littleberry committed a church shooting or that he was an 'avid atheist' employed by the Democratic National Committee. Major news organizations and agency press releases do not corroborate the named individual or the DNC payroll claim, which appears to be a fabricated political rumor.

claim: Says Scott Walker is proposing to add 485 employees "in the category of supervisor and management" to his Department of Administration.
rationale: There is no verifiable record that Governor Scott Walker proposed adding 485 supervisory/management positions specifically to the Department of Administration; such a large, department-specific increase would have been widely documented in budget summaries and news coverage. The claim appears to conflate reclassifications or statewide position changes with a distinct addition to DOA management ranks.

claim: "NASA confirms earth will go dark for 6 days in December 2020."
rationale: This claim is false: NASA did not confirm that Earth would go dark for six days in December 2020. No credible space agency issued such a statement, and scientists have repeatedly debunked viral hoaxes predicting multi-day global darkness as physically implausible without a catastrophic astronomical event.

claim: "At John Lewis funeral Obama told a room full of people that rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote."
rationale: There is no credible transcript or news report showing Obama told mourners at John Lewis's funeral that "rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote." Obama's public remarks at memorial events honored Lewis's civil-rights legacy and urged people to vote, but the specific statement quoted is not supported by available records and appears to be a mischaracterization.

claim: "Why should you get a break for racehorses and not get a break for child care?"
rationale: The statement is a rhetorical question that implies governments give tax breaks to racehorses but not to childcare; that generalization is not universally true. Policy treatment varies by jurisdiction — many countries and states offer childcare tax credits, subsidies, or employer-provided dependent care benefits, while some jurisdictions also provide tax incentives or deductions for the horse-racing industry. Without a specific country or law, the claim cannot be accepted as a factual universal.

claim: "Nearly 20% of our residents" are born abroad.
rationale: The claim is unverified because it omits which jurisdiction and time period 'our residents' refers to; foreign‑born shares vary widely by country and locality. Without that context the statement cannot be confirmed and therefore should be treated as false as a general claim.

claim: "Tommy Thompson wanted to implant data chips in humans."
rationale: As U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary in the mid-2000s, Tommy Thompson publicly endorsed exploring implantable microchip/RFID technology to store medical data and said he would consider getting such a chip himself. Media coverage and his statements tied this idea to electronic health record initiatives rather than a broad forced program.

claim: Says the USMCA is the "biggest trade deal ever made."
rationale: The USMCA is a three-country update to NAFTA (United States, Mexico, Canada) but is not the largest trade agreement ever. Larger trade pacts in terms of membership, population and share of global GDP — for example the EU single market and the RCEP covering 15 Asia-Pacific countries — exceed USMCA, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the company’s board.
rationale: There are no credible news reports or contemporaneous coverage indicating a Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland publicly resigned in a tweet when Elon Musk joined the company’s board. Major outlets documented employee reactions and some departures at the time, but this specific name and tweet do not appear in reliable reporting and appear unverified or fabricated.

claim: "Almost 40% of borrowers with student loan debt didn't finish their degree."
rationale: Multiple analyses of U.S. student-loan cohorts report that roughly one-third to two-fifths of borrowers never complete a postsecondary credential, so saying 'almost 40%' aligns with commonly reported estimates. Different studies and cohorts produce slightly different percentages, but the claim is consistent with reputable research.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Epidemiological data and public-health assessments showed that Omicron subvariants generally caused less severe disease and had lower rates of hospitalization and death than the Delta variant; there is no credible evidence that Omicron is five times more 'toxic' or that its intrinsic mortality rate was higher than Delta's. While Omicron produced large case numbers due to higher transmissibility and immune escape, individual risk of severe outcomes was typically lower.

claim: Says Texas has so few gas-pump inspectors in the field, "the HEBs of this state, the Brookshires of this state, they're calibrating their own gas pumps. The (Texas Department of Agriculture) just sends them the stickers and they calibrate them."
rationale: This statement exaggerates and misrepresents Texas practice. The Texas Department of Agriculture’s Weights and Measures program is responsible for inspecting, testing, and sealing fuel dispensers; while retailers and third‑party service technicians may perform maintenance and adjustments, legal seals and official inspections are performed by TDA inspectors or certified agents rather than the agency merely mailing out stickers and leaving calibration entirely to stores.

claim: Says President Dwight Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out of this country."
rationale: While President Eisenhower did preside over large deportation efforts—most notably the 1954 Operation Wetback—mainstream historical estimates put removals at roughly one million to about 1.1–1.2 million people, not 1.5 million. The 1.5 million figure overstates commonly accepted totals and often conflates different types of removals and voluntary repatriations.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez took a "$10 million payout from Netflix."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez received a $10 million payout from Netflix. Her required congressional financial disclosures list no such payment, and multiple reputable fact-checks have debunked this rumor as baseless or a confusion with unrelated payments to other parties.

claim: "When the union says I want to eliminate tenure, that’s not true."
rationale: This is an unverified denial lacking necessary context (who is speaking, which union, and what specific tenure policy is referenced). There is no supporting evidence provided to confirm the denial or to show the union's original claim, so the statement cannot be treated as factual. Without direct sources (public statements, policy documents, or corroborating records), the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T-shirt with progressive slogans on it.
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence from reputable sources showing Tom Hanks photographed wearing a T‑shirt with explicit progressive political slogans; circulating images making that claim are unverified or appear altered. Because the claim lacks a specific incident, date, or reliable documentation, it cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Says Charlie Crist rode on a jet that "belongs to a serial polluter with a history of environmental violations fined nearly $2 million for polluting water."
rationale: I could not find verifiable public evidence that Charlie Crist rode on a specific private jet owned by an individual accurately described as a “serial polluter” who was fined nearly $2 million for polluting water. The claim bundles an allegation about the aircraft’s ownership and a precise enforcement dollar figure without naming dates or the owner; available reporting and public records do not corroborate that combination. Without a named owner or documented sanction directly tying that owner to Crist’s flight, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Just about everyone everywhere is spending more hours on the job, less time with their families, bringing home smaller and smaller paychecks, while they're paying more and more at the gas pump and the grocery stores."
rationale: The claim is a sweeping generalization that is not supported by data globally. While many countries experienced higher consumer prices (including fuel and food) and some groups faced stagnant or falling real wages and longer hours, trends vary substantially by country, sector, and time period — many workers have seen stable or rising real pay and working hours have not universally increased.

claim: U.S. military uniforms are manufactured in China.
rationale: Most U.S. military uniforms and textiles are procured under U.S. law (notably the Berry Amendment) that requires domestic sourcing, so uniforms are generally manufactured in the United States. While there have been occasional waivers, subcontracting issues, or foreign-sourced components and some non-official “military-style” garments made abroad, the blanket claim that U.S. military uniforms are manufactured in China is incorrect.

claim: "We've had 11,000 attempts to amend the Constitution since 1789."
rationale: Congressional records and summaries commonly report that over 11,000 proposed amendments to the Constitution have been introduced since 1789. The vast majority were bills introduced in Congress that never advanced; only 27 amendments have actually been ratified.

claim: "In the last decade, the average income of the bottom 90 percent of all working Americans actually declined. The top 1 percent saw their income rise by an average of more than a quarter of a million dollars each."
rationale: The statement mixes true elements with exaggeration and depends heavily on ambiguous definitions and time windows. While income growth in recent years has been concentrated at the top, U.S. data for common recent-decade windows (for example 2010–2019) show modest real gains for the bottom 90% on many measures rather than a clear decline, and the reported per-person increase for the top 1% being "more than a quarter of a million dollars each" is an overstatement for typical income definitions and periods. The numbers change substantially depending on whether one uses pre-tax vs after-tax income, households vs workers, and which exact years are compared.

claim: Says Chris Christie "vetoed equal pay for women 3 times. He only let the bill pass once it became a damaging campaign issue."
rationale: This statement is an exaggeration and lacks clear documentary support. Chris Christie did veto or oppose some pay‑equity measures while governor, but credible sources do not clearly show he vetoed an identical "equal pay" bill three separate times and only allowed passage solely because it became a damaging campaign issue. The claim conflates multiple bills, votes, and political messaging in a way that overstates the documented record.

claim: Claims Joe Biden said "coal is more dangerous than terrorists."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Joe Biden uttering the exact line 'coal is more dangerous than terrorists.' Viral posts appear to misquote or take remarks about coal pollution, job declines, or energy policy out of context and present them as a direct comparison to 'terrorists.' Fact-checking outlets have found the phrasing to be a distortion rather than a documented Biden quote.

claim: Huckabee "was one of the highest taxing governors that we had in this country and rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings."
rationale: Cato's Fiscal Policy Report Cards do not show Mike Huckabee as among the very highest-taxing governors nationwide nor clearly 'rivaling' Bill Clinton on those scores. Huckabee did sign multiple tax increases as Arkansas governor, but Cato's overall rankings placed Arkansas in a middling-to-poor position rather than at the extreme top for taxation, so the claim overstates and conflates measures.

claim: A photo of Pete Buttigieg in a military uniform without visible patches shows that "he is a fraud."
rationale: A single photo showing Pete Buttigieg in a uniform without visible patches does not by itself prove he is a fraud. Patches and insignia can be obscured by angle, lighting, cropping, subdued uniforms, or removed for specific contexts, and Buttigieg's Naval Reserve service is a matter of public record, so the image alone is insufficient evidence of deceit.

claim: The average Atlanta resident "spends an extra $924 each year in additional gasoline and wasted time."
rationale: The specific figure of "$924 each year" for the average Atlanta resident is not a reliably verifiable universal fact — major congestion studies (INRIX, TomTom, Texas A&M Urban Mobility) report varying per-driver costs and lost time that differ by year and methodology, and many Atlanta estimates are higher or vary substantially. Because the claim gives a single precise number without citing a year or source, it cannot be confirmed as a general fact.

claim: Rob Cornilles is a Tea Party candidate.
rationale: There is no clear, widely reported evidence that Rob Cornilles was specifically a Tea Party candidate; he has been identified in local politics as a Republican/local office candidate rather than as an expressly Tea Party-endorsed or -branded challenger. The claim overstates an affiliation that isn’t well documented in general reporting about his campaigns.

claim: "By the way, I'm not raising tolls 50 percent....Jon Corzine did."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Jon Corzine himself enacted a single 50% toll increase; toll adjustments in New Jersey were set by toll authorities and any increases during his administration were smaller or spread over time. The statement conflates responsibility and overstates the magnitude of a single Corzine-driven 50% hike, making it misleading.

claim: Image shows Donald Trump’s new Christmas card.
rationale: No image or supporting source was provided to verify that the referenced image is Donald Trump’s new Christmas card. Without the actual image, metadata, or independent reporting confirming its origin and date, the claim cannot be substantiated and is judged false.

claim: "I believe in tax cuts. I believe in being a supply-sider. I cut the income tax I think it was 24 percent. We got 42 percent more revenues."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and likely false: there is no clear evidence that cutting an income tax rate by '24 percent' produced a 42% increase in revenues. Historical major tax cuts (e.g., U.S. Reagan-era cuts and the 2017 TCJA) did not produce immediate 42% boosts in government revenues; revenue outcomes depend on definitions, timing, economic growth, and other policy changes.

claim: On tax inversions, the Wall Street Journal "surprisingly attacked this tax scheme."
rationale: The Wall Street Journal has generally defended corporate tax inversions as lawful tax planning and has criticized U.S. tax policy and government efforts to block inversions; it would be inaccurate to characterize the paper as having 'surprisingly attacked' the practice in general. While specific WSJ news stories or occasional editorials may have criticized aspects of particular deals, the newspaper’s overall editorial stance has tended to support corporations' use of inversions or blame U.S. tax law rather than label inversions broadly as a nefarious 'tax scheme.'

claim: Vaccines "will remove parts of your DNA and replace it with GENETIC CODING (TECHNOLOGY)" that will "cause people to HAVE to cooperate with the New World Order."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that vaccines remove pieces of your DNA or replace them with some 'genetic coding' that compels behavior. mRNA vaccines provide transient instructions to make a harmless antigen and do not integrate into the human genome, and viral-vector vaccines are designed not to alter host DNA; neither mechanism can plausibly create mind-control or force compliance with a conspiracy.

claim: "South Florida ranks No. 1 in the gap between wages and housing."
rationale: The claim is too vague and not supported by a single authoritative source: rankings of the "wages vs housing" gap depend entirely on the metric, dataset and year. Major affordability studies frequently put West Coast and New York metros at the top; while parts of South Florida (e.g., Miami) often show large gaps, they are not consistently ranked No. 1 across reputable analyses.

claim: Says Peter DeFazio votes with Nancy Pelosi 86 percent of the time.
rationale: The precise claim cannot be verified as stated because 'votes with Nancy Pelosi 86 percent of the time' is a statistic that depends on the time period and data source; I find no single authoritative source that confirms that exact figure as a general fact. Vote-alignment metrics (from sources like FiveThirtyEight or GovTrack) vary year-to-year and by methodology, and DeFazio was known to break with House Democratic leadership on a number of votes.

claim: "400 bills have my name on them either as a sponsor or a co-sponsor. You don’t get that done unless you work with folks on the other side."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as presented because the speaker is not identified and no timeframe or legislative body is specified. Whether any particular lawmaker has 400 bills with their name as sponsor or co-sponsor is an empirical fact that must be checked against official legislative records; some lawmakers do accrue hundreds of co-sponsorships while others do not. The accompanying assertion that such a total requires working with the other side is plausible for bipartisan totals but is a generalized inference that cannot be confirmed without examining the party breakdown of those bills.

claim: The Obama administration "raised discretionary spending by 24 percent from President George W. Bush's last full-year budget and will run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years."
rationale: The claim mixes different measures and timeframes to exaggerate the change. Discretionary outlays did not jump 24% from Bush's last full fiscal year when measured on a comparable outlays basis, and the increase in publicly held federal debt during Obama's early years through October did not exceed the roughly $4.8–5.0 trillion increase in debt accumulated over President Bush’s eight years.
