Estimates depend on assumptions about how many children are retained and which portion of per-pupil funding or local costs are counted; using typical Florida per-pupil spending and plausible retention counts produces lower totals and the state does not report a $300M figure for this specific category.

claim: Clicking on this link in a text message lets sex traffickers track you.
rationale: The claim is overly categorical: clicking an arbitrary link does not automatically enable sex traffickers to track you. While malicious links can sometimes collect information (IP address, browser fingerprint), prompt you to reveal location or credentials, or install spyware if you grant permissions or download an app, they do not inherently allow any specific actor (e.g., sex traffickers) to track you without additional actions or vulnerabilities. The risk depends on the exact link, device, and user responses.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: Donald Trump has not explicitly said he wants to 'get rid of' the federal minimum wage; instead he has at times said he would leave minimum-wage decisions to the states or opposed federal increases. Characterizing that rhetoric as an outright stated desire to abolish the federal minimum wage misstates his public comments.

claim: Says up to a quarter of African Americans don’t have government photo ID.
rationale: The claim overstates commonly cited national estimates. Multiple reputable analyses (e.g., studies by the Brennan Center, Pew, and others) generally find the share of African Americans without any government-issued photo ID is lower than 25% nationally, though rates vary by definition, year, and state and can be higher in some local populations.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: This is a long-running urban legend; PepsiCo never admitted that an employee contaminated its products with AIDS and has publicly denied such claims. Public-health experts and fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked the story, noting there is no evidence of contamination and that HIV is not transmitted via food or beverages.

claim: "Live cats have holes drilled into their skulls," posts put into their heads and coils put into their eyes, and some have had their ears cut off or are intentionally deafened or starved at UW-Madison labs that do research to improve hearing in humans.
rationale: The statement mixes descriptions of legitimate invasive neuroscience techniques (small cranial openings for implants and head-posts, and procedures that can induce deafness) with extreme, specific allegations (ears being cut off, intentional starvation) for which there is no reliable public evidence tied to UW–Madison. U.S. research institutions operate under animal-care regulations and oversight, and available public information does not substantiate the most extreme claims in this post.

claim: Says 15,000 IRS employees "have to be added to administer ‘ObamaCare’ and look at the tax implications."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did increase IRS reporting and enforcement work, but there is no firm requirement that exactly 15,000 new IRS employees 'have to be added.' Estimates of staffing needs varied over time and by source, and references to ~15,000 typically conflate temporary surge hiring, full-time-equivalent (FTE) estimates, or speculative claims rather than an explicit legal mandate.

claim: "I've been here almost every day."
rationale: This is a personal attendance claim with no supporting context or evidence, so it cannot be independently verified. Without details (who ‘‘I’’ is, what ‘‘here’’ refers to, the timeframe, or what constitutes ‘‘almost every day’’) there is insufficient basis to accept the statement as true.

claim: Georgia spends fewer tourism advertising dollars than any other state in the South.
rationale: There is no evidence that Georgia spends the least on tourism advertising among Southern states; Georgia operates an active, statewide tourism marketing program with substantial budgets, and smaller states in the region often have smaller total tourism ad outlays. The claim is vague about timeframe and whether it means total or per‑capita spending and is not supported by available summary data.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: The statement gives precise counts and timing for insurance rebates without a verifiable date or source. While the ACA medical-loss-ratio rebate program has issued millions of checks in various years, the exact numbers (13 million last year, 8.5 million this summer, averaging ~$100 each) vary by year and insurer and cannot be confirmed as a blanket fact without a cited source.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: Sanctioning Iran's central bank can sharply curtail foreign transactions, access to reserves, and imports, but it does not automatically 'shut down' the entire Iranian economy. Historically Iran has continued economic activity by using currency controls, domestic production, barter and alternative payment channels, so sanctions cause severe harm but not total cessation.

claim: Says Russ Feingold said that with Obamacare, "we could keep our doctors and our plans, it was rated as the Lie of the Year."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that former Sen. Russ Feingold specifically said the Obamacare promise 'you can keep your doctor and your plan' 'was rated as the Lie of the Year.' While fact-checkers (notably PolitiFact) did label that promise as their 2013 Lie of the Year, the attribution to Feingold appears unverified and likely misattributed.

claim: "So Trump comes to Nashville to oversee damage from the tornado. He flies into the area in a helicopter to get there without further traffic problems in the city. He writes PERSONAL checks to those in need, with his personal accountant in tow."
rationale: There are no credible reports that former President Trump made an unannounced helicopter visit to Nashville to oversee tornado damage and then wrote personal checks to victims with his personal accountant present. Presidential disaster visits and any direct monetary assistance are well documented by news outlets and official statements; routine practice is for federal aid or charitable organizations to provide relief rather than the president handing out personal checks. The specific details claimed (personal check-writing on-site with an accountant) are implausible and unsupported.

claim: Says she couldn't take stimulus money because it required "universal building codes."
rationale: There is no general federal requirement that recipients adopt a single "universal building code" as a condition for taking stimulus funds. While some federal grants for construction or rebuilding require adherence to applicable local, state, or recognized model building codes for safety and compliance, that is not the same as a blanket nationwide mandate and would not bar someone from receiving stimulus money simply for declining a vague "universal building code."

claim: Says he never told anyone he hated the U.S. Senate.
rationale: The claim is underspecified — it does not identify who 'he' is, when or where the statement was allegedly made, or provide a source. Without an identifiable subject and verifiable evidence, the assertion cannot be confirmed and therefore is treated as false for lack of support.

claim: The projected revenue from the Mayweather/Pacquiao fight is "larger than the annual GDP of 29 different countries."
rationale: Contemporary reporting estimated the Mayweather–Pacquiao fight would generate roughly $500–600 million in revenue. That amount exceeds the annual nominal GDPs of many very small economies; using IMF/World Bank nominal GDP data, about 20–40 countries have GDPs smaller than several hundred million dollars, so the statement that it was larger than the GDP of 29 countries is plausible and consistent with published comparisons at the time.

claim: Wisconsin voter turnout jumped from 67% in 2016 to 89% in 2020.
rationale: Statewide turnout in Wisconsin did not jump to 89% in 2020. Official measures put 2020 Wisconsin turnout at roughly the low-to-mid 70s percent of the voting-eligible population (vs about 67% in 2016); an 89% figure likely mixes a different denominator (e.g., percent of registered voters or a local subset) or is incorrect.

claim: The balanced-budget amendment once came within one vote of passing Congress but was defeated because of the no vote from a top Senate Republican, and Rick Santorum says he "stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship."
rationale: The claim bundles several specific assertions that do not match the historical record as stated. While various balanced‑budget amendment proposals in Congress have failed and some votes were close, no well‑documented instance shows a single “top Senate Republican” no vote directly costing passage by one vote with Rick Santorum publicly calling for that senator to resign his chairmanship in the manner described. The statement appears to conflate or misremember separate events and lacks corroboration.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: Multiple official records and Hawaiian state officials have confirmed the authenticity of Barack Obama's birth certificate. In 2011 the White House released a certified long-form copy and Hawaii's Department of Health affirmed its validity, and independent fact-checkers and news organizations have corroborated this, debunking claims it was fake.

claim: Japan's "interest on its own debt" is "25 percent of its national budget"
rationale: This claim overstates the share of Japan’s annual budget that goes to interest. While Japan has very large public debt, extremely low interest rates have kept annual interest outlays well below 25% of the central government budget; the exact share varies by fiscal year and by whether one counts gross versus net interest or central versus consolidated government accounts, but none of those standard measures reaches 25%.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim provides no name, campaign, or specific allegation, so it cannot be verified as stated. Federal investigations leave public records and media coverage; without those identifiers there is no evidence to confirm the assertion.

claim: Says opponent David Dewhurst is a "career politician."
rationale: David Dewhurst has held multiple elected statewide offices and campaigned for higher office over several decades, most notably serving as Lieutenant Governor of Texas for multiple terms (2003–2015). That sustained record in elected positions fits common usage of the term “career politician.”

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Frank Marshall Davis was Barack Obama's biological father; Barack Obama’s father is documented as Barack Obama Sr. in birth records, family testimony, and Obama's own memoir. Davis was a friend and occasional mentor to Obama's maternal family in Hawaii, which has spawned conspiracy claims but no DNA, contemporaneous records, or reliable documentation supporting paternity.

claim: Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted the continued taxation on residents’ properties over 70 percent of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific numeric rate of participation ("over 70 percent of the time") and a particular behavior (seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same) that would require checking official roll-call votes and meeting minutes. I have no verifiable source or timeframe to confirm those records here, so the precise factual assertion cannot be substantiated and is treated as false. The phrase "aided and abetted" is also evaluative rather than a neutral voting record statement.

claim: "666,000 teachers have been laid off already since March."
rationale: The claim gives no source or jurisdiction and is implausible at the global or national level. For example, in the United States there are roughly 3 million public school teachers, so 666,000 layoffs would be an enormous (~20%) reduction that would have been widely reported; major statistical agencies (e.g., BLS) and news organizations have not reported teacher layoffs on that scale since March. Available employment data show much smaller declines in education employment.

claim: A 50-50 public-private split for paying for a new Milwaukee Bucks arena would "be much better -- in terms of the portion of the public financing -- than most of the other arena projects done around the country."
rationale: Arena financing varies widely and in many recent U.S. projects the public share has been smaller than 50% or the project was privately financed, so a 50/50 split would not clearly be "much better than most." Some high-profile arenas were largely or fully privately financed while others had significant public subsidies, making a blanket comparison to "most" projects inaccurate.

claim: "Ten years ago, John McCain offered a bill that said he would ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. John McCain introduced a bill roughly ten years ago that specifically 'banned a candidate from paying registered lobbyists.' McCain did advocate and sponsor various lobbying and campaign finance reforms over his career, but the claimed precise proposal and wording cannot be substantiated from public legislative records or reporting for that timeframe.

claim: Virginia "is home to more veterans per capita than any state in America."
rationale: While Virginia has a large veteran population in absolute terms, it is not the state with the highest number of veterans per capita. Census and VA data historically show states such as Alaska, Maine, West Virginia, and Arkansas among the highest veterans-per-capita, and Virginia does not top those rankings.

claim: The administration has issued rules for "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" and "requires all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay" an abortion premium.
rationale: The HHS rules implementing the Affordable Care Act allowed insurers and exchanges to segregate and collect separate payments for elective abortion coverage so federal subsidies would not be used for abortions, but they did not set a "$1 abortion" price nor require that all enrollees pay an additional "abortion premium." Whether a separate charge is assessed depends on insurer practices and state law; the federal rule permitted, rather than mandated, such separate billing.

claim: "Shakespeare said: ‘I always feel happy. You know why? Because I don’t expect anything from anyone. Expectations always hurt. Life is short. So love your life. Be Happy. & Keep smiling."
rationale: The phrasing and punctuation of the quoted lines do not match Early Modern English and the text does not appear in Shakespeare’s plays or sonnets. The passage is a modern aphorism commonly misattributed to famous authors rather than an authentic Shakespeare quote.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that healthcare.gov contains legal language hidden in its code stating users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information." Publicly available privacy policies and expert fact-checks do not support the claim, and code comments or implementation details would not by themselves create a sweeping legal waiver of privacy rights.

claim: "It has been estimated that only 12% of workers in businesses that are likely to stay open during this crisis are receiving paid sick leave benefits as a result of the second coronavirus relief package."
rationale: The statement cites a precise 12% estimate but there is no widely accepted, authoritative estimate that exactly matches that figure. Analyses of the U.S. Families First Coronavirus Response Act showed that only a minority of workers—particularly at large employers—would be covered, but different studies produced varying percentages and the 12% number cannot be verified without a clear source.

claim: A photo taken on Jan. 6, 2021, at the United States Capitol riot was "doctored to look as if the Capitol was on fire."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a widely circulated Jan. 6 photo of the U.S. Capitol was digitally altered to depict the Capitol itself on fire. Contemporary reporting, official photos, and independent fact-checking found only limited fires inside some adjacent office areas and no verified images showing the Capitol building engulfed in flames due to doctored edits.

claim: "Military arrests former President George W. Bush."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that U.S. military forces arrested former President George W. Bush; such an event would be major national and international news. U.S. legal norms mean civilian arrests (including of former presidents) are handled through civilian law enforcement and courts, not by the military.

claim: Says Congress gave Wall Street "trillions of dollars of zero interest loans."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Congress authorized large rescue and backstop programs (and the Treasury used authority to support markets), and the Federal Reserve extended trillions in emergency liquidity, but Congress did not directly give Wall Street 'trillions of dollars of zero interest loans.' Most support came via the Fed or Treasury facilities that involved purchases, guarantees, or lending at market or low rates rather than blanket zero‑interest loans.

claim: "If Trump had just put his father’s money in a mutual fund ... he’d have $8 billion."
rationale: The statement is a speculative counterfactual without specifying amounts or dates; journalistic investigations report Donald Trump received large but not single-lump transfers (hundreds of millions in inflation-adjusted dollars) from his father over many years, and whether those sums invested would become $8 billion depends critically on timing and returns. No authoritative, reproducible calculation supports the precise claim that simply putting 'his father’s money' into a mutual fund would have produced exactly $8 billion.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke wants "open borders and wants to take our guns."
rationale: The claim conflates two different points: O'Rourke does not advocate 'open borders'—he has supported stronger, more humane border management and comprehensive immigration reform, not abolition of border controls. He has, however, publicly supported bans on certain assault-style weapons and at times endorsed mandatory buybacks, famously saying 'Hell yes, we're going to take your AR-15,' so the 'wants to take our guns' part is a simplified but partially accurate characterization.

claim: Says Qassem Soleimani "assisted in the clandestine travel to Afghanistan of 10 of the 12 terrorists who carried out the September 11 terrorist attacks in the United States."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Qassem Soleimani arranged or assisted the clandestine travel of 10 of the 12 9/11 hijackers. U.S. investigations and the 9/11 Commission found that while a small number of hijackers transited Iran or had limited contacts there, they did not find that Iran or Soleimani orchestrated or facilitated travel on the scale claimed.

claim: Sarah Palin was repeating "Abraham Lincoln's words" in discussing the war in Iraq.
rationale: There is no clear public record or reliable reporting that Sarah Palin repeatedly invoked or quoted Abraham Lincoln specifically when discussing the Iraq War. Palin has been widely quoted on many topics, but major news fact-checks and transcripts of her speeches do not show a recurring practice of repeating Lincoln’s words about that conflict.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: I cannot find verifiable public evidence that the Ohio Republican Party has made nearly 6.6 million voter contacts since 2009 or that it exceeds every other state GOP; such a specific cumulative claim would require a named source and consistent methodology. Party "contact" counts are tracked differently across organizations and larger states (e.g., Florida, Texas) would plausibly report higher totals depending on definitions and measurement periods.

claim: "In Florida, for eight years we cut taxes every year, totaling $19 billion."
rationale: The widely cited $19 billion figure is a cumulative total some state officials and media outlets reported for tax reductions during an eight‑year period, but the claim that taxes were cut every single year is misleading. Different calculations mix one‑time items, fee changes and estimated future savings with recurring tax cuts, and not every year saw a clear net, recurring tax reduction under consistent accounting.

claim: "95 percent of teachers and principals are not implicated in the [Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal] report at all."
rationale: I cannot find authoritative support for the exact claim that 95% of Atlanta Public Schools teachers and principals were not implicated; published investigations identified a specific subset of educators involved in cheating but did not conclude that exactly 95% were uninvolved. The statement presents a precise percentage without citing which report, timeframe, or how 'implicated' and the denominator were defined, so it is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "One of the first nurses to receive the vaccine in AL is now dead."
rationale: The claim is vague and there is no verified reporting that a named nurse who was among the first to receive the COVID-19 vaccine in Alabama (AL) subsequently died as a result of or in connection with that vaccination. Early-vaccine recipients were widely reported and deaths tied to those vaccinations would have been documented by local news and public health statements; I find no reliable evidence supporting this assertion. Given the lack of specifics and corroborating sources, the claim is not supported.

claim: His biography says he was the top ROTC officer in the nation.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it uses an unspecified pronoun—no individual or biography is identified. Without a named person or source, there is no way to confirm that any biography asserts he was 'the top ROTC officer in the nation.'

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: There is no credible transcript or video evidence showing Mika Brzezinski saying the quoted line verbatim; fact-checks and available Morning Joe clips show she has criticized Elon Musk but did not state "That's our job" about controlling how people think. The line appears to be a misattribution or fabrication rather than a documented quote.

claim: "Now there is a new threat that we’re seeing up close: the risk of exposure to powerful drugs that can kill in even tiny amounts."
rationale: Extremely potent synthetic opioids (e.g., fentanyl, carfentanil) are known to be lethal at very small doses, and public-health authorities have documented increasing risks from accidental exposure and contamination. Therefore the claim that there is a new threat from powerful drugs that can kill in tiny amounts is accurate in substance.

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: While many of the poorest counties by income or poverty rate are in Appalachia, a large share of the very poorest counties are elsewhere (for example in the Mississippi Delta, Colonias in Texas, and on Native American reservations). Those counties have diverse racial compositions including majority-Black, majority-Hispanic, and majority-Native populations, so it is incorrect to say the poorest counties “happen to be more than 90 percent white.” The truth depends on the exact poverty metric and year, but the blanket >90% white claim is not supported by county-level Census data.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: While visible surveillance cameras often reduce or displace some types of crime and help identify perpetrators, research shows their deterrent effect is inconsistent and highly context-dependent. Cameras do not 'certainly' prevent robberies because effectiveness depends on visibility, signage, active monitoring, police response, and offender behavior (e.g., use of masks or willingness to take risks).

claim: "We became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and until recently, our exports have exceeded our imports."
rationale: The United States did become a net exporter of natural gas around 2017 according to energy statistics, but the claim's second clause is misleading: net flows have varied month-to-month and depend on definitions (pipeline and LNG flows), and there have been periods when imports exceeded exports. Because the statement presents a sustained, unqualified trend 'until recently,' it overstates how consistently exports exceeded imports.

claim: Says Sandra Bullock said to Hillary Clinton, "If you don’t like our president you can leave and never come back again."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or verifiable source that Sandra Bullock publicly told Hillary Clinton, "If you don’t like our president you can leave and never come back again." The line appears to be a viral misattribution on social media consistent with many fabricated celebrity political quotes.

claim: Federal prosecutions for lying on background checks to buy guns are "down 40 percent" under President Barack Obama.
rationale: Available DOJ/ATF data do not support a consistent, across-the-board 40% decline in federal prosecutions for lying on gun background checks over President Obama's tenure. Numbers for false-statement firearms prosecutions fluctuated year-to-year, and the 'down 40 percent' claim appears to come from a selective comparison of particular years or categories rather than an overall validated trend.

claim: The effort to recall California Gov. Gavin Newsom is "a coup."
rationale: A coup denotes an illegal or violent seizure of state power outside constitutional processes. California’s recall effort is a lawful, statutory procedure (petition, signature thresholds, and special election) defined by state law, not an extra-legal takeover, so calling it a coup is inaccurate if meant literally.

claim: Says Dan Feehan "would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty, putting Minnesota families at risk."
rationale: The statement is an unsubstantiated partisan claim: there is no clear evidence that Dan Feehan has pledged to 'vote with Pelosi' on an agenda described as 'open borders and amnesty.' 'Open borders' and 'amnesty' are charged, vague labels often used in attack ads, and the assertion that such votes would definitively 'put Minnesota families at risk' is opinion, not an established fact.

claim: "No one has died of cancer or heart disease since the COVID-19 thing started."
rationale: This claim is false. Throughout and after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, cancer and heart disease have continued to cause deaths globally and remain among the leading causes of mortality; COVID-19 added excess deaths but did not eliminate other causes.

claim: "Many of the countries in question (in Trump’s travel ban) don't even have a U.S. embassy there to help us vet."
rationale: Some countries targeted by versions of the travel ban (notably Iran, and at times Syria, Yemen and Libya) did not have fully functioning U.S. embassies, but several other countries on various lists (for example Sudan, Chad when included) did have U.S. diplomatic presence. Saying 'many' have no embassy overstates the situation and is misleading without specifying which list and date.

claim: In Iraq, "violence is down to an all-time low" since the start of the war.
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute, countrywide "all-time low" in violence since the war began; while violence in Iraq fell after the 2014–2017 ISIS peak, the country has continued to experience insurgent attacks, militia violence, and periodic spikes. Historical data show much higher casualty rates in earlier waves but also regional variation, so it is not correct to state violence is uniformly at an all-time low since the start of the war.

claim: "Trump on revamping the military: We’re bringing back the draft."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Donald Trump has announced a plan to reinstate the military draft or that he declared “We’re bringing back the draft.” Reinstating conscription in the U.S. would require congressional action and an explicit policy proposal, none of which have been put forward or enacted by Trump as of mid-2024.

claim: "There’s no wildlife" in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
rationale: The claim is false — the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge supports abundant wildlife, including the Porcupine caribou herd (important calving grounds), polar bears that den along the coast, millions of migratory birds, muskoxen, wolves, foxes, and numerous fish species. The refuge was established to protect precisely this biodiversity and critical habitat.

claim: John Boozman supports "privatizing Social Security"
rationale: There is no clear, consistent evidence that Senator John Boozman has called for full privatization of Social Security. While he has supported conservative reform proposals and measures to change benefits or introduce private-account options in line with broader GOP ideas, his public record does not show an explicit endorsement of completely privatizing the entire Social Security system.

claim: "95 percent of the income gains in the last few years have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The claim is presented without a country, timeframe, or income definition, and cannot be verified as a universal fact. While some analyses of U.S. pre‑tax income in very short windows of the post‑2009 recovery reported a very large share of gains going to the top 1 percent, that 95% figure is not robust across different periods, income measures (pre‑tax vs after‑tax, household vs individual), or longer multi‑year windows. Stated as a general claim it therefore overstates what can be supported by available data.

claim: U.S. sanctions mean "Cuba can’t trade with any country or any company whatsoever."
rationale: U.S. sanctions (the embargo) bar most trade and financial transactions between U.S. persons and Cuba and can have extraterritorial effects, but they do not prevent every country or company worldwide from trading with Cuba. Many countries (for example China, Russia, Canada, and EU states) and multinational firms engage in commerce with Cuba subject to their own national laws and commercial constraints. The sanctions are influential and create banking and insurance hurdles, but they are not an absolute global trade ban.

claim: "California has added twice as many jobs as Florida" over the past year.
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because it lacks a specific 12‑month period and data source; statewide job gains fluctuate month to month and must be verified against official labor reports. Without a named timeframe and citation, there is no reliable basis to assert California added exactly twice as many jobs as Florida over “the past year.”

claim: Says Wisconsin payday loans have a 574% average annual interest rate, "exploitative lending that keeps Americans trapped in debt"
rationale: The specific numeric claim that Wisconsin payday loans have a 574% average annual interest rate is not consistently supported by authoritative sources as a statewide average; while payday loans commonly annualize to very high APRs (often in the hundreds of percent), reported averages vary by study, sample, and methodology and 574% is not a universally documented statewide figure. The characterization that payday lending is “exploitative” and can trap borrowers in debt is a policy judgment, though it is supported by research showing high fees and rollovers produce harmful debt cycles for many borrowers.

claim: "Candidate Slotkin had presented herself as a moderate and as someone who’d be independent-minded, but her time in office was making it increasingly clear that no, she was very partisan, voting 96% of the time with Speaker Pelosi."
rationale: While Elissa Slotkin campaigned as a moderate and independent-minded Democrat, the specific assertion that she voted with Speaker Nancy Pelosi 96% of the time is not supported by consistent public roll-call metrics. Public analyses of congressional voting alignment show lower and time-dependent percentages, and the 96% figure appears to be an exaggerated or out-of-context claim.

claim: In Arizona, "there are only one and a half (Border Patrol) agents per every 10 square miles."
rationale: Arizona covers about 113,990 square miles, so 1.5 agents per 10 square miles would imply roughly 17,100 Border Patrol agents stationed in the state. That number is implausibly high compared with known Border Patrol staffing (nationally ~20,000 agents in recent years) and with published sector staffing levels for Arizona, so the stated density is inaccurate.

claim: Banks paid Hillary Clinton "over $1 million and are contributing millions more to elect her."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and campaign finance data show Hillary Clinton accepted more than $1 million in paid speaking fees from Wall Street firms and related entities, and the financial sector (banks, securities and investment firms and their employees) contributed millions of dollars to her 2016 campaign and allied outside groups. Thus the two-part claim — that banks paid her over $1 million and that bankers/financial interests contributed additional millions to elect her — is supported by documented payments and contribution totals.

claim: Says Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "didn't change his position" on a two-state solution.
rationale: Benjamin Netanyahu's stance on a two-state solution has varied over time: he opposed it earlier in his career, publicly endorsed a conditional/demilitarized Palestinian state in his 2009 Bar-Ilan speech, and later issued qualifications and reversals. Because his positions have changed across different periods and statements, the blanket claim that he 'didn't change his position' is false.

claim: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security warned that the SAVE "database is not a foolproof means of verifying (citizenship on) the voter rolls."
rationale: DHS (through USCIS) has publicly stated that the SAVE system was not designed to be a definitive or "foolproof" method for determining U.S. citizenship and should not be relied on alone to verify citizenship for voter registration lists. Officials and fact-checkers have repeatedly noted SAVE is intended to verify immigration status for benefits and has coverage and data limitations that make it unsuitable as a sole means to confirm citizenship.

claim: Says the late Lady Bird Johnson sicced the CIA on actress and singer Eartha Kitt after Kitt spoke out against the Vietnam War during a White House luncheon in January 1968.
rationale: Eartha Kitt did publicly condemn the Vietnam War at a White House luncheon in January 1968 and suffered professional backlash and government scrutiny, but there is no credible evidence that Lady Bird Johnson personally ordered the CIA to target her. Declassified records document surveillance and adverse consequences from government agencies, but not a documented directive from Lady Bird to the CIA.

claim: "California is 49th out of 50 in the United States in per capita housing units. Only Utah can lay claim to being lowest in per capita production."
rationale: The asserted ranking is not supported by census housing-unit-per-person data: California is not consistently 49th and other small, dense states (e.g., New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island) often rank lower in housing units per capita. Utah is not reliably the single lowest in per-capita production; rankings change by year and by whether one measures existing units per capita or new construction (production).

claim: 52 jobs have been saved or created in Florida's 34th Congressional District.
rationale: The claim gives a precise number but provides no source, timeframe, or documentation that would allow independent verification. Specific job counts at the congressional-district level typically require supporting evidence (e.g., company statements, local government reports), which is not supplied here, so the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Rob Portman’s "plan to tax, slash and privatize" Social Security "would devastate Ohioans."
rationale: This claim mixes an inflammatory characterization with a speculative outcome. Publicly available records show Rob Portman supported Social Security reforms to reduce long‑term liabilities (such as benefit adjustments and means‑testing for higher earners) but he did not advance a widely enacted plan to fully privatize benefits or explicitly propose measures described simply as "tax, slash and privatize." Whether any specific reform "would devastate Ohioans" is a value judgment and depends on the precise policy details and implementation, so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Says House Republicans "tried to change the definition of rape."
rationale: The claim is presented as a general, timeless statement but lacks necessary context (which bill, when, and which members). While individual Republican lawmakers in the House have at times proposed or supported legislation and amendments that affect statutory language around sexual assault, there is no single, unambiguous event establishing that 'House Republicans' as a whole tried to change the definition of rape. Without a specific bill or date the statement is too broad to verify as true.

claim: "The daughter of Sen. Coons (D-DE), along with 7 other underaged girls are featured on Hunter's laptop! - Breitbart News"
rationale: There is no credible, independently verified evidence that Senator Chris Coons’ daughter or seven underage girls appear on Hunter Biden’s laptop. The claim originated from partisan outlets and social posts but was not substantiated by mainstream fact-checkers or law-enforcement-confirmed documents or images.

claim: Democrats already agreed to "a deal that Republicans wanted, that Eric Cantor said would be a win."
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks a specific time, bill, or negotiation context; there is no verifiable, general record that Democrats had already agreed to a particular deal described this way and that Eric Cantor explicitly characterized it as "a win." Without identifying the exact policy or quote the assertion cannot be confirmed, so it should be treated as false as stated.

claim: The federal tax code has "loopholes that are giving incentives for companies that are shipping jobs overseas."
rationale: U.S. federal tax rules have historically included provisions that lower the tax burden on income earned abroad or allow companies to shift profits and expenses across borders, which can create financial incentives to move operations or jobs overseas. Examples include deferral of U.S. tax on foreign earnings, favorable treatment for income taxed at lower foreign rates, transfer pricing opportunities, and practices that enabled tax inversions. While some reforms (e.g., the 2017 tax changes) reduced certain incentives, the tax code still contains features that can encourage offshoring.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official announcements indicating that half of the Ottawa police force resigned. A mass resignation on that scale would constitute major, widely reported news and would be verifiable via official statements from the Ottawa Police Service or municipal government, which are absent.

claim: Says Nikita Khrushchev brought an extra shoe to a United Nations session in 1960, which he banged on the desk in protest.
rationale: The famous anecdote that Khrushchev brought an extra shoe and bang it on the United Nations desk in 1960 is widely reported but disputed. Contemporary eyewitnesses, photographs and video do not conclusively show him banging a shoe; many witnesses say he waved or brandished a shoe or slapped the desk, and some participants and historians describe the shoe-banging story as apocryphal or exaggerated.

claim: Says in U.S. Congress, members "don’t even have to be on the floor for debates or votes."
rationale: Congressional rules generally require members to be present on the chamber floor to participate in formal debates and to cast votes. There have been limited exceptions — most notably temporary proxy and remote procedures adopted by the House during the COVID-19 pandemic and remote participation in committee proceedings — but those were special, time-limited measures and are not the ordinary rule for either chamber.

claim: "Texas now has the second-highest high school graduation rate in the country. And it has the highest graduation rate for African Americans and Hispanics."
rationale: Recent federal/state 4‑year adjusted cohort graduation-rate data do not support Texas being overall second-highest nationally; states such as New Jersey, Vermont, and others have typically ranked above Texas. Likewise, subgroup rankings for African American and Hispanic students fluctuate by year and metric and do not consistently show Texas highest, so the blanket claim is unsupported without a specific year and data source.

claim: "Common welfare programs give income of $43,330 or $20.83 an hour."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: there is no single uniform benefit of $43,330 (or $20.83/hr) provided by 'common welfare programs.' Benefits vary widely by program, state, and household size, and most safety-net programs (e.g., TANF, SNAP) provide far less than $43k/year for typical recipients. While $43,330 is the annual equivalent of $20.83/hr at a 2,080-hour work year, that conversion does not reflect how social programs are structured or the typical benefit levels.

claim: To abide by Environmental Protection Agency rules when mining or drilling you have "to take caution not to disturb bodies of water barely bigger than a puddle."
rationale: This statement is misleading. EPA and Clean Water Act authorities can regulate certain wetlands, streams and small water features in some circumstances, but they do not categorically forbid disturbing every tiny puddle; jurisdiction depends on legal definitions (WOTUS), the significant‑nexus standard, specific permits (e.g., Section 404, NPDES), and differing agency and court interpretations. Whether a particular feature is protected is fact‑specific and not as universal as the claim implies.

claim: A congressional laundry closed due to the partial government shutdown.
rationale: During recent U.S. partial government shutdowns (notably the 2018–2019 shutdown), nonessential services in congressional buildings — including on-site laundry operations used by members and staff — were suspended because employees were furloughed. Media reports at the time described laundry services and similar building amenities being closed or curtailed as a result of the shutdown.

claim: Facebook video shows "counting Biden’s votes at 2 a.m."
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to verify the blanket claim that a Facebook video definitively shows ‘‘counting Biden’s votes at 2 a.m.’’ Without a specific link, timestamp metadata, or corroborating sources, the assertion is unverified and may be based on a miscaptioned or edited clip. Social media videos can be reposted, edited, or misattributed, so the claim as stated cannot be confirmed.

claim: Annual precipitation "has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century."
rationale: Regional and state climate analyses show that annual precipitation in Rhode Island and the broader New England region has increased over the 20th century, but the magnitude is much smaller than 12 inches statewide. Long-term station records and NOAA/USGCRP assessments indicate increases on the order of a few inches to under ten inches depending on the baseline period, not a >12-inch rise.

claim: Georgia has led the nation in student fatalities caused by motorists illegally passing stopped school buses.
rationale: The statement is presented as a general, timeless fact but available state-by-state crash data show leadership in student fatalities from motorists illegally passing stopped school buses varies by year. Georgia has had years with a high count and has led the nation in certain single-year reports, but it is not consistently the national leader across all years, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "When I became mayor of Los Angeles, we had a 44 percent (high school) graduation rate. I said that was unacceptable. I challenged that notion. I said the mayor needs to be involved with our schools. We need to partner together. As I left, after a number of reforms, we grew our graduation rate from 44 percent to 72."
rationale: The claim mixes different metrics and timeframes to produce the 44%→72% figure. While Los Angeles graduation rates did rise during the mayor’s tenure, independent fact-checks and district data show the starting and ending percentages vary by which graduation-rate definition is used (cohort vs. on-time vs. different reporting methods), and the straight 44% to 72% jump as stated is misleading.

claim: Says a study indicates up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices.
rationale: I cannot find a credible, specific study that conclusively reports that Texas would lose up to $8.5 billion in GDP and up to 185,000 jobs solely from approving a transgender bathroom restriction. Economic impact estimates for anti-LGBT policies vary widely by author, methodology, and timeframe, and the claim gives no source or period for those figures. Without a named, peer-reviewed or widely cited study matching those exact numbers, the claim is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "I'm the only candidate in the Democratic primary, or actually on either side, who Wall Street financiers and hedge fund managers are actually running ads against."
rationale: The claim asserts exclusive targeting, but historical records show Wall Street financiers and hedge-fund–backed groups have funded ads against multiple candidates in Democratic primaries (and across parties). Notable examples include significant opposition advertising aimed at candidates like Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, and financial-industry PACs routinely spend against various contenders, so the speaker is not uniquely targeted.

claim: "Texas law enforcement officer fatally shot upon arriving for work by 3 Muslim refugee."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official statements documenting a Texas law enforcement officer being fatally shot upon arriving for work by three Muslim refugees. Major local and national outlets and police communications have not reported any incident matching that description, and known shootings in Texas involve different circumstances and perpetrators.

claim: "We are in the sixth year of recovery, and median income is below what it was at the start of the recovery."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as true because it omits key context (which country's recovery, the recovery start date, and whether incomes are inflation‑adjusted or measured per household vs. person). Median income trends vary by dataset and timeframe — in some recoveries and measures incomes rose by year six, in others they had not fully recovered. Because the claim is underspecified and therefore not reliably true as stated, I judge it false.

claim: "We have cut taxes more than 40 times in four years."
rationale: The claim is vague and unverified because it does not name the country, time period, or what counts as a 'tax cut.' At the federal level in major democracies, it is uncommon for an administration to enact more than 40 distinct tax-cut measures in a four-year span; claims that reach such counts typically rely on broad or inconsistent definitions (credits, rate changes, procedural adjustments, state actions). Without specific evidence tying 40+ tax reductions to a particular four-year period and jurisdiction, the statement is not supported.

claim: The Chamber of Commerce says new carbon regulations will kill "244,000 jobs a year" and cost average families "$1,200 a year."
rationale: I cannot confirm that the U.S. Chamber of Commerce explicitly and directly said those exact figures. While the Chamber and allied business groups have published analyses predicting substantial job losses and increased household costs from various carbon rules, reported estimates vary by study, timeframe, and assumptions, and the precise numbers "244,000 jobs a year" and "$1,200 a year" are not reliably attributable to a single, verifiable Chamber statement.

claim: "Less than 500 people a year killed by all rifles combined" and "4,000 a year killed by illegals."
rationale: The two-part claim mixes an arguable partial truth with an unsupported assertion. While rifle-involved homicides are a small fraction of total firearm deaths and in many recent years have been under 500, exact counts depend on year and how 'rifles' are classified. The claim that 4,000 people are killed each year by undocumented immigrants is not supported by DOJ/DHS or academic research; there is no credible evidence of that many homicides annually attributable to undocumented immigrants.

claim: Says in the last 20 years, the French have not "stood by" the United States on foreign policy.
rationale: The absolute claim is false: while France opposed the 2003 Iraq invasion, over the last 20 years France has repeatedly cooperated with the United States on major foreign policy actions (e.g., NATO operations in Afghanistan, the 2011 Libya intervention, joint counterterrorism efforts, and coordinated sanctions and support for Ukraine). Thus France has at times both disagreed with and stood by the U.S., so a blanket statement that the French have not 'stood by' the U.S. is inaccurate.

claim: "Repeated requests for additional security in Benghazi were routinely denied" by Hillary "Clinton’s State Department."
rationale: Multiple investigations (including the State Department Accountability Review Board and congressional inquiries) found that requests for additional security in Libya were made and that the State Department did not provide all requested resources. However, the characterization that such requests were 'routinely denied' by 'Hillary Clinton’s State Department' is an overstatement: decisions involved multiple bureaus, resource constraints, and no credible finding that Clinton personally or her office systematically and repeatedly denied security requests.

claim: "Registered Republican not allowed to vote."
rationale: The claim as a blanket statement is false: being a registered Republican does not disqualify someone from voting. Party registration typically only affects which partisan primary you may vote in; it does not bar participation in general elections. Exceptions to voting eligibility (felony disenfranchisement, residency, age, court-ordered incapacity, or administrative removal) apply regardless of party and are not specific to Republicans.

claim: After Hurricane Katrina, "Dallas and San Antonio took in 5,000 to 10,000 refugees each, but (Bill) White brought in 250,000 and put them up in his 'buddies' empty apartment buildings and let the federal government pay their rents for over two years. They did not return to New Orleans, most of them are on welfare."
rationale: The claim bundles several demonstrably unsupported assertions: contemporary reporting and public records do not show Mayor Bill White 'brought in 250,000' Katrina refugees into apartments owned by his 'buddies' with the federal government paying rents for over two years. Houston did shelter and assist tens of thousands of evacuees and federal programs provided temporary housing and rental assistance, but the specific figure, alleged crony placements, multi-year federally-paid rents, and the blanket claim that 'most of them are on welfare' are not supported by evidence.

claim: Says "about 100,000 kids in this country leave their home state and go to another state to be educated. Out of that 100,000 young people, 30,000 of them are from New Jersey, by far the largest amount."
rationale: The numeric claim is not supported by general U.S. education data and is vague about who “kids” are and what timeframe is meant. National postsecondary enrollment statistics indicate many more than 100,000 students attend school outside their home state overall, and there is no evidence that New Jersey accounts for roughly 30% of that population. Without a precise definition or source, the 100,000/30,000 figures are implausible.

claim: Photo shows R. Kelly being released from prison in 2021.
rationale: There is no credible record that R. Kelly was released from prison in 2021; he remained in custody on federal and state charges through 2021 and was later convicted in 2022. Viral images claiming to show his 2021 release have been debunked or lack verifiable provenance tied to an actual release event that year.

claim: "Between late December of 2020 and last month, a total of 3,362 people apparently died after getting the COVID vaccine in the United States … The actual number is almost certainly higher."
rationale: The statement conflates raw reports of deaths following vaccination with proven vaccine-caused deaths. The Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) and similar sources can show thousands of reports of deaths that occurred after COVID vaccination, but these are unverified temporal associations and do not establish causation; health authorities’ reviews have confirmed only a very small number of vaccine-related fatal events. The claim also gives an ambiguous timeframe ('last month') and implicitly suggests the raw count equals confirmed vaccine deaths, which is misleading.

claim: "Polls show that Floridians don't want to repeal the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization: polling in Florida has produced mixed results depending on timing and how questions are worded. Some surveys have found pluralities or majorities opposing outright repeal, while others show sizable support for repeal or replace options, so it’s inaccurate to claim polls uniformly show Floridians don't want repeal.

claim: Says Obama opposes offshore drilling and a gas tax holiday.
rationale: This claim mixes two different positions: Barack Obama did publicly oppose a short-term federal gas tax holiday, arguing it would do little for consumers and mainly help oil companies. However, he did not categorically oppose all offshore drilling — he opposed opening certain sensitive areas and said drilling alone wasn't the solution, while supporting some domestic oil and offshore leasing under regulation.

claim: "Donald Trump praises Colonel Sanders for his service in the Civil War."
rationale: Harland 'Colonel' Sanders was born in 1890 and died in 1980, while the U.S. Civil War ended in 1865, so he could not have served in that war. There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump praised Sanders for Civil War service; at most public remarks about Sanders refer to his restaurant/brand or persona, not Civil War military service.

claim: Says "I've authored the first bipartisan tax reform bill in a quarter-century."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it lacks any specific bill, author, jurisdiction, or date; without that context there is no way to confirm that no bipartisan tax reform bill existed in the prior 25 years. Tax legislation and the degree of bipartisanship vary by country and time, and multiple tax bills have had bipartisan support in various jurisdictions over recent decades. Because the statement is specific and historical but provides no identifying details, I rate it as false pending corroboration.

claim: The "moon has more than 250 million citizens."
rationale: There are no permanent inhabitants or recognized citizens on the Moon; only a small number of astronauts have visited or walked on the surface (12 people walked on the Moon). No sovereign lunar state or system of citizenship exists, so the claim that the Moon has over 250 million citizens is incorrect.

claim: Says "I never billed a single hour of my time to the City of Portland in the last 10 years -- so, no revolving door."
rationale: I cannot verify the speaker's identity or access to City of Portland billing records, so the specific factual claim that they "never billed a single hour" over ten years is unverified. Even if true, the assertion that this alone means "no revolving door" is logically weak: revolving-door concerns can arise from unpaid consulting, non-billable work, indirect financial relationships, or other forms of influence. Without independent records and a clear definition of "revolving door," the combined claim is not supported.

claim: "Inflation has gone up every month of the Biden presidency and just hit another 40-year high."
rationale: This is false. Consumer inflation did not rise every month of the Biden presidency—CPI monthly changes were not monotonically increasing and there were months with smaller increases and some with declines—and although year‑over‑year inflation hit a roughly 40‑year high in mid‑2022 (around 9.1%), it did not 'just hit another' 40‑year high afterward.

claim: "I can tell you with certainty (cap and trade) would have a devastating impact on our economy."
rationale: The statement asserts certainty that cap-and-trade would have a 'devastating' impact on the economy, which is a predictive and value-laden claim that cannot be known with certainty. Empirical analyses and economic models show a wide range of outcomes depending on program design, scope, allowance allocation, and revenue recycling; many implemented cap-and-trade programs produced modest macroeconomic effects and concentrated costs in particular sectors rather than uniformly devastating results.

claim: Says a photo shows an ambushed Los Angeles police officer and that the NFL intends to "honor and praise the organization" that stood outside of the hospital chanting, "We hope she dies."
rationale: The claim conflates a misidentified photo with an unsubstantiated accusation about the NFL. There is no credible reporting or official NFL statement showing the league intended to 'honor and praise' an organization that stood outside a hospital chanting 'We hope she dies,' and similar social-media posts have been debunked for misidentifying images and inventing links between unrelated events.

claim: Seth Magaziner "plans to spend billions more of your money."
rationale: The statement is a vague political attack without specific context (timeframe, what 'more' is compared to, or which proposals are meant). I cannot verify that Seth Magaziner made or proposed an identifiable plan that indisputably entails 'spending billions more of your money' as phrased. Without concrete policy proposals or documented budget figures tied to this claim, it is not supported as stated.

claim: "Bernie Sanders wants free health care for all and was asked how he would pay for it. His answer was raise taxes to 52% on anybody making over $29,000 per year."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has advocated Medicare-for-All funded through tax changes and other revenue sources, but he did not propose raising taxes to a 52% rate on everyone making over $29,000. Independent fact-checkers and the text of Sanders' proposals show the 52% figure is a mischaracterization or conflation of different tax measures or combined burdens, not a stated policy to tax all earners above $29k at 52%.

claim: The Obama administration "went to court to keep one of these five in jail at Guantanamo just three years ago because he was such a huge risk."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by the public record: while the Obama administration did defend detentions in habeas litigation and used Periodic Review Boards, there is no clear, documented instance where the administration 'went to court to keep one of these five in jail at Guantanamo just three years ago' in the way the statement implies. The well-known case of the 2014 exchange of five Taliban detainees (for Bowe Bergdahl) involved review processes and diplomatic arrangements rather than a discrete recent court filing to retain one of those five in custody. The timeline and phrasing in the claim do not match available facts.

claim: "In 2014 ... in McDowell County, W.Va., one of the poorest counties in the nation, life expectancy for men was 64 years. In Fairfax County, Va., a wealthy county, just 350 miles away, life expectancy was nearly 82 years, an 18 year differential. The life expectancy gap for women in the two counties was 12 years."
rationale: County-level life-expectancy estimates for 2014 show that men in McDowell County, WV had an unusually low life expectancy (around 64 years) while men in Fairfax County, VA were near 82 years, yielding roughly an 18-year gap; the female gap between the two counties is reported to be about 12 years. These specific figures have been widely reported based on 2014 county life-expectancy estimates.

claim: "Women in Oregon are paid 79 cents for every dollar paid to men. If the wage gap was eliminated, a working woman in Oregon would have enough money for 2,877 gallons of gas, 72 more weeks of food for her family or nearly 12 more months of rent."
rationale: The claim bundles a specific pay-gap ratio and precise purchasing-power calculations without citing a year, data source, or assumptions. State pay-gap figures vary by year, data set (median vs. mean, full-time vs. all workers) and demographic adjustments, and the stated gallons/weeks/months numbers depend on arbitrary price and earnings assumptions so cannot be verified as a general factual statement.

claim: Says "in Oregon only 41 percent of adults have ever been tested" for HIV.
rationale: The 41% figure corresponds to a national estimate often cited by the CDC for U.S. adults who have ever been tested for HIV, not a confirmed statistic specifically for Oregon. State-level survey data (BRFSS and state health department reports) vary by year and demographics, so attributing the 41% figure directly to Oregon without a dated source is likely incorrect.

claim: Florida’s coastal and stormwater infrastructure are "two of the most critical areas during a storm, and received D-plus and D ratings, respectively, by the American Society of Civil Engineers in 2016."
rationale: The American Society of Civil Engineers’ 2016 Florida Infrastructure Report Card gave Florida’s coastal infrastructure a D+ and its stormwater infrastructure a D, and highlighted both as especially important vulnerabilities during storms. The quoted ratings and the characterization of them as critical in storm events match the 2016 ASCE assessment.

claim: "Greg Abbott said it would be a ‘waste’ to expand pre-k to all Texas children."
rationale: I am not aware of any reliable record of Gov. Greg Abbott using the exact phrase that expanding pre-K to all Texas children would be a ‘waste.’ While Abbott has expressed skepticism about large, costly universal programs and emphasized targeted early education spending, I could not confirm a direct quote with that wording. Without a verifiable citation, the specific claim as quoted should be treated as false or unverified.

claim: Says Kelly Loeffler is "for getting rid of health care in the middle of a pandemic."
rationale: The statement is a misleading oversimplification. Kelly Loeffler has a record of opposing the Affordable Care Act and supporting repeal or state flexibility around federal health rules, but there is no clear evidence she explicitly advocated eliminating all health care “in the middle of a pandemic”; she also supported COVID-19 relief measures in Congress. The claim appears to be political hyperbole rather than an accurate description of a specific policy position or statement.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "has pledged to eliminate" the U.S. Department of Education, which would end federal aid to college students.
rationale: Ted Cruz has publicly advocated abolishing the U.S. Department of Education, but dismantling the agency would not automatically end federal student aid. Federal grants and loans are authorized by statute and could be transferred to another agency or continued by Congress unless those programs were specifically repealed.

claim: Under a public health care option, 120 million Americans will "lose what they now get from private companies and be forced onto the government-run rolls as businesses decide it is more cost-effective for them to drop coverage."
rationale: This specific claim is unsupported and appears exaggerated. Reputable nonpartisan analyses of public-option proposals have not projected that 120 million people would be forced to lose private coverage; effects depend on policy design and tend to show smaller, voluntary shifts rather than employers uniformly dropping coverage. Typical public-option designs do not compel businesses to terminate employer-sponsored plans or 'force' workers onto government rolls.

claim: "The gas station where they initially attacked" Kyle Rittenhouse "is owned by his grandparents."
rationale: Contemporary news reports and publicly available information do not show that the gas station where Kyle Rittenhouse was initially confronted was owned by his grandparents. Rittenhouse did live with his grandparents, which may have led to confusion, but ownership of that gas station has not been credibly tied to them.

claim: A lawyer demanded "several Houston pastors hand over to the city government many of their private papers, including their sermons."
rationale: I find no credible reporting or historical record that a lawyer formally demanded multiple Houston pastors turn over many private papers and sermons to the city government as quoted. Such a sweeping compelled seizure of clergy records would be a major First Amendment and privacy controversy and almost certainly would have been widely reported; the absence of reliable sources makes the claim unverified and likely false.

claim: "A golf course closes somewhere in America every 48 hours."
rationale: The claim presents a sweeping present-tense rate that is not supported by current industry data. While industry reports (e.g., from the National Golf Foundation and trade press) documented high closure rates in past decades—sometimes approaching one course every 48 hours for specific years or periods—closure rates have varied over time and by region and are not uniformly one course every 48 hours across 'America' today.

claim: Says she "wiped out" the state Agriculture Department’s inspections of eggs at retail sites like grocery stores.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and lacks a named subject, date, location, or source; I could not verify any specific instance in which a identified official explicitly said she 'wiped out' state Agriculture Department inspections of eggs at retail sites. Without a verifiable attribution or corroborating evidence (quotes, press release, legislation, or reputable reporting) the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: The Affordable Care Act "will likely go down as the biggest tax increase in history."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did include new taxes (e.g., net investment income tax, additional Medicare payroll tax, excise taxes) but budget analyses from the Congressional Budget Office and Joint Committee on Taxation scored the law as a modest revenue raiser and net deficit reducer over its first decade, not an unprecedented tax surge. Historically, U.S. tax increases tied to World War I, World War II, and major revenue acts were far larger when measured in absolute terms and as a share of GDP.

claim: "Military tribunals start Jan. 20, 2021."
rationale: There is no evidence or official order that 'military tribunals' were set to begin on January 20, 2021; that date was the presidential inauguration and no nationwide military tribunal process began then. Claims that mass military trials would start on that day were part of unfounded speculation and misinformation and were not borne out by government announcements or reporting.

claim: Says President Obama has "doubled" the deficit.
rationale: The claim is false as stated: President Obama did not "double" the annual federal budget deficit. Annual deficits peaked around the 2009 crisis and then generally fell through his terms; what did rise substantially during his presidency was the federal debt (the accumulated national debt nearly doubled), which is a different measure than the yearly deficit.

claim: "We’re losing almost 6,000 state jobs."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it provides no jurisdiction, timeframe, or source. Without those specifics, the precise figure of "almost 6,000 state jobs" cannot be confirmed and is unsubstantiated; such a claim would require official state payroll, layoff, or budget documentation to verify.

claim: "This past (legislative) session, we passed out of the Legislature a resolution requiring Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment to the (U.S.) Constitution."
rationale: A single state legislature cannot unilaterally require Congress to enact a constitutional amendment. States can pass nonbinding resolutions urging Congress to act or submit applications under Article V for a convention of states, but those measures do not compel Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment on their own.

claim: "Withheld union dues fund half of Dem (Democratic) campaigns in Florida."
rationale: There is no evidence that 'withheld union dues' fund half of Democratic campaigns in Florida. Campaign finance disclosures show Florida Democrats are financed by a mix of individual donors, PACs, party committees, and some union political spending, but union political contributions (which are typically made via separate voluntary PACs or opt-in deductions) do not constitute 50% of Democratic campaign funding. U.S. and state rules also generally prohibit using compulsory dues directly for political contributions, so the phrasing 'withheld union dues' is misleading.

claim: "Last year, there were an additional 81,000 pages of government regulations. If you stack that up, it would be a three-story building."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions: that ‘last year’ exactly 81,000 pages of government regulations were added, and that those pages stacked would form a three‑story building. The precise 81,000 figure is unverified because the number of regulatory pages (e.g., Federal Register pages) varies year to year and the claim gives no year or definition of what counts as ‘government regulations.’ While a stack of ~81,000 standard sheets would plausibly be on the order of 25–35 feet (roughly 2.5–3.5 stories depending on story height and paper thickness), the factual core — that last year produced 81,000 new regulatory pages — is not supported as stated.

claim: Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker’s estimate of a $3.6 billion state budget deficit is "manufactured" and a "bogus figure."
rationale: The $3.6 billion shortfall cited by Gov. Walker was derived from official state budget projections (Department of Administration and the nonpartisan Legislative Fiscal Bureau) for the relevant biennium; opponents criticized the assumptions and inclusion/exclusion of one‑time fixes and fund shifts but offered no evidence that the figure was fabricated. The dispute was over accounting and presentation, not that the number was a purely 'manufactured' or 'bogus' invention.

claim: "Trump’s DHS secretary confirms they are preparing to arrest sanctuary city leaders."
rationale: There is no verifiable public statement from a Trump-era DHS secretary confirming a plan to arrest sanctuary-city leaders. DHS and DOJ officials at times threatened enforcement measures or withholding funds, but arresting municipal officials for adopting sanctuary policies would be legally unusual and was not announced as an operational policy by DHS.

claim: Marc Molinaro "has cut taxes, his budget now is lower than it was six years ago" in Dutchess County
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely false as stated: county budgets and spending typically increase over multi‑year periods due to inflation and service needs, and there is no clear evidence that Dutchess County’s overall budget is lower than it was six years earlier. While Marc Molinaro has at times highlighted tax savings or rate changes, such statements often refer to specific measures (tax rate, levy, or particular fees) rather than total county budget. Without a precise metric and year range the broad claim that the county budget is now lower is unsupported.

claim: "We have spent $7 trillion, trillion with a T, $7 trillion in the Middle East."
rationale: The claim is presented as an unqualified fact but is misleading: direct U.S. war appropriations for post‑9/11 conflicts are on the order of about $1.5–$2.5 trillion, while broader estimates that add long‑term veterans' care, interest, and economic costs vary widely and are often cited in the $4–8 trillion range. Whether the total is exactly $7 trillion depends entirely on which costs and time period are included, so the categorical statement without context is inaccurate.

claim: The newly created state Immigration Enforcement Review Board "can actually prosecute, and get them [violators] into jail, if we bring in the attorney general."
rationale: Administrative review boards generally have civil enforcement powers (fines, license actions) but do not themselves bring criminal prosecutions. Only prosecutors (such as a state attorney general or local district attorney) can file criminal charges that could lead to jail, and they will do so only if the evidence and statutes support criminal conduct. Saying the board "can actually prosecute, and get them into jail" conflates the board's administrative role with prosecutorial authority.

claim: Says Donald Trump "says organized crime runs wild on reservations."
rationale: I am not aware of a clear, attributable quote in which Donald Trump explicitly said the exact phrase 'organized crime runs wild on reservations.' While he has on occasion criticized crime and governance on some Native American reservations, there is no well-documented source for that precise wording and the claim appears to be a paraphrase or possible misattribution.

claim: "PELOSI says if President TRUMP wins, she will resign!!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news reporting that Nancy Pelosi said she would resign if Donald Trump wins. The statement appears to be a social-media rumor or misattribution rather than a documented public pledge by Pelosi.

claim: Says a military Humvee labeled "COVID-19 quarantine team" was on Interstate 696 in Michigan.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an official military Humvee labeled 'COVID-19 quarantine team' was traveling on I-696 in Michigan; similar images circulated early in the pandemic were shown to be doctored or miscaptioned. U.S. military and National Guard units do not use informal, alarmist signage like that on operational vehicles, and independent fact-checks found no confirmation of this specific incident.

claim: Teachers "are working their third consecutive year -- some longer than that -- without salary increases."
rationale: The claim is presented as a general statement without specifying a location or time period, but teacher salary changes are determined locally and vary widely. Some districts and states did authorize raises in recent years while others implemented freezes or cuts, so the blanket assertion that teachers broadly are in a third consecutive year without increases cannot be verified and is misleading as stated.

claim: "There aren't too many people outside protesting" his speech at the Phoenix Convention Center.
rationale: The statement asserts a specific crowd size at a particular event but provides no date, time, or supporting evidence. Crowd levels at protests fluctuate and require contemporaneous photographic, media, or official counts to verify; without such evidence the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as unverified/false.

claim: Trump supporters are heading to the border as the migrant caravan approaches.
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks verifiable, contemporary evidence: it does not specify which border, which caravan, or when, and there are no authoritative reports confirming a broad, coordinated movement of "Trump supporters" to the border tied to a specific caravan. While isolated individuals or small groups have in the past traveled to borders in response to migration events, that does not substantiate the generalized present-tense statement as stated.

claim: America’s federal business tax rate is the highest "in the world."
rationale: The U.S. statutory federal corporate tax rate was cut to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which is not the highest national corporate tax rate in the world. Other countries have statutory national corporate rates or sector-specific rates that exceed 21%, and historically the U.S. top federal rate (35% before 2018) was high but not uniquely the highest globally.

claim: Says Iranian Gen. Qassem Soleimani "was a designated terrorist by President Obama, who didn't do anything about it."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate in two ways: U.S. sanctions and terrorism designations are typically issued by agencies (Treasury/State), not personally 'by President Obama,' and although the U.S. had sanctioned Qassem Soleimani and his Quds Force, the Obama administration did not personally 'designate' him in the manner implied. It is also misleading to say Obama "didn't do anything about it" — the administration took sanctions and other measures but did not carry out a lethal strike against Soleimani (the strike that killed him occurred under President Trump).

claim: Joe Biden’s eyes were black during the debate because he was wearing Mojo Vision lenses.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden wore Mojo Vision contact lenses during the debate, and Mojo Vision’s AR contact-lens technology has been a prototype research product not distributed for public use. The dark appearance of his eyes in some footage is plausibly explained by camera lighting, exposure, reflections, or natural pupil dilation and video processing artifacts rather than specialized contacts.

claim: Says the Trump administration’s new policy for legal immigrants on welfare "has been around for a while. This is not a new thing that the president is trying to implement here, that the United States has been this way."
