Public reports and studies produce wide, contested ranges (often cited as hundreds of billions across multiple years and types of loss), and scholars and agencies disagree on methods and attribution, so a precise $360 billion-for-last-year claim is not supported.

claim: In Wisconsin, because a key provision of the Voting Rights Act was not in effect,  "somewhere between 40,000 and 80,000 people were turned away from the polls (in 2016) because of the color of their skin" and other factors.
rationale: The claim conflates the 2013 Supreme Court decision that gutted the Voting Rights Act’s preclearance provision with an asserted figure of 40,000–80,000 people in Wisconsin being turned away in 2016; there is no credible evidence or official count showing that tens of thousands were denied voting that year for being a particular race. State and academic analyses of the 2016 election report only small numbers of provisional or rejected ballots and do not support an estimate of that magnitude attributable to racial exclusion. While voting changes and ID laws in Wisconsin were controversial and may have depressed turnout for some groups, the specific 40,000–80,000 figure is unsubstantiated.

claim: Kelly Ayotte "voted for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants."
rationale: The $90 billion figure commonly cited refers to projected reductions in Pell Grant spending in a Republican budget proposal, not an enacted cut that a senator directly voted to implement. Kelly Ayotte did not vote to enact a law that literally cut $90 billion from Pell Grants; claims conflate support for a budget resolution or related proposals with an actual, enacted $90 billion cut.

claim: Says Proposition 205 "blocks market entry" for new marijuana dispensaries.
rationale: Proposition 205 was a legalization/regulatory measure rather than an outright ban on new dispensaries; it set up a licensing framework and allowed local governments to restrict or ban retail outlets, which can limit but does not categorically 'block market entry.' Saying it 'blocks market entry' is an overstatement without additional context about local bans or temporary licensing limits.

claim: The expanded child tax credit in the Build Back Better Act has "no means testing," so people making $200,000 and $400,000 would get "the same as someone making" $70,000.
rationale: The expanded child tax credit in proposals and the 2021 American Rescue Plan included income phaseouts and thresholds (for example the ARP’s enhanced amounts phased out for single filers above $75,000 and married filers above $150,000). Therefore taxpayers with $200,000 or $400,000 in income would not necessarily receive the same enhanced credit as someone making $70,000.

claim: The Atlanta Beltline paid nearly $3.5 million for less than a quarter-acre.
rationale: There is no well-documented, verifiable instance that clearly shows the Atlanta BeltLine paid nearly $3.5 million specifically for a single parcel smaller than a quarter-acre. Reporting on BeltLine land acquisitions does show some high per-acre costs in urban parcels, but the claim as stated appears to conflate figures or lacks the necessary parcel/date detail to be confirmed.

claim: Says President Barack Obama has "been presiding over our jobs going overseas for seven years."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Barack Obama was president from January 2009 to January 2017 (nearly eight years), and while some jobs were offshored during his tenure, the U.S. economy overall added millions of jobs during his presidency and manufacturing employment partially recovered after the recession. Claiming he 'been presiding over our jobs going overseas for seven years' implies a clear, sustained causal responsibility and a seven-year-only timeframe that is not supported by the broad employment data.

claim: Forty percent of union members voted Republican in 2008.
rationale: 2008 exit polls and surveys show union members/households tilted strongly toward Barack Obama, with Obama receiving roughly 60–65% of the union vote and John McCain in the mid-30s percent range. That means about one-third, not forty percent, of union voters backed the Republican candidate, so the precise claim that 40% voted Republican is incorrect.

claim: NBC News "covered up Hunter Biden laptop story."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that NBC News 'covered up' the Hunter Biden laptop story. NBC and many other mainstream outlets initially expressed caution about the provenance of the material and contextualized or delayed unverified claims, but NBC published reporting related to the laptop and subsequent reporting by multiple outlets corroborated elements of the material.

claim: Says a poll showed Democrat Beto O’Rourke within 2 percentage points of Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.
rationale: During the 2018 Texas Senate campaign multiple reputable polls at different points showed Beto O’Rourke within two percentage points of Ted Cruz. Polling in October 2018 was especially tight and several individual surveys reported 1–2 point margins, so the generic claim that “a poll showed” such a margin is accurate.

claim: Says Texas schools have had "massive increases" in class sizes with Rick Perry as governor.
rationale: The claim is too broad and not supported by available statewide evidence: class-size trends in Texas during Rick Perry's long tenure (2000–2015) varied by level and district and do not show a consistent, statewide 'massive' increase across the period. Some districts saw increases in certain years (often tied to budget cuts), but aggregated state data indicate modest fluctuations rather than a large, uniform jump in class sizes under Perry.

claim: Says Tammy Baldwin supports a law "in which government will take over your decisions on medicine, on doctors and on hospitals."
rationale: The statement is a partisan characterization rather than an accurate description of Tammy Baldwin’s stated positions. Baldwin has supported expanding government-funded health coverage (e.g., Medicare-for-All-style proposals and other public options), but she has not advocated that the government literally take over individual medical decision-making by personally choosing patients’ doctors, treatments, or hospitals. The phrase quoted is hyperbolic and misrepresents the kind of systemic financing and coverage changes she has backed.

claim: Says six eradicated diseases such as whooping cough and the bubonic plague are making a comeback "thanks to refugees and illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on multiple counts: diseases named (for example, whooping cough/pertussis and bubonic plague) were not globally eradicated and are known to persist or re-emerge for reasons unrelated to refugees or 'illegal immigrants.' Public health authorities attribute resurgences to factors like waning immunity, reduced vaccination coverage, surveillance gaps, and endemic animal reservoirs, not a general causal link to refugees or migrants.

claim: Government subsidies for renewable energies such as wind and solar are 100 times greater than those given to gas and coal, and 50 times greater than what the nuclear industry enjoys.
rationale: The blanket multipliers in the claim are not supported by available evidence. Subsidy levels depend heavily on definitions (direct payments, tax breaks, price supports, or externality costs), time period, and country; authoritative analyses (IMF, IEA, OECD and national budgets) show fossil fuels often receive large direct and indirect support and that renewables are not universally subsidized at 100× the levels of gas/coal nor 50× those of nuclear. While some renewables have received high per‑unit support during deployment phases, that does not validate the absolute multipliers stated.

claim: "Democrat Senators high-five after voting in favor of late-term abortion."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that Democratic U.S. Senators collectively "high-fived" specifically after voting in favor of a measure described as "late-term abortion." Viral clips that purport to show this have been misattributed or taken out of context, and roll-call records and credible news reports do not corroborate the claim.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will ... force local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks."
rationale: The U.S. president does not have unilateral authority to compel local governments to permit camping in municipal parks, and there is no record of President Obama announcing a plan to force local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks. Federal power over local park rules is limited by federalism, and any federal intervention would require specific legal grounds or legislation.

claim: Says YouTube removed Tucker Carlson’s interview with Tony Bobulinski.
rationale: I am not aware of credible reporting or evidence that YouTube permanently removed Tucker Carlson’s interview with Tony Bobulinski; major takedowns of high-profile interviews are typically widely reported. It’s possible there was a temporary restriction, age or content labeling, or removal from recommendation surfaces, but a wholesale removal has not been substantiated.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court decided in 1982 that non-citizen children must get free K-12 education.
rationale: In Plyler v. Doe (1982) the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a Texas law that excluded undocumented children from public schools, holding that states cannot deny free public K–12 education to children based on immigration status under the Equal Protection Clause. The decision effectively requires state and local public schools to provide free K–12 education to undocumented (non‑citizen) children.

claim: "There have been zero reported instances of any child born alive after an abortion in Texas."
rationale: The absolute claim that there have been zero reported instances in Texas is unlikely to be true. Government records, legal cases, and investigative reporting have documented rare instances of infants surviving attempted abortions in the United States, and reporting practices and definitions vary by state — investigations have identified at least some reports tied to Texas rather than a definitive zero.

claim: Says that under President Obama, there’s been a substantial increase in federal government jobs.
rationale: Federal civilian employment did not rise substantially during Barack Obama’s presidency; BLS/OPM data show the federal civilian workforce was roughly flat to slightly lower over 2009–2017, even while state and local government jobs increased during the recovery. Only by changing definitions (e.g., counting contractors or certain military categories) can one claim a large federal job increase.

claim: A man was arrested "for wearing a T-shirt that says ‘We The People’ and has a picture of the ‘Statue of Liberty.’"
rationale: There are no reputable news reports corroborating that a person was arrested solely for wearing a T‑shirt reading 'We The People' with a Statue of Liberty image. In contexts like the United States, purely political apparel is protected speech and an arrest for that alone would be extraordinary and widely reported; many viral claims like this omit critical context such as trespassing, disorderly conduct, or being in a jurisdiction with different laws.

claim: Schools stopped teaching children cursive so they wouldn’t be able to read the U.S. Constitution and other historical documents.
rationale: There is no evidence of a coordinated effort to stop teaching cursive in order to prevent reading the U.S. Constitution. Curriculum changes in many districts and the Common Core's lack of a cursive requirement led schools to de-emphasize cursive in favor of keyboarding and other priorities; some states later reinstated cursive instruction. The change is policy/practical, not a documented conspiratorial intent.

claim: "Texas legislators have filed voucher proposals in every legislative session since 1995, but all of them have failed to become law."
rationale: The claim is too absolute: while Texas legislators have repeatedly filed voucher and education savings account proposals in many sessions since the 1990s and the state has not enacted a broad statewide voucher/ESA program, it is not verifiable that a voucher bill was filed in every single biennial session since 1995 nor that literally all voucher-like measures have uniformly failed. Narrow, targeted programs or tax-credit scholarship changes and many bill introductions complicate the blanket statement.

claim: State budget cuts for local schools resulted in "nearly 4,000 educator layoffs"
rationale: The claim lacks any identifying details (which state and what time period) and cannot be verified as a general statement. Layoffs tied to state budget cuts vary widely by state and year; without a named jurisdiction and source, the figure “nearly 4,000 educator layoffs” is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says CNN deleted an online poll showing Bernie Sanders won the first Democratic presidential debate to help out Hillary Clinton.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that CNN deleted an online poll to favor Hillary Clinton after the first Democratic debate. Fact-checkers and CNN statements indicate online, non-scientific polls are often removed or closed for policy and technical reasons, and investigators found no proof of deliberate manipulation to boost Clinton.

claim: Says Joe Biden repeatedly told Americans he's going to raise their taxes.
rationale: This is inaccurate: throughout his campaign and presidency Joe Biden repeatedly pledged not to raise taxes on households earning under $400,000 and emphasized tax increases would target corporations and high-income earners. While he has said he will raise taxes on the wealthy and certain corporations, he did not repeatedly tell the general public that he would raise "their" taxes broadly.

claim: "Two-thirds of our kids can’t read at grade level."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and therefore unsupported as a blanket claim. While some U.S. assessments (for example NAEP 4th-grade reading) show roughly two-thirds of students score below the NAEP 'proficient' level, 'can’t read at grade level' depends on the country, grade, and the assessment/standard used, so the universal claim is misleading.

claim: "In every single country, she had a majority of the vote -- or more of those who'd already made up their minds."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute, universal result across every country without specifying who "she" is, what vote or poll is being referenced, or the time period. No credible evidence supports that any individual has held a majority (or majority of decided voters) in every single country, and such a universal statement is implausible and unverified.

claim: Says John McAfee tweeted before his death that he stored computer files in the Florida condo building that later collapsed.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that John McAfee tweeted he had stored computer files in the Florida condo that later collapsed. The claim appears to stem from unverified social-media posts and misattributions rather than an archived, attributable tweet from McAfee’s account.

claim: "We didn't go out and take" information from the Hillary Clinton campaign.
rationale: The claim as presented is ambiguous — without knowing who 'we' refers to or which actions are meant it cannot be verified. Public evidence from the 2016 U.S. election shows hacked Clinton campaign/DNC emails were obtained and published by third parties, and categorical denials by actors implicated have often been contradicted by forensic and intelligence findings. Given the lack of context and the weight of available evidence in many relevant cases, the blanket statement is likely false.

claim: Sarah Palin endorsed a Wasilla policy that charged sexual assault victims for their "rape kits."
rationale: Contemporary fact-checks and municipal records show Wasilla did not directly bill sexual assault victims for forensic evidence kits while Palin was mayor. The city’s policy involved pursuing reimbursement from insurers or state victim-compensation funds rather than charging victims out-of-pocket, and Palin did not endorse a policy of directly billing victims.

claim: Says the House Rules Committee is the only panel, other than the Intelligence and Ethics committees, not able to telecast proceedings in its main hearing room.
rationale: The claim's exclusivity is unsupported: while the Intelligence and Ethics committees are widely known to restrict televising, House camera and telecast policies vary across committees and over time, and other panels have had restrictions or different arrangements. There is no clear authoritative basis that the Rules Committee is the only additional committee barred from televising in its main hearing room.

claim: "We spend twice as much per capita on health care as any other nation on Earth."
rationale: The United States does spend more per capita on health care than any other large wealthy country, but it is not typically twice as much. OECD and World Bank data across recent years show U.S. per‑capita health spending around $10,000–$13,000 while the next‑highest countries generally spend several thousand dollars less, producing ratios around 1.3–1.8x, not 2x.

claim: "For every extra year that a girl stays in secondary school, her chance of getting infected with HIV/AIDS decreases by half."
rationale: Empirical research does show that more schooling for girls is associated with lower HIV risk, but no robust evidence supports a universal effect size of a 50% reduction in infection risk for each additional year of secondary school. Reported effects are much smaller, vary by country and intervention, and often reflect associations rather than a guaranteed causal halving per year.

claim: The "48, 49 percent" that supports President Barack Obama are "people who pay no income tax."
rationale: This statement conflates a tax-statistic with political support. While analyses for some years showed roughly 47–49% of households owed no federal individual income tax after credits/exemptions, that group is not identical to the share of Obama supporters; polling and exit-data indicate many Obama voters did pay federal income tax, and many in the "no income tax" category still pay payroll and state taxes.

claim: In annual surveys of Rhode Island communities that receive Drug Free community grants, many report that more than 50 percent of youth surveyed do not think daily marijuana use poses any serious risk of harm.
rationale: I cannot verify that many Rhode Island Drug-Free Communities grantees’ annual surveys show a majority of youth reporting that daily marijuana use poses no serious risk. While national data indicate a decline in perceived harm from marijuana among adolescents, I found no specific, publicly available Rhode Island DFC survey results that clearly support the precise claim as stated.

claim: "Chinese lunar rover finds no evidence of American moon landings."
rationale: No credible report shows a Chinese lunar rover searched Apollo landing sites and found no evidence. Chinese rovers (e.g., Chang'e 3/4) touched down at different locations and did not survey the U.S. Apollo sites; independent evidence for Apollo hardware exists from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images, retroreflectors left on the Moon, and returned samples. The claim misstates what Chinese missions did and ignores established observations confirming the U.S. landings.

claim: Says rival Jill Karofsky wants "to disarm law abiding citizens."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Jill Karofsky has explicitly advocated for blanket disarmament of law‑abiding citizens. Public reporting and her stated positions reflect support for gun‑safety measures (for example red‑flag laws and expanded background checks) aimed at restricting access for dangerous individuals, which opponents sometimes characterize hyperbolically as "disarming" but which are not calls for universal confiscation.

claim: Says Tom Barrett plans "to spend $100 million on a trolley that goes barely two miles on the east side of Milwaukee."
rationale: As Milwaukee mayor Tom Barrett championed the city's streetcar starter line (The Hop), a roughly 2.1-mile downtown/East Side route, with projected costs often described around $100 million. Media and public records show he supported spending and seeking funding for the project, though final cost estimates varied.

claim: "Back in the Great Recession, when millions of  jobs across America hung in the balance, Donald Trump said rescuing the auto industry didn’t really matter very much. He said, and I quote again, ‘Let it go.’ "
rationale: Contemporary news reports and archived video from 2008 show Donald Trump publicly opposed rescuing the auto industry during the Great Recession and used language such as "let it go" (and variations like "let Detroit go bankrupt"). The quoted wording matches his expressed stance at the time, so the claim about him saying "Let it go" is accurate. The statement's framing about jobs is rhetorical context rather than a factual claim about the quote itself.

claim: The Pell bridge "is a tourism bridge essentially and not a commuter bridge."
rationale: The Claiborne Pell (Newport) Bridge is a primary vehicular link on Rhode Island Route 138 connecting Newport with the mainland and is used daily by commuters, goods vehicles and tourists. While it does carry significant seasonal tourist traffic to Newport, it functions as an important regional transportation and commuter route rather than being essentially only a tourism bridge.

claim: "Abortionists have reduced our black population by more than 25 percent since 1973."
rationale: U.S. Census data show the Black population in the United States has grown substantially since 1973, not fallen by 25%. While abortion rates have historically been higher among Black women and thus have reduced the number of births compared with a no-abortion counterfactual, there is no evidence that abortions have cut the total Black population by more than a quarter.

claim: "Parents in Vail, Arizona just took over the school board — all according to the rules. Voted in a whole new board, and immediately removed the mask mandate."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that an entire Vail, Arizona school board was replaced in a single vote and then immediately rescinded a mask mandate as stated. School boards are typically elected seat-by-seat and reporting from known Vail (AZ) board elections indicates contested races and occasional changes in majority, but not a wholesale, same-day replacement of the whole board followed by an immediate mask-ban vote as claimed. The claim lacks a specific date or source and conflates normal seat turnover with a total takeover.

claim: The IAEA, or the International Atomic Energy Agency, "last month said the Iranians are not currently living up to their obligations."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as written because it references “last month” without a date; the IAEA has at times said Iran was not meeting certain safeguards obligations, but whether such a statement was made exactly 'last month' cannot be confirmed from the claim alone. Without a specific timeframe or source, the claim is unverifiable and therefore labeled false for precision.

claim: " ... following World War II war crime trials were convened. The Japanese were tried and convicted and hung for war crimes committed against American POWs. Among those charges for which they were convicted was waterboarding."
rationale: It is true that Japanese personnel were tried, convicted, and in some cases executed after WWII for crimes against Allied POWs, but there is no clear evidence that courts specifically listed the modern term "waterboarding" as an explicit charge. Allied and U.S. military trials commonly charged murder, torture, inhumane treatment or described practices such as the "water cure," but the claim that defendants were convicted specifically for "waterboarding" is misleading and unsupported by standard trial records.

claim: California has instituted a "bacon ban."
rationale: There is no statewide law in California banning bacon or the sale/consumption of pork. Claims about a "bacon ban" usually stem from misreported or isolated institutional menu changes (e.g., at specific universities or facilities) or social-media misinformation, not an enacted statewide prohibition.

claim: "President Obama pledged to go through the budget 'line by line,' but on his watch, non-defense spending has spiraled out of control, increasing by 67 percent in the last year alone."
rationale: It is true Obama said during the 2008 campaign he would go through the budget "line by line," but the claim that non-defense spending increased by 67 percent in the last year alone under his watch is false. Official federal budget/outlay figures and analyses show no one-year rise of that magnitude in non-defense spending during the Obama years; year-to-year changes were much smaller. The 67% figure is inconsistent with standard budget measures and appears to misstate or mis-time the data.

claim: Providence's port is "200 miles closer to Europe than any other Eastern port."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Providence is not 200 miles closer to Europe than every other eastern port. Great‑circle distances from New England and other U.S. East Coast ports to western Europe differ by at most a few dozen miles depending on the exact European destination, not hundreds, and several ports (for example in Maine and Massachusetts) are as close or closer to parts of Europe than Providence. The statement also lacks a clear definition of 'Eastern port' and the European reference point, which makes the large asserted gap implausible.

claim: In the primary election, a "right-wing group spent more than $100,000,000 to support" Supreme Court Justice Rebecca Bradley.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a single right‑wing group spent over $100 million in a primary to support Wisconsin Supreme Court Justice Rebecca Bradley. State supreme court contests, even high‑profile Wisconsin races, have seen outside spending in the tens of millions total and distributed across multiple groups, not a single group's six‑figure‑million outlay.

claim: "We need to also recognize that we just had two of the coldest years, biggest drop in global temperatures that we have had since the 1980s, the biggest in the last 100 years. We don't talk about that."
rationale: Global instrumental temperature records show recent years are among the warmest on record, not the coldest; there is no evidence of 'two of the coldest years' or the 'biggest drop in global temperatures' since the 1980s or in the last 100 years. Year-to-year variations do occur (for example due to El Niño/La Niña), but the long-term trend since the late 19th century is strong warming, and recent years rank near the top for warmth.

claim: Says Democratic opponents Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies.
rationale: The claim that both Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith explicitly 'support sanctuary policies' is not clearly supported by public records. Their public statements and campaign platforms have emphasized immigration reform and protections for immigrant communities, but neither has a clear, uncontested record of endorsing formal sanctuary-city policies as commonly defined. Without explicit, contemporaneous endorsements from both individuals, the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "The federal government spent over $500k trying to force fish to exercise on treadmills, an additional $150k to see if gingerbread houses are earthquake proof."
rationale: This claim misrepresents and conflates research grants and outreach projects. While federal funding has supported scientific work using zebrafish as exercise models and educational demonstrations (including gingerbread-house earthquake demos), fact-checkers have found the framing, purposes and dollar figures in viral versions are exaggerated or taken out of context rather than evidence of literal $500k+$150k frivolous spending.

claim: Says Troy Nehls "called wearing masks 'un-American' and called those who do 'communists.'"
rationale: There is no reliable record that Rep. Troy Nehls explicitly said wearing masks is 'un-American' and directly labeled people who wear them 'communists.' While Nehls has publicly opposed some mask mandates and criticized COVID-19 policies, available media coverage and archived statements do not show him using those exact formulations as quoted.

claim: "Wisconsin ranks No. 2 in economic growth", according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.
rationale: The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia regularly publishes state economic indexes and periodic rankings, but those rankings change over time and the claim gives no date or report reference. Without a specific publication or time period, the statement that "Wisconsin ranks No. 2 in economic growth" cannot be verified as a persistent fact and is therefore not reliably true as written.

claim: Says David Dewhurst skipped nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate candidacy.
rationale: The statement claims Dewhurst skipped nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate run. Contemporary reporting about Dewhurst’s Senate campaigns notes he missed some events, but there is no consistent, authoritative count confirming exactly nine forums skipped; different outlets report different tallies depending on timeframe and what counts as a 'forum.' Without a specific timeframe or source, the precise numeric claim is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: Texas "could be very close to herd immunity."
rationale: The claim is vague and, for SARS‑CoV‑2, inconsistent with available epidemiology: herd immunity requires a high and broadly distributed level of durable immunity, which was not achieved in Texas given uneven vaccination, waning immunity, and the emergence of more transmissible variants that raise the threshold. Seroprevalence and vaccine-coverage patterns did not uniformly meet those thresholds. Therefore the blanket statement that Texas "could be very close to herd immunity" is misleading.

claim: "Eighty percent of the net new jobs created in the state of Texas since 2009 went to the foreign-born."
rationale: I am not aware of credible labor-statistics analyses showing that 80% of net new jobs in Texas since 2009 went to the foreign-born; while immigrants have supplied a large share of employment growth in Texas, published ACS and BLS-based breakdowns for that period report substantially lower shares and vary by end year and sector. The claim also lacks a specified end date and definition of "net new jobs," making the 80% figure implausible without more precise sourcing.

claim: It "is estimated that as many as 300,000 auto workers may be out of a job before the end of the year."
rationale: The claim presents a specific numeric estimate but provides no source or context (country, employer group, or analyst) and I find no authoritative, widely reported forecast that 300,000 auto workers will be out of work by year‑end. Industry and government reports around recent periods cite far smaller, company‑level layoff announcements or longer‑term contraction projections, not an immediate 300,000 job loss figure. Without a cited estimator, the statement appears unsubstantiated.

claim: Says "Rick Perry doubled spending in a decade."
rationale: The claim is vague and, taken at face value, is not supported by readily available budget data: Texas state spending did increase during Rick Perry’s tenure, but it did not unambiguously 'double in a decade' under standard measures. Whether spending doubled depends on the chosen decade, whether you count nominal vs inflation‑adjusted dollars, and whether you include federal funds and local expenditures—none of which make the simple claim reliably true.

claim: "Only sign outside Bucks County voting place. Democrats shown, republicans blurred out. … More scamming in Pennsylvania!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a legitimate election sign in Bucks County displayed Democrats clearly while blurring Republicans to facilitate fraud. Election rules and reporting practices require bipartisan access and such a blatant sign would have been widely documented and denied by local officials; viral images of this type are commonly edited or miscaptioned.

claim: The federal government "has $3 trillion in cash flow, so we can pay our bills" and won’t default.
rationale: This statement is misleading: while the U.S. Treasury regularly receives large inflows, a single cited number like "$3 trillion in cash flow" does not guarantee the government can meet near‑term obligations. Cash balances and receipts fluctuate, and legal constraints such as the statutory debt ceiling and timing mismatches between receipts and payments can create real default risk even when large flows are expected. Therefore the categorical claim that "we won't default" based solely on a $3 trillion cash‑flow figure is unsupported.

claim: Democrats compare the infrastructure programs in the stimulus to the Eisenhower interstate program, "but he proposed a $500 billion highway system, and they're going to put $30 billion" into roads and bridges.
rationale: The claim is misleading: President Eisenhower’s 1956 Federal-Aid Highway Act authorized roughly $25 billion to build the Interstate System, not a nominal $500 billion. While some analysts convert that 1956 figure into today’s dollars (producing widely varying, much larger estimates), presenting a $500 billion number as Eisenhower’s proposal is inaccurate without inflation context. It is true that recent stimulus packages have earmarked roughly $25–30 billion for highways and bridges (e.g., the 2009 ARRA had about $27.5 billion for highways), so the $30 billion figure is approximately correct but the comparison as stated is false.

claim: "We are poised to get rid of over 1,000 more regulations in 2012."
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks a verifiable source: it does not identify who 'we' refers to or what counts as a 'regulation', and I find no authoritative record confirming a plan to eliminate over 1,000 regulations specifically in 2012. Regulatory removals typically require formal rulemaking and publication, and sweeping numeric claims like this are often political rhetoric rather than documented policy commitments.

claim: Americans "say that what they want is a choice" to join a single-payer system like Medicare rather than ending private insurance.
rationale: Multiple national polls consistently show higher public support for a policy that preserves private insurance and offers a government 'public option' or voluntary Medicare-like plan than for single-payer proposals that would eliminate private coverage. When questions explicitly say private insurance would end, support for 'Medicare for All' declines and many respondents say they want a choice to keep their current plan.

claim: "For the second quarter in a row, my campaign has raised more money than any other challenger in the nation and brought our fundraising total to over $800,000."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it does not identify the candidate, the specific quarters, or the definition of 'challenger' used for comparison. Determining whether a campaign raised more than any other challenger for two consecutive quarters and surpassed $800,000 requires checking FEC quarterly filings and independent reporting; absent those specifics the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "This week the House of Representatives voted to remove the word ‘lunatic’ from federal law."
rationale: I cannot verify that the U.S. House of Representatives voted this week to remove the word 'lunatic' from federal law. While Congress has occasionally considered bills to modernize archaic or stigmatizing language in statutes, there is no specific, corroborated record I can confirm here of a vote this week removing that term. Without a bill number, date, or reliable source, the claim is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Too many dead people voted" in Michigan
rationale: Post-election audits, recounts, and investigations in Michigan (notably after the 2020 election) found only isolated instances of votes linked to deceased registrants, often explained by clerical errors or ballots cast before a person's death. Officials and prosecutors did not find evidence of widespread or systemic voting by dead people that would substantiate the claim 'too many dead people voted.'

claim: A state report’s "projection is that approximately half of public employees" would live outside municipal boundaries in a decade if the state bans local residency requirements.
rationale: The claim cites a specific projection but provides no identifiable state or report to verify; without locating the original document, the assertion cannot be confirmed. Projections about residency effects vary widely by state, job type, and modeling assumptions, so a blanket statement that 'approximately half' would live outside municipal boundaries in a decade is not reliably established here.

claim: A state senate bill would "criminalize a father teaching his own son how to use a hunting rifle."
rationale: This phrasing is a common mischaracterization of proposed state gun bills; while some bills restrict minors' possession or require storage/supervision, they generally include exceptions for parental instruction, hunting, or licensed training. Without a specific bill cited, there is no evidence that any recent state senate bill would categorically criminalize a father teaching his own son to use a hunting rifle.

claim: DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz "denied unemployment went up under Obama."
rationale: There is no well-documented record that DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz publicly denied that unemployment rose at the start of Barack Obama’s presidency. Official U.S. labor data show unemployment increased during the 2008–2009 recession early in Obama’s term and then fell during the recovery; Democratic officials typically framed the narrative as inheriting a recession and overseeing recovery rather than denying the initial rise.

claim: "Forty percent of people in this country, illegally, are overstaying visas."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated because it omits which country and what time period, and the share of unauthorized residents who are visa overstays varies widely by country and by year. While some U.S. estimates in certain years and by certain methods have put the share of overstays near 40%, other estimates and other countries show very different breakdowns, so the blanket claim as written is misleading.

claim: "Donald Trump is the first president in modern history (who) did not start a new war."
rationale: The claim is false: several 20th-century U.S. presidents did not begin new large-scale wars—e.g., Gerald Ford (1974–77) and Jimmy Carter (1977–81) did not initiate new wars—so Trump is not the first. Also many modern presidencies involved limited strikes or interventions that are debated as 'starting' wars, and Trump himself ordered major strikes (e.g., Syria, the strike that killed Qasem Soleimani) even if he did not start a declared full-scale war.

claim: "Wisconsin is #1 in the Midwest for personal income growth over the year."
rationale: The claim gives no year or data source and cannot be verified as stated; state personal income growth rankings change annually and are reported by agencies like the BEA. Without a specific timeframe and citation, the blanket statement that Wisconsin is #1 in the Midwest for personal income growth is unsupported and likely incorrect.

claim: In 2008, "only 54 percent of Latinos in Texas were registered to vote and only 35 percent actually turned out."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because official voting statistics use different denominators (citizen voting-age population vs total Latino population) and available sources do not support the precise 54% registered / 35% turnout numbers for Texas Latinos in 2008. Depending on whether noncitizens are included or whether turnout is measured as percent of all Latinos or of eligible/citizen Latinos, reported registration and turnout figures differ substantially from the quoted pair.

claim: "Thanks to Washington, nearly everyone will pay more in taxes in 2013. Somehow people think it's just the wealthy. It's not."
rationale: While the 2-percentage-point payroll tax holiday expired at the start of 2013 (raising Social Security payroll taxes for most wage earners), Congress largely prevented income tax rate increases for the vast majority by passing the American Taxpayer Relief Act, which kept lower income-tax rates in place for taxpayers below the high-income thresholds. So many people saw higher payroll taxes, but it is incorrect to say "nearly everyone" paid higher overall income taxes — the increases were concentrated in payroll taxes and the highest earners for income-tax rate changes.

claim: Says photos show the Trump-Ukraine whistleblower with Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, Nancy Pelosi and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Multiple reputable fact-checkers and news organizations found no credible evidence that those photos show the Trump–Ukraine whistleblower; the whistleblower’s identity was not publicly confirmed and the circulated images were misattributed or depicted other people. Therefore the claim that photos show the whistleblower with Schumer, Warren, Pelosi and Clinton is false.

claim: Says Texas high school "graduation rates are at an all-time high—the third-highest in the nation—which represents a significant turnaround from just a few short years ago."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while Texas graduation rates have risen in recent years, saying they are an 'all-time high' and 'third-highest in the nation' is not supported consistently by federal or state data. Other states (e.g., New Jersey, Iowa, Vermont, Massachusetts and several others) have often reported higher adjusted cohort rates, and Texas’s national rank has varied by year and data source. The claim also glosses over differences in timing and measurement that affect comparisons.

claim: A video shows "the COVID-19 vaccine when it hits your blood."
rationale: Ordinary videos cannot show a COVID-19 vaccine 'hitting your blood' because vaccine components (mRNA and lipid nanoparticles) are microscopic and not visible to the naked eye or consumer cameras. Footage presented as that is typically an animation, unrelated microscope imagery, or mislabelled content rather than a real-time recording of vaccine entering bloodstream.

claim: "Bob Menendez just voted to increase the government's debt ceiling to $1.9 TRILLION! In his 19 years in Congress, Menendez has helped overspend America over $15 TRILLION into debt."
rationale: The claim mixes an unverified, context-free claim about a single $1.9 trillion debt‑ceiling vote with a misleading attribution that Menendez alone ‘helped overspend’ $15 trillion. Debt‑limit adjustments are tied to specific bills and timeframes (and the cited $1.9T figure lacks context), and the growth in federal debt over many years is the result of votes by many members of Congress, multiple administrations, and economic conditions — it cannot be accurately ascribed to one senator.

claim: "Foster children are disproportionately victims of identity theft."
rationale: Multiple government audits, child-welfare research, and advocacy reports indicate that youth in foster care face higher rates of identity theft than other children. Factors such as frequent placement changes, many caregivers and caseworkers with access to personal data, and limited ongoing credit monitoring make foster children disproportionately vulnerable to identity fraud.

claim: "Bill Nelson actually voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times."
rationale: There is no authoritative roll-call record showing Bill Nelson explicitly voted to raise taxes 272 times; that number originates from partisan tallies that count a wide mix of amendments, procedural votes, and measures not actually enacting tax increases. Nonpartisan fact-checkers have reviewed similar claims and found them misleading because they use a broad definition of "voted for higher taxes."

claim: Obama served on a board with former Weather Underground member William Ayers and "that relationship with Mr. Ayers on this board continued after 9/11."
rationale: Barack Obama and William Ayers did serve together on the board of the Woods Fund of Chicago, with overlapping terms from 1999 through 2002. Because their overlap included late 2001, their board association did indeed continue after the September 11, 2001 attacks.

claim: "CDC confesses: Vaccines are failing, and the vaxxed can be superspreaders."
rationale: The CDC has not "confessed" that vaccines are failing; vaccines remain effective at preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death. While breakthrough infections can occur and vaccinated people can sometimes transmit SARS-CoV-2 (especially with more transmissible variants), evidence does not support the blanket claim that the vaccinated are a primary source of superspreading or that vaccines as a whole are failing.

claim: "Condemning violence against the police and urging support for the police" is "markedly absent" from President Barack Obama’s public remarks.
rationale: President Obama repeatedly condemned violence against police and urged support for law enforcement in public remarks — for example he issued statements after the 2016 Dallas attack and other incidents, and frequently praised and met with police leaders. Therefore the claim that such condemnations and calls for support were "markedly absent" from his public remarks is incorrect.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. While many public-option proposals are designed to be primarily financed by enrollee premiums, most legislative designs include public subsidies, tax-credit funding for low-income enrollees, start‑up or administrative support, and potential government backstops—so it is not solely funded by private insurance premiums and can involve public money.

claim: "Parents and teachers are already worrying about what they call the ‘Trump Effect.’ They report that bullying and harassment are on the rise in our schools, especially targeting students of color, Muslims and immigrants."
rationale: Multiple news outlets, teachers’ groups, parent organizations, and civil-rights groups reported after the 2016 campaign and election that parents and educators were expressing alarm about increased bullying and harassment in schools, particularly toward students of color, Muslim students, and immigrant students. Surveys and incident-tracking by organizations such as the SPLC, ACLU, and school districts documented rises in reported bias incidents and complaints consistent with these concerns.

claim: Says Austin trains are "full" at rush hour and "packed" for special events.
rationale: Urban commuter rail services, including Austin's CapMetro rail, typically see higher ridership during morning and evening peak periods, and local reporting and transit operator statements note crowded trains at rush hour and during large events. Major Austin events (e.g., music festivals, sports, university events) reliably produce surges that can leave trains 'packed.'

claim: "The Cleveland police has issued a stand down order to officers."
rationale: There is no specific, corroborated public report or official announcement that the Cleveland Police Department issued a blanket 'stand down' order to officers. Without a date, jurisdiction (e.g., Cleveland, OH versus other Cleve lands), or source, the claim cannot be verified and is not supported by known public records. Routine police communications occasionally mention 'stand down' in narrow contexts, but that is not the same as a citywide order.

claim: "If there were not derivatives, there would be no bank loans at all today."
rationale: Bank lending long predates modern derivatives: loans have been made for centuries while widespread use of modern derivatives (swaps, options, futures) rose in the late 20th century. Derivatives are risk-management and hedging tools that help banks manage interest-rate, currency, and credit risks, but they are not a prerequisite for creating or granting loans, which can be funded by deposits, equity, or central-bank liquidity.

claim: Says Bruce Poliquin "voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance."
rationale: While Bruce Poliquin did vote for the House Republican health bill in 2017 (the AHCA), which independent analyses said would reduce coverage for many people, I cannot find authoritative evidence that the measure he voted for would specifically 'strip 117,000 Mainers' of their insurance. State-level estimates of coverage losses varied by model and year, and the precise 117,000 figure is not clearly tied to Poliquin’s vote by a reliable source.

claim: "Piles of bricks are being staged in cities around the country, indicating riots are planned."
rationale: There is no credible evidence of a coordinated nationwide effort to ‘stage’ piles of bricks in cities as part of planned riots. Reports and viral images have typically been isolated, often showing ordinary construction materials, landscaping supplies, or photographs taken out of context rather than proof of an organized campaign.

claim: Says George Soros and Bill Gates are funding a bioweapons lab in Sierra Leone that caused the Ebola outbreak.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that George Soros or Bill Gates funded a bioweapons laboratory in Sierra Leone or that such a lab caused the Ebola outbreak. WHO and independent epidemiological investigations traced Ebola outbreaks to natural zoonotic spillover and human-to-human transmission, and reporting on Gates and Soros shows philanthropic public-health and development funding, not biological weapons programs. The claim appears to originate from conspiracy sources and is not supported by reliable reporting or scientific investigation.

claim: Says House Democrats’ impeachment inquiry of President Donald Trump "doesn’t feature the opposition party, it doesn’t feature cross-examination."
rationale: This characterization is inaccurate as a blanket statement. Republican members of the House committees were involved in the 2019 impeachment inquiry (they attended depositions, issued statements, and Republican members questioned witnesses in public hearings), although some closed-door staff-led depositions did not use adversarial courtroom-style cross-examination.

claim: "If you need to call 911 but are scared to because of someone in the room dial and ask for a pepperoni pizza."
rationale: There is no widely adopted or reliable protocol in which asking for a "pepperoni pizza" on a 911 call covertly summons help. Emergency dispatchers use direct information, silent-call procedures, or specific local protocols—relying on a pizza request is not a recognized method and could delay assistance.

claim: "This rule could prevent children under 18 from using such tools as a power screwdriver, a milking machine or something as simple as a wheelbarrow on the family farm . . . "
rationale: The statement is presented as a broad consequence but lacks context about which regulatory "rule" and jurisdiction it refers to. Under U.S. federal law and many state rules, family-farm exemptions and age-based allowances mean minors commonly perform routine tasks (including wheelbarrow use) and many regulations target specific hazardous machinery rather than banning all tool use by under‑18s. While some rules restrict certain powered or hazardous equipment for minors, it is unlikely a typical regulation would categorically bar all the listed simple tasks on family farms.

claim: "A Cornell University research study concludes that ethanol generates a 29 percent energy loss, meaning it takes more than a gallon of gasoline to produce a gallon of ethanol."
rationale: Cornell researcher David Pimentel (with coauthors) published analyses concluding that corn ethanol has a negative net energy balance on the order of ~29%, i.e., that more fossil-fuel energy is used in its production than is contained in the ethanol produced. That conclusion has been reported as meaning it takes more than a gallon (energy-equivalent) of petroleum fuel to produce a gallon of ethanol. However, the result is contested by many other studies using different methods.

claim: "We have developed a wind industry (in Washington state) from zero to $6 billion in 12 years."
rationale: The claim is vague and likely inaccurate: Washington State had wind projects and related economic activity before the unspecified 12-year window, so it did not start from “zero,” and I could not find corroborating evidence that the state's wind industry reached exactly $6 billion in the claimed period. Without a clear definition of what the $6 billion measures (annual revenue, cumulative investment, asset value, exports, or jobs+payroll) the statement cannot be verified and appears to overstate or mischaracterize commonly reported figures.

claim: "Wikileaks also shows how John Podesta rigged the polls by oversampling Democrats, a voter suppression technique."
rationale: Wikileaks published John Podesta’s campaign emails, but they do not provide evidence that he ‘rigged the polls’ by deliberately oversampling Democrats to manipulate results. Discussions in campaign emails about polling often concern weighting, subgroup oversamples for analytical purposes, or targeted turnout efforts, which is not the same as covertly tampering with public polls. Moreover, oversampling in a poll is a methodological choice affecting representativeness and reporting, and is not a conventional voter suppression technique (which aims to prevent or deter voting).

claim: "I have returned money every year since taking office."
rationale: The statement is a specific factual claim but provides no identifying speaker, timeframe, or supporting evidence. Without a named officeholder and corroborating records (payback receipts, financial disclosures, or independent reporting) the claim cannot be verified and therefore should be treated as false.

claim: "Faced with $1 million in campaign debt," Scott Walker "is unloading his campaign security costs onto the backs of Wisconsin taxpayers."
rationale: This statement mixes two separate facts to imply intentional wrongdoing. Scott Walker did carry campaign debt after his presidential bid and state law-enforcement routinely provides security for governors, but public reporting does not establish that he deliberately shifted campaign security expenses to Wisconsin taxpayers to cover campaign debt; many security costs are official and routinely state-funded. Without clear evidence that campaign-related security was billed to taxpayers as a way to retire campaign debt, the claim overstates and misattributes intent.

claim: "Almost 1 million children ... have no health insurance in this state."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not name which state or timeframe is meant; most U.S. states have far fewer than 1 million uninsured children, though a couple of very large states might approach that scale in certain years. Without a specific state, year, or source, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Here in Florida, despite 14 school shootings in eight years, we still have some of the weakest gun laws in the nation."
rationale: The claim bundles a specific numeric count and a broad policy judgement that are both unverifiable as stated. Whether Florida saw '14 school shootings in eight years' depends on how 'school shooting' and the eight-year window are defined, and authoritative tallies do not universally report that exact figure. Likewise, assessments of whether Florida has 'some of the weakest gun laws' vary by metric and time: the state adopted notable restrictions after Parkland (e.g., age limits and some safety measures) but also has permissive elements and subsequent legislative changes, so it is inaccurate to assert the blanket statement without a clear source and timeframe.

claim: "We don’t allow filming inside of the City Hall unless there is a specific reason."
rationale: The claim is framed as a blanket policy but rules on filming in City Halls vary by jurisdiction; many municipalities permit recording in public areas while others require permits or impose restrictions. Without specifying which City Hall or legal jurisdiction, the statement cannot be affirmed as generally true.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi diverted "$2.4 billion from Social Security to cover impeachment costs."
rationale: There is no evidence that Speaker Nancy Pelosi diverted $2.4 billion from Social Security to pay for impeachment. Impeachment expenses are covered through House appropriations and general Treasury funding; Social Security trust funds are legally separate and not used to finance congressional operations without explicit statutory action.

claim: Says under his leadership "Wisconsin median household income" is up 2.7%, while it is down 1.3% nationally under President Obama.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and lacks a clear timeframe. Census Bureau data show U.S. median household income did not fall by 1.3% across Obama’s presidency overall and, depending on the start/end years chosen, Wisconsin’s median income change also differs from +2.7%; the stated percentages do not match standard Census series and appear to cherry-pick periods.

claim: Says Conor Lamb "ran on a campaign that said very nice things about me."
rationale: The claim is presented without attribution or context and there is no verifiable public record that Conor Lamb ran a campaign explicitly saying 'very nice things about me' about an unspecified person. Without a source, timing, or clear target of the alleged praise the statement cannot be confirmed and appears unverified.

claim: Says Mitch McConnell's "biggest donor" is a "Russian oligarch that the GOP just lifted sanctions on."
rationale: Mitch McConnell’s largest reported personal donor and longtime supporter is Harlan Crow, an American real-estate heir, not a Russian oligarch. There is no evidence that the GOP recently lifted sanctions on a Russian oligarch who is McConnell’s biggest donor; the claim appears to conflate different donors and sanction actions.

claim: "Immigrants are responsible for 96 percent of our small biz growth since 2000."
rationale: There is no credible national evidence that immigrants drove 96% of U.S. small‑business growth since 2000; while immigrants are an outsized and important share of new entrepreneurs, published data show much smaller shares and the 96% figure appears to be a misinterpretation or a citation of a narrow subset. National statistics and academic analyses report substantial but far lower contributions by immigrants to business formation and employment growth.

claim: "Our jobless rate, our unemployment rate, is the lowest of all of the big cities in New Jersey."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which city "our" refers to, which months/years are being compared, or how "big cities" are defined. Unemployment rates change over time and vary by municipality, so without specific jurisdiction and timeframe the statement cannot be confirmed. Because of that missing context, the claim cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Says that Biden’s ban on new federal leases will kill 120,000 Texas jobs.
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes a specific, large job loss to the Biden administration’s pause on new federal leases. That pause applied to new federal land and offshore leasing for review and did not halt existing production; the 120,000-job figure traces to industry-funded, worst-case projections and is not supported by independent government or academic analyses, which found the immediate employment impact would be much smaller and dependent on markets and long-term policy changes.

claim: Says "the Kardashians donate whopping sum to Las Vegas mass shooting victims"
rationale: There are no credible, widely reported sources indicating that the Kardashian family made a publicly announced ‘whopping’ donation to victims of the 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting. Major celebrity contributions to that disaster were broadly reported and the Kardashians were not listed among donors; while an individual could have given privately, the claim as stated is unsupported.

claim: Two federal government buses "stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in the very small town of Green Cove Springs Florida… The passengers were illegal immigrants, straight from the southern border."
rationale: I found no reliable, independent reporting or official confirmation that two federal government buses carrying migrants from the southern border stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in Green Cove Springs, Florida. Viral social media posts making this claim have not been corroborated by local news, law enforcement, or federal agencies, and the identities/origins of passengers and bus operators are not established.

claim: Says Donald Trump has outlined "policies that read like a Kremlin wish list."
rationale: The claim is a value judgment rather than an objectively verifiable fact: whether Trump’s policies "read like a Kremlin wish list" depends on interpretation and which specific policies are meant. While some journalists and critics have made similar critiques pointing to his comments on NATO, sanctions, and Russia, the statement as presented lacks attribution or concrete evidence to be treated as a factual claim.

claim: "Half the kids coming out of college this year … can't find a job, or a job that's consistent with a college degree."
rationale: This statement overstates available evidence. Official labor data show unemployment for recent college graduates is typically in the single digits, and while underemployment (working in jobs that don’t require a degree) exists and can be substantial for some cohorts or majors, most measures put that share in the roughly 20–40% range rather than a flat 50% who either have no job or one inconsistent with their degree.

claim: On immigration, what reports say President Barack Obama "plans to do is roughly on the same scale" as what President George H.W. Bush did.
rationale: There is no clear, widely cited reporting that characterizes President Obama’s planned immigration actions as 'roughly on the same scale' as what President George H.W. Bush did. Obama’s 2014 executive actions (expanded DACA/DAPA) were described as historic and affecting millions, whereas George H.W. Bush did not implement a comparable large-scale executive relief; most media comparisons invoked other administrations or different policy acts.

claim: "Since 1904, the Ohio victor has won the presidency 25 out of 27 times "
rationale: Counting presidential elections from 1904 through 2008 (27 contests), Ohio voted for the national winner in 25 of them; the two exceptions were 1944 (Ohio backed Dewey while FDR won) and 1960 (Ohio backed Nixon while Kennedy won). This is a commonly cited bellwether statistic about Ohio's historical record.

claim: Says Charlie "Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money."
rationale: The claim as presented is ambiguous and no verifiable source is provided to confirm that any public figure named Charlie actually said the quoted line. Without clear identification of who “Charlie” or “Duke” refers to and lacking a traceable citation, the statement cannot be confirmed as factual. Absent corroborating reporting or a primary source, the claim should be treated as unverified and therefore false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Says Dennis Miller said that if he didn’t see women protesting the Ghislaine Maxwell trial verdict "you're all frauds. This isn't justice for those women, this is a joke."
rationale: There is no reliable, corroborated reporting or primary source evidence that Dennis Miller uttered this exact line about women protesting the Ghislaine Maxwell verdict. The quotation appears to be unverified and likely misattributed on social media rather than traceable to a confirmed Miller statement.

claim: "In the last five years only one out of 60 -- one out of 60 -- appropriations bills has been passed on time before the end of the fiscal year."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and likely false because it asserts only 1 of 60 regular appropriations bills were enacted on time across an unspecified five‑year span. While Congress often fails to pass all 12 annual regular bills before the fiscal deadline, congressional records show that multiple individual appropriations bills have been enacted on time in recent five‑year intervals, and many others were passed as regular bills or consolidated into omnibus measures near year‑end. The statement appears to be a mischaracterization or exaggeration absent a precise timeframe and definition of “on time.”

claim: "...Over 30 years, federal spending on education has grown by 375 percent, but test scores remain flat."
rationale: The statement is misleading and lacks necessary context. Whether federal education spending rose '375 percent' depends on the exact 30-year window and whether figures are inflation-adjusted, and federal K–12 spending is only a small portion of total education funding; real federal spending did not uniformly increase by that amount across common 30-year periods. National assessment data (NAEP) show mixed results — substantial math gains since the 1990s and variable reading trends — so it is inaccurate to assert that test scores have simply 'remained flat' without specifying subject, grade, and timeframe.

claim: "We have less Americans working now than in the ’70s."
rationale: The absolute number of employed Americans today is much higher than in the 1970s — current employment totals are well over 150 million compared with roughly 70–80 million in the early 1970s, reflecting population and labor force growth. The claim would only be plausible if it were referring to an employment rate or specific demographic groups rather than the total number employed.

claim: "The (ARC Tunnel) project was originally estimated to be $8.7 billion, and New Jersey alone was on the hook for all overruns."
rationale: While early Port Authority estimates for the ARC tunnel project were commonly cited around $8.7 billion, the claim that New Jersey alone was on the hook for all cost overruns is inaccurate. Funding agreements envisioned a mix of Port Authority contributions, federal grants, bond financing and state participation, and legal/liability arrangements did not make New Jersey solely responsible for every potential overrun.

claim: The Obama administration is using as its "legal justification for these airstrikes (on the Islamic State), an authorization for military force that the president himself has called for repeal of."
rationale: The Obama administration principally cited the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force (and related inherent/self‑defense authorities) in defending airstrikes against ISIS, while President Obama had publicly called for repeal of the 2002 Iraq AUMF—not the 2001 AUMF. Therefore the claim misstates which AUMF the president had sought to repeal.

claim: "You're more likely to be the victim of a violent crime in Milwaukee than in 96 percent of the country."
rationale: The claim states a precise percentile (higher than 96% of the country) but that specific ranking depends on the year, data source, and whether you compare cities, counties, or all places. While Milwaukee consistently reports a high violent-crime rate compared with many U.S. cities, available rankings vary and do not uniformly place it above 96% of all jurisdictions across datasets and years.

claim: Says James Clapper "and virtually everyone else" said "there is no collusion" in the Russia investigation findings.
rationale: The claim overstates consensus. While the Mueller investigation and the Department of Justice concluded they did not establish a criminal conspiracy between the Trump campaign and Russia, responses varied: some officials (including statements by James Clapper at times) said they had not seen evidence of collusion, but many analysts and officials emphasized the report documented numerous contacts and declined to endorse a blanket "no collusion" formulation. The term "collusion" itself is imprecise and was used differently by different people.

claim: Says the FDA said that Pfizer "falsely misled" the agency about the safety of the COVID-19 vaccines and that the shots are killing more people than they save.
rationale: The FDA has not issued a public finding that Pfizer "falsely misled" the agency about vaccine safety, nor has it stated that COVID-19 vaccines kill more people than they save. On the contrary, the FDA authorized and later fully approved the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine based on clinical trial and post‑authorization safety data, and large-scale studies and surveillance systems show the vaccines reduce COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths. Assertions that the FDA made those accusatory statements are mischaracterizations of documents and media reports.

claim: Says voter roll purge would mean "more than 200,000 registered Wisconsin voters will be prohibited from voting."
rationale: The statement conflates being flagged or removed from a voter roll with being categorically prohibited from voting. In recent Wisconsin actions, roughly 200,000+ registrants were reported as potentially affected or flagged for removal, but removal from the rolls alone does not automatically bar someone from voting — many can confirm or restore registration and Wisconsin permits mechanisms (including registering at the polls with ID/proof of residence) to vote. Exact numbers and outcomes vary by specific purge, so the absolute claim that 'more than 200,000 ... will be prohibited' is inaccurate.

claim: "North Korea is telling its people that their men’s national team is in the World Cup final."
rationale: There is no evidence that North Korea’s men's team is in any World Cup final; historically the North Korean men's team has never reached a World Cup final and World Cup finals are globally reported events. A claim that the state is telling citizens their team is in the final would be easily contradicted by international coverage and official tournament records.

claim: Says with the ongoing economic downturn, child abuse is on the rise.
rationale: Economic downturns and household financial stress are established risk factors for increased child maltreatment, but empirical measurements vary by place and indicator; overall administrative reports sometimes fall during downturns (due to reduced detection) even when some indicators (hospitalizations, hotline reports) rise. Because the claim is a broad, unqualified statement about an unspecified ongoing downturn and does not specify which measures or jurisdiction, it cannot reliably be stated as universally true.

claim: "Over 81 percent of the babies that are born at LBJ Hospital right here in Houston are born of women who are not here legally."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that over 81% of babies born at LBJ Hospital are to women who are 'not here legally.' Hospital and state birth records do not record immigration status, independent fact-checkers have found the claim unsupported, and any percentages inferred from billing or program data can be misleading. Available public data and reporting do not corroborate an 81% figure.

claim: Says Paul Manafort "played a very limited role" in the Trump presidential campaign.
rationale: Paul Manafort was campaign chairman of the Trump 2016 presidential campaign from June to August 2016 and continued to serve as a senior adviser with access to campaign operations and strategy; characterizing his role as "very limited" is misleading given those responsibilities and documented participation. Reports and court filings show he had substantive influence over campaign strategy, delegate operations, and had repeated interactions with senior campaign staff.

claim: "Kansas City Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes has left training camp and says he will ‘not play another down in the NFL’ until the team changes their name."
rationale: There are no credible reports or verified statements that Patrick Mahomes left training camp or declared he would refuse to play until the Kansas City team changed its name. Mahomes has continued to participate in team activities and has not publicly made that demand. This claim appears to be fabricated or a misattribution.

claim: "Governor Carcieri has not been campaigning with me."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it omits who 'me' refers to and the relevant time period. There are no specific public records or sources provided to confirm that Governor Don Carcieri did not campaign with the unnamed person, so the claim cannot be established as factual.

claim: Political activists are "being paid" to protest members of Congress.
rationale: The broad claim that political activists are being paid to protest members of Congress is unsupported as a general statement. Investigations and fact-checks have found only isolated incidents or instances where organizers reimburse travel or pay staff/contractors, not widespread, systematic payment of protesters across the board.

claim: The Freedom to Vote Act "automatically registers ineligible voters."
rationale: The Freedom to Vote Act would expand automatic voter registration at agencies like DMVs, but it requires individuals to attest to eligibility and includes verification and data-matching safeguards. It does not indiscriminately register everyone or intentionally register people who are ineligible; any registrations flagged as ineligible would be rejected or subject to follow-up.

claim: After pushing through a red flag law in the New Mexico Senate, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham "has had the firearms of her guards and household seized."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s guards’ or household firearms were seized simply because a red flag law passed. Red flag (ERPO) laws enable courts to order temporary removal of firearms after a petition and hearing, not automatic confiscation upon passage, and reporting and fact-checking outlets found no verified incidents of her security detail or household weapons being taken. Claims to the contrary appear to be unsubstantiated political assertions.

claim: "Thousands of Westerners and Americans" are fighting with extremists in eastern Syria and Iraq.
rationale: While thousands of foreign fighters from Western countries did join extremist groups in Syria and Iraq at the conflict’s peak, the number of U.S. citizens who fought there was much smaller—on the order of a few hundred rather than thousands. The claim as phrased implies thousands of Americans specifically, which is not supported by available estimates.

claim: "'Wrong precinct' rules exacerbate our provisional ballot problems (and) HB 194 does nothing to solve the wrong-precinct problem."
rationale: The statement is too general to verify because "wrong precinct" rules and any given "HB 194" vary by jurisdiction. In some places wrong-precinct rules can increase provisional ballot rejections, but whether a specific HB 194 fails to address that depends on the bill's actual text. Without identifying the state and examining the bill language and local election rules, the blanket claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Sen. Cory Booker wants to require a federal license for gun owners but criticizes voter ID laws as discriminatory.
rationale: Sen. Cory Booker has publicly supported stricter federal gun controls including proposals for mandatory licensing/registration for gun owners as part of his platform. He has also repeatedly criticized voter ID laws as discriminatory and a form of voter suppression, particularly affecting minorities and low-income voters.

claim: Ethylene oxide used in COVID-19 testing swabs "literally changes the structure of the building blocks of your own body."
rationale: Ethylene oxide (EtO) is indeed a reactive alkylating sterilant and at high exposures can modify DNA or proteins, but properly sterilized medical swabs contain only very low residual EtO that dissipates and does not 'literally change the structure of the building blocks of your own body.' Routine brief contact with an EtO‑sterilized swab is not biologically equivalent to the high exposures required to cause cellular alkylation or measurable damage.

claim: Says Mitt Romney did not pay taxes for 10 years.
rationale: Public reporting and the limited tax returns Mitt Romney released do not support the blanket claim that he paid no taxes for a continuous 10-year period. While Romney had years with low or no federal income tax liability due to business losses, deductions, and offsetting credits, available records show he paid federal taxes in some of the years in question and the broad claim is misleading without specifying tax type or timeframe.

claim: "When you pull up to the gas pump to fill up your car, get your cell phone and search for Bluetooth devices. If a sequence of letters and numbers show up don’t pay at the pump. One of the pumps has a credit card skimmer inside of it. All of these skimmers run on bluetooth."
rationale: While some gas-pump skimmers have used Bluetooth to transmit stolen card data, not all skimmers use Bluetooth and many legitimate devices at a station will also broadcast seemingly random identifiers. Relying on a generic Bluetooth scan as a definitive test will produce both false positives and false negatives and is therefore unreliable advice.

claim: "Two out of our last three governors in Virginia were investigated by the FBI. One went to jail and one is running for office again in this election."
rationale: This is incorrect. While former governor Bob McDonnell was federally investigated and prosecuted, his convictions were later overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court and he did not serve prison time; no other recent Virginia governor served jail time. Also the phrase about one running again is ambiguous and not accurate as stated — recent ex-governors have had varying candidacy activity but none of the last three both went to jail and is now running.

claim: "Moderna has been pulled in Iceland and pulled for everyone under age 30 in Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark due to heart issues."
rationale: This overstates and misstates national policies. Nordic health authorities did impose age‑based restrictions on Moderna (Spikevax) at various times because of a small myocarditis/pericarditis risk, but the exact limits varied by country, sometimes applied primarily to younger men or only to certain doses/boosters, and Iceland did not issue a blanket nationwide permanent withdrawal for all ages. The claim's blanket statement that Moderna was "pulled in Iceland" and "pulled for everyone under age 30" across Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark is therefore inaccurate.

claim: This is the first time since World War II that five nuclear-powered aircraft carriers were docked together.
rationale: Nuclear-powered aircraft carriers did not exist during World War II—the first nuclear carrier, USS Enterprise (CVN-65), entered service in 1961—so it is impossible for five nuclear carriers to have been docked together during WWII. Therefore describing a recent grouping as the 'first time since World War II' is incorrect. If five carriers recently were together, the WWII comparison is logically invalid.

claim: "More than 27,000 Rhode Island jobs depend on trade with Canada."
rationale: I could not corroborate an authoritative source stating that over 27,000 Rhode Island jobs depend on trade with Canada. Rhode Island is a small state and published state-level trade employment estimates from federal sources typically report trade-supported jobs in the low thousands rather than tens of thousands; the claim likely conflates direct, indirect, and induced jobs or uses a broader regional/timebound estimate. Without a clear source and definition, the figure appears to be an overstatement.

claim: "Of our 98,000 teachers who are K-12, over 53,000 of those teachers today are over 50 years old."
rationale: The statement gives precise counts but provides no source, time frame, or named jurisdiction, so it is not verifiable as presented. Teacher workforce age distributions vary by district and state and such a specific claim requires named data (e.g., NCES or state HR reports) to confirm.

claim: "As we near the 10th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, we should not forget that some of the hijackers used New Jersey driver’s licenses to board those aircraft."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that any of the 9/11 hijackers specifically used New Jersey driver’s licenses to board the aircraft. While several hijackers used state-issued IDs and passports to pass security, public records and the 9/11 Commission reporting do not single out New Jersey licenses as what they used to board the flights.

claim: "Moscow was engulfed in flames" after a giant explosion.
rationale: There is no credible or corroborated reporting that the entire city of Moscow was "engulfed in flames" after a single explosion. While Moscow has experienced isolated explosions or fires at times, mainstream news, eyewitness accounts, and satellite imagery have not shown the whole city ablaze, so the claim is hyperbolic and unsupported.

claim: "American coronavirus vaccine killed five Ukrainians."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or authoritative reporting that a U.S.-made COVID-19 vaccine killed five Ukrainians. Global health agencies and national authorities monitor vaccine safety closely, and such a specific, confirmed fatality cluster would have been documented and investigated publicly; instead this appears to be an unverified social-media claim.

claim: "I've been outspent by my opponents every time I've run for U.S. Senate."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as phrased because it does not identify the speaker or the specific Senate campaigns. Determining whether a candidate was outspent in every Senate run requires comparing official campaign finance and independent expenditure records for each election cycle; without those data this claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unproven.

claim: "Under the Obama plan . . . all the health care in this country is eventually going to be run by the government."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act increased government involvement in financing and regulation (Medicaid expansion, subsidies, and insurance marketplaces) but did not nationalize health care or replace private insurers. Employer-sponsored coverage, private insurance companies, and private health providers remained central to the U.S. system, so it is incorrect to say all health care would be run by the government.
